title: [EPIC] Native Asupersync cutover and async compat collapse
description:
# Goal
Finish the async migration as a real Asupersync adoption, not an executor swap. The target end state is native `&Cx`-aware, structured, cancel-correct async across FrankenTerm’s supported control-plane and mux-server surfaces.

This epic exists because current debt is architectural, not cosmetic. `runtime_compat` still leaks Tokio semantics, `smol` is still used directly in important mux and server code, and several core lanes still rely on dual-runtime patterns that prevent a trustworthy finish line.
design:
# Design
1. Follow the Asupersync migration guidance explicitly: `&Cx` first in owned async APIs, region-owned tasks instead of detached spawning, shrinking compat boundaries, deterministic tests during migration.
2. Migrate by domain seam: Smol-based legacy crates, core runtime loops, IPC and watch sockets, TCP TLS HTTP boundaries, then final compat collapse.
3. Treat any remaining compat layer as a temporary quarantine with a named owner bead and removal path.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Direct `tokio`, `smol`, and `async-io` usage is removed from supported shipping paths covered by this epic.
2. `runtime_compat` no longer acts as a long-term dual-runtime home for core business logic.
3. Async APIs owned by the project follow native Asupersync semantics rather than Tokio-shaped compatibility shims.
4. Deterministic and remote verification evidence exists for each migrated seam.
notes: If a stubborn third-party boundary must temporarily remain, isolate it behind a named quarantine adapter and keep it out of core control-plane logic. Still compiles is not the acceptance test here.
close_reason: All 6 children closed (.1-.6) - epic rollup complete

title: Replace direct Smol I O and task surfaces in wezterm-client and frankenterm-mux-server-impl with native Asupersync
description:
# Goal
Remove the direct Smol and async-io dependency from the legacy client and mux-server implementation surfaces that still carry important runtime behavior.

This task exists because `wezterm-client` and `frankenterm-mux-server-impl` still use `smol::Async`, Smol channels, and related reactor assumptions. Those crates are not done simply because the broader repo has some Asupersync already.
design:
# Design
1. Replace direct Smol I O registration and task orchestration with native Asupersync equivalents.
2. Avoid an executor-swap anti-pattern. The outward API should become Asupersync-shaped, not a Smol shim wearing a new runtime.
3. Preserve cancellation, shutdown, and transport semantics while moving to native `&Cx` and structured ownership where the project controls the API.
4. Add deterministic and remote verification for the migrated behavior.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Supported code paths in `wezterm-client` and `frankenterm-mux-server-impl` no longer depend directly on `smol` or `async-io`.
2. The migrated surfaces expose native Asupersync semantics instead of generic executor-neutral wrappers that keep Smol concepts alive.
3. Tests cover shutdown, cancellation, connection failure, and normal operation.
4. Completion evidence records the exact remote verification commands and artifacts.
5. This bead follows `ft-xbnl0.1.4`'s shared verification contract: comprehensive unit coverage for touched code paths, at least one deterministic integration or E2E script with detailed timestamped logging and artifact capture, and exact `rch exec -- ...` verification commands recorded in the completion evidence.
notes:
This is the direct continuation of `ft-riz42`, but with the finish-line expectation that the result be native, not half-ported.

Inventory cross-link (`ft-xbnl0.1.1`): this lane owns the remaining direct Smol / `async-io` shipping-path surfaces in `crates/frankenterm-mux-server-impl/src/dispatch.rs`, `frankenterm/client/src/client.rs`, `frankenterm/client/src/domain.rs`, `frankenterm/codec/src/lib.rs`, `frankenterm/ssh/src/lib.rs`, `frankenterm/uds/src/lib.rs`, and `frankenterm/async_ossl/src/lib.rs`, with adjacent executor debt still visible in `frankenterm/promise/src/spawn.rs`.

Native target shape: `&Cx`-threaded APIs, native Asupersync I/O registration and timers, scope-owned tasks, and no executor-neutral Smol compatibility shims surviving in client/mux-facing crates.

comments.author: OliveDesert
comments.text:
Code-grounded execution split after validating current sources and Asupersync primitives on 2026-04-03.

What the code says now
- `frankenterm/client` and `crates/frankenterm-mux-server-impl` are the direct Smol entrypoints.
- Support crates already partially know about native Asupersync:
  - `codec` defaults to `async-asupersync` and only stays on Smol when callers force `async-smol`.
  - `frankenterm-ssh` defaults to `async-asupersync` and already exposes a runtime shim (`runtime::block_on`, channel/io reexports).
  - `frankenterm-uds` and `async_ossl` default to `async-asupersync`, but today they only expose blocking `Read`/`Write` wrappers plus optional `async_io::IoSafe`.
- The hard blockers are therefore not abstract runtime folklore; they are concrete call sites and wrapper gaps:
  1. local Unix / mux-server dispatch path
  2. SSH proxy / pipe path
  3. TLS/OpenSSL path

Important design correction
- The first idea in this bead description about creating an Async<T>-like generic adapter should NOT be the default architecture.
- Asupersync's native pattern is per-type `Option<IoRegistration>` plus `rearm(...)` on `WouldBlock`, as seen in its own `net::unix::UnixStream` and `process` pipe wrappers.
- The finish-line-safe approach is: use concrete per-type native adapters where the project owns the type, and only fall back to a narrow local adapter when there is no better owned boundary.

Recommended implementation slicing
1. Local Unix + mux-server dispatch first.
   files: `frankenterm/uds/src/lib.rs`, `crates/frankenterm-mux-server-impl/src/dispatch.rs`, `frankenterm/client/src/client.rs`, relevant `Cargo.toml` files.
   plan: add native Asupersync `AsyncRead`/`AsyncWrite` + readiness registration to `frankenterm-uds::UnixStream`; stop forcing `codec`/`uds`/`async_ossl` into Smol mode from client and mux-server manifests; replace `smol::Async` + `smol::channel` + `smol::future::or` in dispatch and the local client path with native Asupersync-shaped loops.

2. SSH proxy / pipe path second.
   files: `frankenterm/client/src/client.rs`, possibly `frankenterm/ssh/*` only if needed.
   plan: remove direct `smol::block_on` in favor of the SSH runtime shim immediately; then decide whether `SshStream` should gain a small local Asupersync pipe-registration adapter or reuse an existing process-pipe pattern from Asupersync. This path is not the same problem as Unix sockets and should not be conflated with them.

3. TLS/OpenSSL path third, coordinated with finish-line networking work.
   files: `frankenterm/client/src/client.rs`, `frankenterm/async_ossl/src/lib.rs`.
   plan: either give `AsyncSslStream` a native Asupersync readiness wrapper using the same `IoRegistration`/`WouldBlock` pattern, or deliberately hand this slice to the broader native-network/TLS lane if the correct answer is to stop using this wrapper entirely. Do not hide TLS behind another executor-neutral shim.

Immediate low-risk cleanup opportunities once the first slice starts
- direct `smol::block_on(sess.exec(...))` in `client.rs` should route through `frankenterm-ssh`'s runtime shim rather than calling Smol directly.
- `smol::Timer::after(...)` in `client.rs` should move to a native timer path (`asupersync::time` or a repo-local native shim) rather than survive as a stray holdout.

This bead should now be read as: concrete per-transport native cutover, not "invent a new generic Async<T> compatibility layer".

title: Collapse frankenterm-core runtime observation, workflow, and maintenance loops onto Cx-first structured concurrency
description:
# Goal
Move the core runtime hot path onto native Asupersync semantics.

This task exists because observation loops, workflow runners, maintenance paths, channels, locks, and sleeps are where the project’s long-lived behavior actually lives. If those remain Tokio-shaped or dual-runtime, the finish line is fake.
design:
# Design
1. Thread `&Cx` through owned async APIs in the core runtime hot path.
2. Replace detached spawning with scope-owned work and explicit region structure.
3. Replace legacy channel, lock, select, and sleep patterns with native Asupersync primitives.
4. Add deterministic tests for lifecycle, cancellation, backpressure, and shutdown-sensitive loops as the code moves.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Core runtime observation and workflow hot paths follow native Asupersync semantics.
2. The runtime no longer depends on Tokio-shaped spawn, time, or channel assumptions in the covered surfaces.
3. Deterministic tests exercise lifecycle, backpressure, and cancellation behavior.
4. Remote verification demonstrates that the migrated hot path still operates under real build and test conditions.
5. This bead follows `ft-xbnl0.1.4`'s shared verification contract: comprehensive unit coverage for touched code paths, at least one deterministic integration or E2E script with detailed timestamped logging and artifact capture, and exact `rch exec -- ...` verification commands recorded in the completion evidence.
notes:
This is the heart of the migration. If this task is compromised by compat shortcuts, the rest of the finish-line story will remain weak.

Inventory cross-link (`ft-xbnl0.1.1`): this lane owns the core `runtime_compat` hot path inside `crates/frankenterm-core/src/runtime_compat.rs` plus the observation/workflow/runtime consumers in `runtime.rs`, `events.rs`, `search_bridge.rs`, `watchdog.rs`, `telemetry.rs`, `restore_process.rs`, `session_retention.rs`, `survival.rs`, `retry.rs`, `wait.rs`, `workflows/mod.rs`, `workflows/runner.rs`, `workflows/engine.rs`, `caut.rs`, and `tui/query.rs`.

Native target shape: thread `&Cx` through owned async APIs, replace detached spawn with `Scope`, and replace Tokio-shaped channels/locks/time/select assumptions with native Asupersync semantics.
close_reason: runtime observation/workflow/maintenance loops threaded through Cx-owned spawn primitives; search_bridge, ipc, native_events, runtime.rs runner migrated.

title: Migrate IPC, watch-daemon control sockets, and local control-plane streams to native Asupersync
description:
# Goal
Remove legacy async assumptions from the local transport layer that binds CLI, daemon, and watch-style control paths together.

This task exists because JSON-line IPC, local sockets, and related control streams are structural parts of the operator experience. They need native Asupersync ownership, not a migration seam that happens to pass tests today.
design:
# Design
1. Move accept loops, per-connection handlers, buffered reads and writes, and shutdown paths onto native Asupersync networking and structured concurrency.
2. Preserve protocol compatibility while changing the runtime semantics under the hood.
3. Make connection lifecycle and backpressure behavior deterministic and testable.
4. Fold any remaining compat use into explicit quarantine or remove it entirely.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Local control sockets and IPC code paths covered by this bead no longer depend on Tokio-like runtime helpers.
2. JSON-line protocol behavior remains stable while lifecycle semantics become native and structured.
3. Tests cover malformed input, concurrent clients, disconnects, and shutdown.
4. Remote verification is captured with exact commands and artifacts.
5. This bead follows `ft-xbnl0.1.4`'s shared verification contract: comprehensive unit coverage for touched code paths, at least one deterministic integration or E2E script with detailed timestamped logging and artifact capture, and exact `rch exec -- ...` verification commands recorded in the completion evidence.
notes:
This task is intentionally transport-focused. Higher-level command semantics belong to other beads.

Inventory cross-link (`ft-xbnl0.1.1`): this lane owns the local control-plane transport slice currently still reached through `runtime_compat`, specifically `crates/frankenterm-core/src/ipc.rs`, `native_events.rs`, `event_stream.rs`, and related local socket/control-stream helpers. Inherited blocker `wa-16hou` remains relevant context, but ProudSalmon already completed a bounded `ipc.rs` shutdown-semantics support slice on 2026-04-01, so this lane should build on that work rather than redoing it.

Native target shape: Asupersync-owned Unix socket accept loops, buffered line I/O, structured per-connection task ownership, deterministic shutdown, and stable JSON-line protocol behavior.
close_reason: IPC/native event migration verified

RusticMaple tick 165 — sixteenth post-storage tick: replay.rs Pause-branch cancellation hole (commit 7ee66b9e).

Fixed a latent cancellation hole in `handle_control` that survived the initial replay.rs cx-first migration.

Problem: legacy `handle_control` Pause branch spins on `control_rx.changed(&watch_cx)` where `watch_cx = crate::cx::for_request()` — a fresh orphan cx. Even when the caller of `play_with_cx` cancels their cx, the paused player blocks forever in the watch-channel wait until an external Play/Stop signal wakes it. The outer `cx.checkpoint()` runs only between frames, not during a Pause wait.

New sibling:
- handle_control_with_cx (same match structure; Pause branch now runs `cx.checkpoint()` each loop iter AND passes caller's cx into `control_rx.changed(cx)` — watch-channel wait becomes interruptible by cx cancellation, not just by control-channel closure)

Effect: a paused player under a cx-first caller now exits within one cancel-signal tick (one `changed()` wake-up) instead of requiring external control input. This plugs the last behavioral gap between `play` and `play_with_cx`.

RusticMaple tick 169 — twentieth post-storage tick: WriteCommandSender::send_with_cx root-level orphan plugged (commit 71718653).

Built a call-graph scanner following tick 168's pattern. Found THE LARGEST SINGLE orphan-cx hole in the codebase: `WriteCommandSender::send` uses `crate::cx::for_request()` for its inner mpsc reserve. Every single storage `_with_cx` write method (~60+) ultimately hits this orphan — a cancellation-chain break for the entire storage write surface.

Pre-flight `cx.checkpoint()` in each sibling catches cancel before the enqueue, BUT if the writer queue is backpressured (queue-full), the reserve wait blocks with the orphan cx — the parent cancel is ignored until backpressure drains. Rare but not impossible under high storage load.

New sibling:
- WriteCommandSender::send_with_cx (threads caller cx into `self.inner.send(cx, command)`; legacy `send` preserved for ambient-cx callers — critical since the ~50+ legacy `foo(...)` paired writes don't have cx in scope)

- add_event_label_with_cx

- add_event_mute_with_cx

Migration pattern captured: each cx-first sibling inlines the WriteCommand construction + `send_with_cx(cx, ...)` call directly. The delegate-to-legacy pattern wouldn't work because the legacy fn constructs and sends in one unit — no way to thread cx into the send without duplication.

RusticMaple tick 191 — EventWaiter::wait_with_cx per-recv cx routing (commit cc449372).

Pivot target after the workflows/ cx-first sweep: `event_stream.rs` EventWaiter::wait_with_cx was using ambient-cx `subscriber.recv()` inside its recv_loop. The outer `timeout_with_cx(cx, timeout, recv_loop)` bounds the overall wait by cx, so cancel still lands — but only via drop-cancel of the inner future when the outer wrapper observes cancel.

Under LabRuntime virtual time this had a determinism gap: if virtual time advanced past timeout but the inner recv was blocked on a broadcast channel, cancel would land asynchronously (via future drop) rather than at the recv boundary.

Both WaitCondition branches (AllOf tracker loop and default condition loop) migrated. The outer `timeout_with_cx` is preserved as the timeout bound — this is belt-and-suspenders cancellation at BOTH boundaries (per-recv and overall-wait).

No separate `_with_cx` sibling needed here — `wait_with_cx` IS the cx-first entry; the legacy `EventWaiter::wait` function still lives separately with its own ambient-cx recv_loop and is untouched.

RusticMaple tick 192 — IpcServer::run_with_context_with_cx accept-poll cx-threaded (commit 7e75ddd2).

Found a concrete orphan-cx hole in `ipc.rs`: `run_with_context_with_cx` was using `crate::runtime_compat::timeout(IPC_ACCEPT_POLL_INTERVAL, self.listener.accept())` for its accept-poll loop. The ambient `timeout` helper (runtime_compat.rs L2159) internally falls back to `Cx::current()` thread-local lookup — which means if the IPC server loop is spawned outside a thread-local cx scope (e.g. directly from CLI startup, or from a context that didn't install the caller's cx into the thread-local), the accept poll runs under a fresh request-scoped cx rather than the explicit cx the caller threaded in.

Tick 192 routes the accept poll through `crate::runtime_compat::timeout_with_cx(cx, IPC_ACCEPT_POLL_INTERVAL, self.listener.accept())` — matching the pattern already used by `native_events::run_with_cx` (native_events.rs L291). This guarantees the caller's explicit cx bounds the poll regardless of thread-local state.

- shutdown_signal_pending_with_cx uses cx for the shutdown select ✅

RusticMaple tick 193 — ipc shutdown_signal_pending_with_cx outer timeout cx-threaded (commit 2c08e46f).

Second orphan-cx hole in ipc.rs closed in two ticks. `shutdown_signal_pending_with_cx` at L1130 was a classic "mostly cx-threaded with an orphan-cx outer wrapper":

// Before:
match crate::runtime_compat::timeout(

That's asymmetric cx ownership — under LabRuntime virtual time the timer could advance independently of the caller's budget.

comments.text:
RusticMaple tick 195 — vendored/mux_pool execute_with_recovery_with_cx retry-backoff cx-threaded (commit d4d77103).

Note: second concurrent code landing in a row — agent committed the same 1-line fix I was preparing. Per AGENTS.md concurrent-edits rule, treating as own work. The diff is bit-identical to my prepared change.

Inside `execute_with_recovery_with_cx` (vendored/mux_pool.rs L391), the retry-backoff sleep used:

    cx::with_cx_async(cx, |_| sleep(delay)).await;

The closure takes `|_|` and DISCARDS cx. `with_cx_async` just passes cx to the closure parameter — it does NOT install cx into the thread-local scope. So the inner ambient `sleep(delay)` then fell back to `Cx::current()` thread-local lookup.

Net effect: retry-backoff timer was bound to a different cx than the enclosing execute_with_recovery_with_cx path. Under LabRuntime virtual time, the backoff delay could advance independently of the caller's budget/cancellation — an operator cancelling a slow-recovery mux op would have to wait the full delay before the retry loop noticed.

Tick 195 routes the backoff through `crate::runtime_compat::sleep_with_cx(cx, delay)` directly. Now the backoff timer and the parent execute path observe the same cx.

RusticMaple tick 198 — notifications handle_detection_with_cx mute-check cx-threaded (commit 81709e4d).

comments.text:
RusticMaple tick 200 — ipc handle_client_with_context_with_cx request-line read cx-threaded (commit 5ce0c3d5). Tick MILESTONE.

**200 ticks** into the ft-xbnl0.2.3 cx-first migration. Fittingly, this tick closes one more orphan-cx hole in the ipc server per-connection handler using an existing `_with_cx` sibling.

`handle_client_with_context_with_cx` takes the caller's cx by value and is spawned from `run_with_context_with_cx`'s accept loop with a child cx clone. The handler body threads cx into downstream calls (`handle_request_with_context_with_cx`), BUT the entry point — the JSON request-line read — used ambient `compat_unix::next_line(&mut lines)` despite `next_line_with_cx(&cx, &mut lines)` existing in runtime_compat.rs L1389.

The ambient variant doesn't observe cx cancellation at any entry checkpoint. A client that connects and stalls without sending a full line would block the per-connection handler indefinitely even when the outer IPC server's cx has been cancelled — leaked task staying alive until the client drops or the process exits.

Tick 200 fixes L1338 by switching to `next_line_with_cx(&cx, &mut lines)`. Matches the pattern already used by `native_events::handle_connection_with_cx` (native_events.rs L465).

RusticMaple tick 202 — simulation execute_until_with_cx routes inject via MockWezterm::inject_with_cx (commit 9f467982).

Inside `Scenario::execute_until_with_cx` (simulation.rs L722), each loop iteration did:

2. `Self::to_mock_event(event)?` — pure CPU ✅

`MockWezterm::inject` uses `self.panes.write().await` — a plain RwLock acquire that picks up cx via `Cx::current()` thread-local fallback. The cx-first sibling `MockWezterm::inject_with_cx(cx, ...)` (wezterm.rs L6815) routes through `write_with_cx(cx)` so the caller's explicit cx bounds the write-lock wait.

Tick 202 switches L745 to `mock.inject_with_cx(cx, pane, event)`. A long-held write lock (concurrent harness) plus outer cx-cancel now deterministically interrupts the write-lock wait rather than inheriting whatever thread-local cx happens to be installed.

- `execute_until` is the ambient-cx legacy path.
- `execute_until_with_resize_timeline_with_cx` is a pre-flight-only wrapper that intentionally delegates to the legacy timeline fn so nanosecond-scale telemetry is consistent across runs. Per-event cx checkpoints would perturb measurements. Per docstring: "Callers that need per-event cancellation should use the non-timeline variants (`execute_until_with_cx`)."

RusticMaple tick 205 — runtime_compat output_with_cx watcher sleep cx-threaded (commit fad3646b).

Used a python-based precise scan (re.finditer for async fn bodies with depth tracking) to hunt orphan-cx holes. Three `task::spawn` sites inside `_with_cx` bodies surfaced — metrics.rs clean (passes task_cx clone), web_framework.rs clean (child_cx), but runtime_compat.rs `Command::output_with_cx` had an orphan.

The fn spawns a watcher task that polls the caller's cx for cancellation (via `watcher_cx.is_cancel_requested()`) and flips an AtomicBool the blocking child-exec observes. But the watcher's inter-poll sleep used ambient `super::sleep(PROCESS_POLL_INTERVAL)`.

`super::sleep` falls back to `Cx::current()` thread-local lookup for its budget timer. In LabRuntime virtual-time tests, the watcher's cancel-check and the sleep-timer were therefore bound to DIFFERENT cx values — classic asymmetric ownership. The watcher would still notice cancel eventually (next wakeup), but the timer wasn't part of the caller's explicit cx budget.

Tick 205 routes the sleep through `super::sleep_with_cx(&watcher_cx, PROCESS_POLL_INTERVAL)`. Now both the cancel check and the timer observe the same cx clone.

comments.text:
RusticMaple tick 207 — protocol_recovery execute_with_cx per-attempt checkpoint (commit e407562a).

Precise-scan surfaced `ProtocolRecoveryEngine::execute_with_cx` as having a retry loop with 2+ awaits per iteration but no per-iteration cx.checkpoint. Closer inspection confirmed a real gap.

Before this tick:
- pre-flight `cx.is_cancel_requested()` check at entry ✅
- between-attempt `sleep_with_cx(cx, delay)` surfaces cancel as `RecoveryError::Cancelled` ✅
- **BUT**: no cancel observation at the top of the retry loop ❌

Consequences:
1. If cx is cancelled DURING `operation(attempt).await`, cancel wasn't observed until the following iteration's `sleep_with_cx` ran — adding one full operation's latency.
2. On the final attempt (`attempt + 1 == max_attempts`), the between-attempt sleep is SKIPPED — so final-attempt cancel was completely invisible, and the loop would exit with `RetriesExhausted` swallowing the cancel signal.

Tick 207 adds a top-of-loop `cx.is_cancel_requested()` check. Fires BEFORE calling `operation(attempt).await`, so:
- Cancel fired during previous operation's await lands at the next attempt boundary.
- Final-attempt cancel is now observed correctly (returns `Cancelled` instead of `RetriesExhausted`).

`attempts` field in the `Cancelled` outcome reports the completed-attempt count (not +1) — matches the semantics of legitimate early exits.

Legacy `execute()` (L548) non-cx retry loop is unchanged — no cx parameter there.

Verification: 88 / 88 protocol_recovery:: tests pass under `--features asupersync-runtime` via fork bypass (CC=llvm clang, CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/ft-rusticmaple-target).

comments.author: RusticMaple
comments.text:
RusticMaple tick 208 — retry.rs cx-first retry loops honor cancel (commit d1d06e6a).

**This tick closed a real bug, not just an orphan-cx hole.**

Both `with_retry_outcome_cx` (L230) and `with_smart_retry_cx` (L470) did:

    let _ = crate::runtime_compat::sleep_with_cx(cx, delay).await;

The `let _ = ...` DISCARDS sleep_with_cx's Err, which is the signal that cx was cancelled during the sleep. Net effect: **cancel during backoff was swallowed and the next retry operation fired anyway.**

Additionally, neither loop had a top-of-iteration cancel check, so even if the operation itself observed cx cancellation, the outer retry loop would keep retrying.

Tick 208 fixes both fns symmetrically:

1. **Per-attempt cancel check** at top of loop. Returns `Error::Cancelled(...)` when fired. Catches cancel fired during previous operation().await.

2. **Sleep result checked**. When `sleep_with_cx(cx, delay).await` returns Err (cx cancelled during backoff), returns `Error::Cancelled("backoff cancelled during sleep")` with a distinct message so callers can distinguish cancel-at-boundary vs cancel-mid-sleep.

For `with_retry_outcome_cx`, the cancelled result goes into `RetryOutcome { result: Err(..), attempts, elapsed }` so timing telemetry is preserved. For `with_smart_retry_cx`, the Err is returned directly.

Legacy `with_retry_outcome_inner` (L292) and `with_smart_retry_inner` (L526) are non-cx paths and unchanged.

`with_retry_and_circuit_cx` (L370) delegates to `with_retry_outcome_cx` and inherits the fix transitively.

Verification: 60 / 60 retry:: tests pass under `--features asupersync-runtime` via fork bypass (CC=llvm clang, CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/ft-rusticmaple-target). Key contract pins:
- `retry_runs_deterministically_under_labruntime_with_cx`
- `smart_retry_exhausts_attempts_on_retryable_errors`
- `circuit_records_success_on_retry_success` (transitive via with_retry_and_circuit_cx)

Tick 207 closed a "cancel invisible on final attempt" responsiveness gap. **Tick 208 closed an actual correctness bug**: retry loops under cancel would complete extra operations the caller had explicitly cancelled. A service under backpressure cascading cancels into retry loops would have run those operations anyway, wasting budget and potentially aggravating upstream load.

comments.author: RusticMaple
comments.text:
RusticMaple tick 209 — wait::wait_for_cx honors cancel during loop + backoff (commit a95c5a9f).

Follow-up audit after tick 208's retry.rs bug-fix: ran `grep "let _ = .*sleep_with_cx"` to find other cancel-swallowing sites. 12 hits total. Most were OK (top-of-loop cx.is_cancel_requested() check catches cancel on next iteration; cancel-swallowing during sleep just means one extra iteration). But `wait::wait_for_cx` had the same exact bug as retry.rs: no top-of-loop cancel check AND `let _ = sleep_with_cx(...)` swallowing cancel during backoff.

Net effect pre-tick-209: once a `wait_for_cx` loop started, cancel fired on the caller's cx was swallowed. The predicate kept being polled until natural timeout or retries-exhausted fired. For long-running quiescence waits with expensive predicates, this wasted budget and potentially delayed shutdown.

Tick 209 fixes wait_for_cx symmetrically:

1. **Top-of-loop cancel check** → returns `WaitError` with `last_observed = Some("cancelled")`. Callers can distinguish cancel from natural timeout via the marker AND via `elapsed < timeout`.

2. **sleep_with_cx result checked** → returns the same WaitError-with-"cancelled" marker on Err.

API-stable: no new error variants. The existing `WaitError` struct now carries a conventional "cancelled" marker in `last_observed`. Display format still reads as "timeout waiting for X (retries=N, last_observed=cancelled)" which is semantically accurate.

Because `wait_for_quiescence_cx` (L403) and `wait_for_quiescence_with_backoff_cx` (L430) both route through `wait_for_cx`, the fix propagates transitively across the public wait API.

Legacy `wait_for_inner` (non-cx path at L224) unchanged.

Verification: 116 / 116 wait:: tests pass under `--features asupersync-runtime` via fork bypass (CC=llvm clang, CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/ft-rusticmaple-target).

RusticMaple tick 212 — DesktopNotifier::send_with_cx override with pre-flight cx check (commit 425fddd2).

Audit of NotificationSender trait impls:

- Returns structured NotificationDelivery with error="cancelled before desktop notification dispatch" on cancel
- Otherwise delegates to `send()` (the sync Command::output can't observe cx mid-exec)

Pattern matches cass/caut clients' sync-subprocess boundary scoping. This isn't about making the subprocess cancellable — it's about skipping queued sends cleanly on outer-scope cancel.

RusticMaple tick 223 — WorkflowRunner::run_with_cx — top-level event-loop cx-first sibling (commit fc262753).

**Final closure on tick 187's "deep remaining work" list.** Tick 187 identified `run` at L1792 as requiring "cross-crate signature changes" and left it as future work because it's the top-level event-loop driver.

Threads cx through 5 layers of the event-loop driver:

1. **Startup**: `resume_incomplete_with_cx(cx)` (tick 222) replaces ambient `resume_incomplete`.

2. **Loop top-of-iteration**: `cx.checkpoint()` gates each iteration — cx-cancelled caller breaks the loop cleanly between events.

4. **Detection dispatch**: `handle_detection_with_cx(cx, ...)` (tick 190 inlined body) routes to `engine.start_with_id_cx`.

5. **Per-spawn child_cx clone**: each spawned workflow-execution task receives a `cx.clone()`, tying the detached future to the caller's cancellation tree. Inside the spawn, `run_workflow_with_cx(&child_cx, ...)` (tick 178 entry) → `run_workflow_inner(Some(&child_cx), ...)` → fully cx-threaded step execution.

Result: a cx-cancel on the caller's explicit cx bubbles through the runner loop AND all child workflow executions currently in flight. Loop exits cleanly; child tasks terminate at their next cx-observing await.

Legacy `run` preserved verbatim.

**Cross-crate caller migration** — the `frankenterm` CLI crate now drives `WorkflowRunner::run_with_cx` (tick 223) instead of the legacy `run` at the spawn site (main.rs L15115).

Change is minimal, 3 lines:

```rust
let cx = frankenterm_core::cx::Cx::current()
    .unwrap_or_else(frankenterm_core::cx::for_request);
workflow_runner.run_with_cx(&cx, &event_bus_clone).await;
```

Uses `Cx::current().unwrap_or_else(for_request)` — the same pattern already used elsewhere in main.rs (L11805) — so the runner picks up any ambient cx installed by the runtime driver, falling back to a fresh request-scoped cx.

**Concrete benefit**: a cx-cancel on the caller's explicit cx now bubbles through the runner loop AND all child workflow executions currently in flight. Previously `runner.run(...)` silently dropped cx context at the spawn boundary.

Each arm treats Cancelled as a timeout-like error surface since ambient `wait_for` (not `wait_for_with_cx`) should not return Cancelled in practice — the arms exist purely for exhaustiveness.

Before: `self.storage.upsert_action_plan(execution_id, &plan)` — always ambient.

After: dispatches on `cx: Option<&Cx>`:
```rust
#[cfg(feature = "asupersync-runtime")]
let persist_result = if let Some(cx) = cx {
    self.storage.upsert_action_plan_with_cx(cx, execution_id, &plan).await
} else {

title: Replace TCP, TLS, and HTTP client or service boundaries with native Asupersync networking
description:
# Goal
Finish the network-facing runtime migration so service and client boundaries stop dragging Tokio-era dependencies into the system.

This task exists because TCP listeners, TLS handshakes, HTTP client work, and related service boundaries still define a large part of the remaining async debt. They also create transitive dependency pressure that blocks a true no-Tokio finish line.
design:
# Design
1. Replace direct TCP and TLS surfaces with native Asupersync networking where the project owns the boundary.
2. Replace outbound HTTP client usage with native Asupersync HTTP semantics.
3. Keep compatibility boundaries explicit and temporary if any framework cannot be removed immediately.
4. Add tests and benchmarks for handshake behavior, concurrent connections, and request latency so the migration is not justified purely by ideology.
acceptance_criteria:

RusticMaple tick 319 — non-2xx response handling contract (commit acabeaf9).

**New test**: `distributed_http_client_returns_non_2xx_as_ok_response` — pins that 404/500 responses come back via `Ok(Response{status, body})`, not `Err`.

**Why this matters**: `Err` is for transport/connection failures; `Ok` with non-2xx status is a successful HTTP round-trip the caller must interpret. Confusing the two breaks retry logic — a caller that retries on `Err` would retry a 404 forever (will never succeed), while a caller that checks `.status` can correctly distinguish permanent from transient failures. This is a contract the caller can depend on.

**Test structure**:
- Server: one task, sequentially accepts 2 connections, sends `404 Not Found / gone` then `500 Internal Server Error / broken`.
- Client: 2 sequential GETs through `DistributedHttpClient`, asserts each comes back as `Ok(_)` with the matching status code and body bytes.

comments.text:
RusticMaple tick 322 — metrics server mid-flight cx-cancel contract (commit 7c68b9bb).

**New test**: `metrics_server_start_with_cx_mid_flight_cancel_stops_accept_loop` — pins that cancelling the cx *after* the metrics TCP accept loop is running causes the loop to exit without requiring the shutdown flag.

**Pivot from HTTP client** to the **server-side TCP accept** path. The metrics server at `metrics.rs:540-587` binds a `TcpListener` and clones `cx` into the spawned accept-loop task (`task_cx` at L545) for cancel propagation. Two shutdown signals exist side-by-side — `shutdown_flag` (atomic) and `task_cx.is_cancel_requested()`. Prior tests covered pre-cancel (refuses-to-bind, tick from 2.3 era) and wait_with_precancelled_cx. The **mid-flight cancel** path (cx cancelled after start) was not pinned.

**Why this matters**: An operator cancelling on program termination (signal handler) can reliably cancel the ambient request cx but may not flip the shutdown flag. If a regression removed the cx check from the accept loop, the server would only stop via the flag — the operator-cancel case would hang forever.

**Test structure**:
1. Start server via `start_with_cx(&cx)` — binds listener, spawns loop task.
2. Cancel cx without touching shutdown flag.
3. Wait for handle completion; assert < 2s (generous over 250ms accept-poll interval).
4. Sanity: assert shutdown flag is still `false` → proves cancel took effect via the cx path, not the flag.

**Verification**:
```
test metrics::tests::metrics_server_start_with_cx_mid_flight_cancel_stops_accept_loop ... ok
test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed
```

**New test**: `distributed_http_client_sends_host_header_matching_authority` — pins that the `Host:` header value matches the URL's authority component.

- Assert response round-trips, AND the server saw the correct Host header.

RusticMaple tick 326 — empty-body POST Content-Length: 0 contract (commit 96a0bd6d).

**New test**: `distributed_http_client_post_empty_body_sends_content_length_zero` — pins that POST with `Vec::new()` body sends `Content-Length: 0` and zero body bytes.

**Why**: Empty-body POST is common (health pings, webhooks, idempotent-create APIs). 1. Request contains `Content-Length: 0` (case-insensitive).
2. After `\r\n\r\n` separator, zero body bytes (buffer is zero-init; any non-zero trailing bytes mean client wrote data it shouldn't have).
3. Happy-path 200 OK roundtrip.

RusticMaple tick 327 — large-body POST roundtrip contract (commit fb0627e7).

**New test**: `distributed_http_client_post_large_body_roundtrips` — pins 128 KiB POST body round-trips intact.

**Why**: Small-body (tick 316, 11 bytes) and empty-body (tick 326, 0 bytes) both fit in a single kernel write() syscall. A regression that only surfaced for payloads crossing the kernel send-buffer boundary — dropping bytes past the first EWOULDBLOCK, failing to await between partial writes, truncating the final chunk — would not fire on either. Production bodies routinely hit 128 KiB: captured pane scrollback, detection events with rich context, rollup event-batch forwarding.

**Test structure**:
- Body: 128 KiB total, with sentinels (`RMS:` head + `:END` tail) for targeted corruption detection independent of bulk byte-equality.
- Server: accumulates read chunks (read may return partial data at this size), then asserts length matches, head/tail sentinels preserved, and full body byte-for-byte equal.
- Client: POST via `DistributedHttpClient::plaintext()` with `Cx::for_testing()`.

comments.text:
RusticMaple tick 328 — documented timeout_with_cx cancel semantics (commit 73e59bc1).

**Pivot tick**: started by trying to add a mid-flight cx-cancel test for `EventWaiter::wait_with_cx`, then a pre-cancel test for `timeout_with_cx` itself. Both exposed that **`timeout_with_cx` does not observe cx-cancel directly** — only the cx budget deadline. A pre-cancelled cx with infinite budget runs for the full requested duration (30s test confirmed this empirically).

**Root cause**: `timeout_with_cx` calls `asupersync::time::budget_timeout`, which calculates `effective_timeout = min(requested, remaining_budget)` then defers to `crate::time::timeout`. No direct `is_cancel_requested()` check.

**Why the system works anyway**: every cx-first function in frankenterm-core that uses `timeout_with_cx` already adds explicit `cx.checkpoint()?` at function entry (MetricsServer::start_with_cx, start_web_server_with_cx, EventWaiter::wait_with_cx, etc.) — so the user-facing behavior is correct. The pattern is: callers short-circuit pre-cancel, then call timeout_with_cx for budget-bounded timing.

**The risk**: a future cx-first migration that added a new `_with_cx` surface WITHOUT the pre-flight checkpoint would silently hang on pre-cancel. There's no compile-time enforcement of the pattern.

**Fix chosen — documentation**: added a "Cancellation semantics" section to `timeout_with_cx`'s doc comment making the contract explicit. Prevents future regressions by making the cancel-vs-budget distinction obvious to anyone wiring up a new cx-first surface.

**Why not a test**: a pre-cancel short-circuit test would require either:
1. Changing `timeout_with_cx` to check cancel directly (scope creep — belongs in the primitive, not this bead)
2. Documenting+pinning the current slow-cancel behavior (anti-pattern — would block the fix if anyone wanted it later)

Documentation is the right fix for a latent design gap that doesn't yet manifest as a user-visible bug.

RusticMaple tick 331 — extended cancel-semantics doc to sleep_with_cx (commit ce432cc5).

**Docs extension**: `sleep_with_cx` shares the tick-328 contract shape of `timeout_with_cx` — both wrap asupersync's `budget_*` primitives which observe cx budget deadline but NOT direct cancel.

**Why extend to sleep_with_cx**: both primitives use identical semantics (budget-aware, cancel-unaware), but only `timeout_with_cx` had the warning. A future migration that wired a new polling loop around a naive `sleep_with_cx` call would silently hang for the full sleep window per iteration on cancel. Parallel docs prevent this.

**Contract now explicitly documented on both primitives**:
- Budget deadline caps effective duration (honored).
- Cancel is NOT directly observed (not honored by primitive alone).
- Callers MUST pre-flight with `cx.checkpoint()?`.
- Inside polling loops, callers MUST re-check cancel at iteration boundaries.
- All existing cx-first callers in this crate already follow this pattern (watchdog.rs, backpressure polling, metrics accept loop, etc.).

No behavior change — docs-only.

RusticMaple tick 334 — build_tls_server_name contract tests (commit 32310f5e).

**New tests** (4): pin `build_tls_server_name`'s behavior across the key input shapes:
- IPv4 literal → `ServerName::IpAddress` (NOT `DnsName`)
- DNS hostname → `ServerName::DnsName`
- Empty bind addr → defaults to `"localhost"`
- Invalid host (spaces) → `DistributedTlsError::Config(_)`

**Why the IPv4/DNS variant split is load-bearing**: rustls `ServerName::IpAddress` verifies against IP SANs in the certificate; `ServerName::DnsName` verifies against DNS SANs. If a regression mis-routed between them (e.g. accepted `127.0.0.1` as a DnsName), cert verification would either fail unexpectedly or — worse — succeed against the wrong SAN. This is the SNI / server-name-verification surface; regressions here open cert-verification holes.

**Discovery during development**: `":8443"` does NOT trigger the empty-host default branch. `distributed_bind_host` returns the input unchanged when the host-before-colon is empty, and then `ServerName::try_from(":8443")` fails. The default-to-localhost branch only fires for truly empty or whitespace-only bind. Test adjusted + comment added to preserve the finding for future readers.

**Verification**:
```

**New tests** (2):

RusticMaple tick 339 — resolve_tls_versions positive-path contracts (commit bfb016b2).

**New tests** (3): pin that `build_tls_bundle` accepts each supported `min_tls_version` config string:
- `"1.2"` builds cleanly
- `"1.3"` builds cleanly
- `"1.2+"` (suffix form, explicitly permitted per `distributed.rs` L122-L123) builds cleanly

**Why**: min-TLS-version is a security-relevant knob. Setting it to `"1.3"` must mean the server refuses TLS 1.2 clients; `"1.2"` accepts both. A regression that silently collapsed both into a single version list would either weaken security (if `"1.3"` downgraded to include 1.2) OR break compatibility (if `"1.2"` upgraded to exclude 1.2). RusticMaple tick 342 — HTTPS URL against plaintext server → Err (commit c5e98bec).

**New test**: `distributed_http_client_https_url_against_plaintext_server_returns_err` — pins that the client returns `Err` on scheme mismatch (https:// URL, plaintext server).

**Why** — URL scheme is a security-critical signal:
- A client that silently stripped `https://` and connected plaintext would defeat TLS entirely.
- A client that silently accepted a plaintext response on an https request would expose session data.
- In either case the caller asked for encrypted transport, got unencrypted, and has no way to know anything went wrong.

**Contract pinned — three observable properties**:
1. Result is `Err(_)` — caller sees the failure.
2. Failure happens fast (<10s bound) — does not hang on TLS handshake.
3. No panic on TLS handshake failure with wrong server.

**Test design**: plaintext server accepts connection and immediately closes. The client's TLS handshake attempt gets invalid handshake bytes or EOF before completion, surfacing as Err.

**First scheme-dispatch contract test** for `DistributedHttpClient`. Prior HTTP client tests all used `http://` (plaintext loopback); this one exercises the `https://` branch of the URL-parsing + transport dispatch.

**Verification**:

comments.text:
RusticMaple tick 344 — IPv6 literal URL (bracketed authority) roundtrip (commit 34798ab2).

**New test**: `distributed_http_client_handles_ipv6_literal_url` — pins correct handling of bracketed IPv6 URLs like `http://[::1]:<port>/path`.

**Why** — RFCs 3986 §3.2.2 + 7230 §5.4: IPv6 authorities use square brackets to disambiguate the colons in the address from the host:port colon. Brackets must be preserved in both the TCP connect path AND the Host header.

**Two regression modes caught**:
1. Client strips brackets before TCP connect → `[::1]:port` and `::1:port` parse differently; stripping causes connect failures or mis-addressed connections.
2. Client fails to bracket the Host header → `Host: [::1]:port` is RFC-compliant and many reverse proxies route on the bracketed form.

**Test structure**:
- Bind a loopback IPv6 listener via `TcpListener::bind("[::1]:0")`.
- GET `http://[::1]:<port>/ipv6` via `DistributedHttpClient::plaintext()`.
- Assert happy-path response (200 + "ok") AND server-received Host header contains `host: [::1]:<port>` (case-insensitive).

**Graceful skip**: on CI hosts without IPv6 loopback, the test prints a skip note and returns — the contract is only meaningful when v6 is actually available. Most macOS/Linux dev + CI environments have v6 loopback enabled.

**Verification** (this host has v6 loopback):
```

test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed
```

comments.text:
RusticMaple tick 345 — premature server close → Err (commit dbdab3a1).

**New test**: `distributed_http_client_surfaces_premature_server_close_as_err` — pins that the client returns `Err` when the server closes connection after sending headers promising 100 bytes but only 5 bytes of body.

**Why**: Realistic network interruption — flaky link, server OOM-killed mid-response, upstream restarted. The client has three possible behaviors under this scenario:

| Behavior | Outcome |
|----------|---------|
| **Return `Err(_)`** ← **contract** | Caller knows response is incomplete, can retry / log / surface to operator |
| Return `Ok(Response{body: partial})` | Silently leaks truncated data — downstream code would deserialize corrupt JSON, accept partial scrollback, etc. |
| Hang waiting for remaining bytes | Stalls containing agent workflow indefinitely |

A regression from behavior 1 → behavior 2 would silently corrupt distributed event forwarding WITHOUT any observable error at the call site. This test is specifically designed to pin the Err branch so that regression fires loudly.

**Test structure**:
- Server: send `HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 100\r\n\r\nshort` (5 body bytes, not 100), then close.
- Client: GET; must return Err within 5s.

**Verification**:
```

test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed
```

comments.author: RusticMaple
comments.text:
RusticMaple tick 349 — 3xx redirect current-behavior snapshot + security finding (commit 4013f6e9).

**Key finding this tick**: `DistributedHttpClient` **follows 3xx redirects transparently** by default (inherited from asupersync HTTP client's default RedirectPolicy). A peer-injected 302 with `Location: http://attacker.com/` would route the request there before the caller sees anything.

**Test added**: `distributed_http_client_3xx_redirect_current_behavior_snapshot` — a snapshot test pinning the observed status quo. Server responds 302 with `Location: http://does-not-resolve.invalid./`; client follows the redirect, hits DNS failure, returns `Err(ConnectError-shaped error)`. Test asserts `result.is_err()`.

**SECURITY CONCERN documented in the test doc comment**: transparent redirect following is a real risk for a distributed RPC client where URLs are supposed to point at trusted peer nodes. A compromised peer could exfiltrate the next request's body via a 302 redirect. **Fix**: configure `RedirectPolicy::none()` at the `DistributedHttpClient` construction site.

**Why this is a snapshot not a contract**: fixing the underlying behavior is a policy-level change that belongs in a separate bead — ft-xbnl0.2.4 is about migrating OFF tokio, not about changing default client policy. The snapshot:
1. Pins the current behavior so any caller relying on "Err on bad redirect" stays working.
2. Provides a signal-flip trigger — a future commit switching to `RedirectPolicy::none()` causes this test to fail with a clear signal to update the assertion and file a security-follow-up bead.

Recommend filing a new bead: "DistributedHttpClient must not transparently follow 3xx redirects" as a security hardening task (distinct from this bead's scope).

**Verification**:
```

test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed
```

**Test design**:
- Primary listener responds `302` with `Location: http://127.0.0.1:<secondary_port>/redirected`.
- Secondary listener (a separate loopback port) would accept any connection that came from a redirect follow, flip an atomic flag, and respond `200 "followed!"`.
- Assertions:
  1. `resp.status == 302` (the primary's response, not 200 from secondary).
  2. `resp.body != b"followed!"` (the 302 has an empty body, not the secondary's text).
  3. After a 100ms settling window, `secondary_was_hit` atomic is still `false` — proves the follow did not race-land on the secondary after the primary response was read.

This closes step 4 of ft-kfkyi's verification checklist (recorded in the closed bead's description).

RusticMaple tick 364 — Send+Sync type-level assertion (commit 8be1f2e7).

**New test**: `distributed_http_client_is_send_and_sync` — compile-time assertion that `DistributedHttpClient` implements `Send + Sync + 'static`.

**Why**: Distributed RPC use case wants `Arc<DistributedHttpClient>` shared across concurrent request tasks. That requires Send + Sync + 'static. If a future refactor adds a non-Send/Sync field to the inner asupersync HttpClient, this test fires at **build time** — before any callsite would encounter the restriction.

**Pattern** (standard zero-runtime-cost type-level):
```rust
fn assert_send<T: Send>() {}
fn assert_sync<T: Sync>() {}
fn assert_send_sync_static<T: Send + Sync + 'static>() {}
assert_send::<DistributedHttpClient>();
// ...
```

The `#[test]` body is three function calls with no runtime exercise. The test passes iff the trait bounds hold at compile time.

**Complements** `distributed_http_client_concurrent_gets` (tick 318):
- Tick 318 exercises concurrent **creation** of per-task clients.
- Tick 364 proves concurrent **sharing** via `Arc` is type-safe.

Together they cover both the one-client-per-task and shared-client concurrency patterns.

**Verification**:
```

test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed

RusticMaple tick 371 — response body byte-verbatim contract (commit 0956db00).

**New test**: `distributed_http_client_response_body_bytes_pass_through_verbatim` — pins the client returns body bytes exactly as received, without CRLF normalization, null-byte stripping, or UTF-8 transcoding.

**Why**: Distributed RPC bodies are opaque. Real payloads include binary serialized data (bincode, msgpack, protobuf), JSON with embedded `\r\n` in string fields, captured scrollback with mixed line endings. Any client-side normalization would silently corrupt these.

**Test body covers edge-case byte values**:
- CR (`\r`), LF (`\n`), CRLF (`\r\n`) sequences
- Null byte (0x00)
- High-bit byte (0xFF)
- Tab (`\t`)
- ASCII interleaved between them

Server writes the bytes verbatim under Content-Length. Client reads, must return the identical byte sequence (asserted byte-equal).

RusticMaple tick 380 — mid-flight cx-cancel snapshot + finding (commit 4d925607).

**New snapshot test**: `distributed_http_client_mid_flight_cancel_does_not_hang`. Fires cx-cancel 50ms into an in-flight GET against a stalled server.

**Finding** (recorded in the test's doc comment): the DistributedHttpClient's response-read path does NOT observe mid-flight cx-cancel. Measured elapsed = **10.02s** — the test's defensive 10s outer timeout fired, NOT the cx-cancel. Same class of gap as tick 328 documented for `timeout_with_cx` (budget observed, cancel not).

**Severity**: lower than ft-kfkyi (redirect exfil). Not a security issue — a hung distributed RPC call will eventually time out via its own internal limits (if configured) but won't observe operator cancel. An operational-ergonomics gap rather than a correctness/security gap. Recorded as snapshot test + doc comment rather than a separate bead.

**Pre-cancel vs mid-flight cancel pair**:
- Tick 313 `..._honors_pre_cancelled_cx`: cancel BEFORE get → fast Err (cancel observed at entry).
- Tick 380 `..._mid_flight_cancel_does_not_hang`: cancel DURING get → outer timeout fires (cancel not observed mid-read).

**Implementation note**: initial test had a bug — `let _ = listener.accept().await` dropped the accept return immediately, closing the stream, client saw UnexpectedEof in 9ms. Fixed to `let _stream_hold = listener.accept().await` so the stream is actually held. With the proper stall, the real 10s-outer-timeout behavior surfaces.

**Verification**:
```

RusticMaple tick 396 — tightened tick-313/314 pre-cancel assertions (commit 03e33a70).

**Test refinement tick** — tightened ticks 313 + 314 (GET + POST pre-cancelled cx) to the specific `Err(ClientError::Cancelled)` contract now enabled by tick-387's ft-l9mxa fix.

**Before** (loose):
```rust
assert!(result.is_err(), "...some error, just not a hang...");
assert!(elapsed < 5s, "...fail fast...");

**After** (tight):
```rust
match &result {
    Err(ClientError::Cancelled) => {}

| Path | Test | Latency | Variant |

| Pre-cancel (pre-flight check) | Ticks 313+314 | <1s | `Err(Cancelled)` |
| Mid-flight cancel (watcher race) | Ticks 380+389 | ~70ms | `Ok(Err(Cancelled))` (through outer timeout) |

RusticMaple tick 402 — chunked transfer-encoding response contract (commit 5d6febd5).

**New test**: `distributed_http_client_parses_chunked_transfer_encoding` — pins `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` responses decode correctly.

**Why**: Real HTTP/1.1 servers use chunked encoding for responses without known-ahead length (SSE, streaming APIs, compressed pipelines). A client assuming Content-Length always exists would fail or hang.

**Test**: Server sends chunked response with body "HelloWorld" split into 3 chunks (5+3+2 bytes) + 0-size terminator:
```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
\r\n
5\r\nHello\r\n
3\r\nWor\r\n
2\r\nld\r\n
0\r\n\r\n
```
Client must reassemble as `b"HelloWorld"`.

**Pairs with tick 319** (non-2xx with Content-Length-bounded body): together they cover **both response-body-framing strategies** allowed by HTTP/1.1.

comments.text:
RusticMaple tick 432 — mpsc::recv mid-flight cancel gap discovered + caller pattern pinned (commit 9a868dd2).

**Finding** (new): asupersync `mpsc::Receiver::recv(cx)` observes
**pre-cancel** via its per-poll `cx.checkpoint()` short-circuit
(tick 422 pins that) but does NOT register a cx-cancel-waker.
A recv already suspended on the send-side waker will NOT wake when
`cx.cancel_with(...)` fires afterwards.

Same class of gap as:
- ft-l9mxa: HTTP client mid-flight cancel (resolved tick 387 via
  race_with_cx_cancel helper wrapping DistributedHttpClient)
- sleep_with_cx / timeout_with_cx: documented (ticks 328/331) to
  observe BUDGET but not DIRECT cancel

**Discovery path**: attempted a naive mid-flight cancel test during
tick 432. The 2 s outer wrapper's timeout fired before the recv
observed the 100 ms mid-flight cancel — definitive evidence that
the waker path is not wired.

**New test**: `mpsc_recv_with_cx_mid_flight_cancel_via_select_race_pattern`
pins the caller-side WORKING pattern — wrap the recv in a
`futures::future::select` against a poll-sleep cx-cancel watcher.
The watcher branch catches the cancel within its 50 ms poll interval,
surfacing within ~150 ms of the cancel firing.

The match-arm structure tolerates a future improvement in asupersync
where mpsc.recv itself gains cx-cancel-waker support — the test
accepts `Either::Left(Err(RecvError::Cancelled))` as an alternative
valid outcome, so the test stays green if observability improves.

**Takeaway for callers needing mid-flight mpsc cancel**: follow the
tick-387 `DistributedHttpClient::race_with_cx_cancel` pattern —
wrap the inner recv in a `select!` against a poll-sleep watcher.

comments.text:
RusticMaple tick 514 — transient check-script flake observed, re-run 109/109 green.

**First regression-like signal in ~35 observation ticks** since tick 479:
- 1st check-script run: `ONE OR MORE RUNS FAILED (87 tests passed before failure)`
- 2nd check-script run (immediately after): all 6 runs PASS (109 tests)

The "87" count on the failing run (34 HTTP + 45 TLS + 3 guards + 3 metrics = 85, plus partial) suggests a run in Run 5 or 6 flaked under load. Most likely culprit:
- Run 5 web mid-flight cancel test (tick 417): 200 ms wait-to-bind + 100 ms poll-cycle tolerance. Under load the server bind + shutdown orchestration could slip past the 5s assertion envelope. Less likely since I've observed 0.3s consistently.
- Run 6 mid-flight select-race tests (ticks 432-439): 100 ms cancel trigger + 50 ms watcher poll + 500 ms assertion envelope. Under heavy concurrent-agent load, the spawned cancel task's sleep could drift past the 500 ms boundary.

The fact that the immediate re-run passes cleanly confirms this is a **timing flake**, not a correctness regression. Mid-flight tests are inherently timing-sensitive; the 500 ms envelope may be too tight under peak multi-agent contention on this machine.

Not filing a follow-up bead — the flake rate is very low (1 in ~35 check-script runs) and the underlying contract (cancel observed eventually via select-race) is still correct.

Cumulative this session: **328 ticks (187-514)**.

comments.author: RusticMaple
comments.text:
RusticMaple tick 515 — mid-flight select-race envelopes 500ms → 1000ms (commit 53997864).

Proactive flake-reduction response to tick 514's transient check-script
flake. All 6 mid-flight select-race tests had their elapsed-envelope
assertion loosened from 500ms to 1000ms.

**Rationale**: cancel task sleeps 100ms, watcher polls every 50ms —
typical observation is ~150ms. Under concurrent-agent load on this
machine, the cancel task's spawn + sleep can drift past the tight
500ms envelope. 1000ms gives ~850ms headroom which should absorb
peak contention while staying well under the 2000ms outer safety-net
(unchanged).

**Not a correctness change**: same caller-side select-race contract
is pinned. Typical observation still ~150ms; the looser envelope only
allows more drift before the test fails the assertion.

**Untouched**: Command::output pre-spawn test (line 6372) — that
test doesn't involve a cancel-trigger sleep; the checkpoint fires
<20ms locally. Its 500ms envelope is already very loose for that
semantic.

**109/109 local still pass** after the change.

title: Collapse runtime_compat quarantine and remove dual-runtime feature seams from core APIs
description:
# Goal
Shrink the compatibility seam down to what is genuinely unavoidable and remove dual-runtime logic from core project-owned APIs.

This task exists because a repo can claim Asupersync while still keeping Tokio-shaped abstractions alive in `runtime_compat`, feature flags, and helper APIs. That is migration debt, not a finished architecture.
design:
# Design
1. Identify which compat exports are still used by project-owned core logic after the preceding migration tasks.
2. Replace those uses with native Asupersync primitives or move them behind explicit quarantine adapters.
3. Remove dead feature branches and comments that describe a dual-runtime future that is no longer intended.
4. Leave only deliberately isolated boundaries, each with a named owner and removal path if it still exists.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Core project-owned APIs no longer rely on `runtime_compat` as a long-term abstraction layer.
2. Dual-runtime feature seams are removed from covered surfaces.
3. Remaining compat code, if any, is explicit quarantine with a named reason and owner.
4. The codebase narrative now matches the intended native-Asupersync architecture.
5. This bead follows `ft-xbnl0.1.4`'s shared verification contract: comprehensive unit coverage for touched code paths, at least one deterministic integration or E2E script with detailed timestamped logging and artifact capture, and exact `rch exec -- ...` verification commands recorded in the completion evidence.
notes:
This task is the architectural cleanup step that makes the migration real instead of forever in progress.

Inventory cross-link (`ft-xbnl0.1.1`): this lane owns final collapse of the `runtime_compat` quarantine after lanes `2.1` through `2.4` land, plus removal of direct runtime dependency declarations and dual-runtime feature seams that still exist in root/core/client/mux manifests.

Native target shape: core project-owned APIs no longer present Tokio-shaped abstractions; any surviving foreign boundary is explicit quarantine with a named reason and removal path.
close_reason: Fixed across dab704d3 + 1b3def54 + 9e1bd63b + fdd1e817 + f58ed8f1 — asupersync non-optional, all cfg gates stripped, cx blocks collapsed, tokio::select replaced. Zero dual-runtime feature seams remain in core APIs.

title: Enforce zero tokio, smol, and async-io gates in supported builds, tests, benches, and docs
description:
# Goal
Turn the no-Tokio and no-Smol intent into a durable invariant.

This task exists because migration work is not closed until the repo actively prevents regression. Without hard gates, future contributions will quietly reintroduce runtime debt and undo the finish-line push.
design:
# Design
1. Add machine checks that fail when direct `tokio`, `smol`, or `async-io` usage returns in supported surfaces.
2. Extend doctor or audit surfaces so contributors can diagnose violations locally.
3. Sweep docs and comments so the narrative matches the final architecture.
4. Make the gate broad enough to defend shipping paths, tests, benches, and key docs without blocking legitimate quarantine that is explicitly owned.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Supported builds, tests, benches, and core docs are guarded against direct `tokio`, `smol`, and `async-io` reintroduction.
2. Violations fail in a way that is actionable for contributors.
3. Allowed quarantine cases, if any, are documented and intentionally exempted.
4. This bead provides the durable no-regression gate for the async migration lane.
5. This bead follows `ft-xbnl0.1.4`'s shared verification contract: comprehensive unit coverage for touched code paths, at least one deterministic integration or E2E script with detailed timestamped logging and artifact capture, and exact `rch exec -- ...` verification commands recorded in the completion evidence.
notes:
This is the enforcement step that turns the migration into a maintained property rather than a one-time cleanup.

Inventory cross-link (`ft-xbnl0.1.1`): this lane owns the permanent no-regression gate for the async migration, including manifest checks, source/doc sweeps, and explicit exemption handling for any named quarantine left after `ft-xbnl0.2.5`. The inherited final-cleanup bead is `wa-2h1ha`.

Guard scope should treat `runtime_compat.rs` as the only intentional temporary Tokio quarantine root during migration and fail fast if new direct `tokio`, `smol`, or `async-io` usage appears elsewhere in supported builds, tests, benches, or core docs without an explicitly documented owner.

Stale-allowlist check forces ratchet-down: as upstream beads migrate files, allowlist must shrink. Commit a72fb92c. Level A satisfied (unit+integration+fmt+clippy clean). Level B rch substrate refused offload (fail-open guard); local cargo test --no-default-features ran as fallback. Level C artifact bundle present. Closed under upstream blockers ft-xbnl0.2.5 and wa-2h1ha by design - this bead delivers the gate; those beads drive the allowlist toward zero.

title: [EPIC] Supported-path capability completion and placeholder closure
description:
# Goal
Finish or honestly narrow every supported-path capability that still behaves like a placeholder, partial implementation, or misleading promise.

This epic exists because a swarm operator cannot trust a terminal or control-plane whose advertised pane lifecycle, alt-screen truth, scrollback visibility, detach semantics, renderer support, or mux-server operations still hide `todo!()` branches or fake state.
design:
# Design
1. Reuse the placeholder-remediation program where it already owns the surface.
2. Add explicit new tasks for gaps that are real but not yet represented cleanly, especially mux-server sessionhandler operations and any final supported-path sweep.
3. Prefer small honest capability surfaces over broad imaginary ones: either ship the behavior for real or narrow the contract in code, tests, and docs.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Every supported-path capability covered by this epic is either implemented for real or explicitly narrowed with operator-visible semantics.
2. Safety-relevant state such as alt-screen, detach support, pane lifecycle, and scrollback availability is no longer based on placeholders.
3. Renderer and platform support claims match actual tested behavior.
4. Shared mux-server implementation no longer contains supported-path `unimplemented!()` branches for pane and window operations.
notes: This epic is about truth. If a feature is intentionally unsupported, say so explicitly and prove callers can distinguish that from not implemented yet.
close_reason: done

title: Finish machine-control and client-domain truth needed for safe robot actions
description:
# Goal
Make robot and client-domain actions rely on real state instead of placeholders or stale assumptions.

This task exists because pane creation, alt-screen truth, and safety-sensitive input behavior are core to swarm orchestration. If those surfaces are not authoritative, the control plane is not trustworthy no matter how much else is implemented.
design:
# Design
1. Build on the existing client-domain placeholder-remediation work for remote spawn and alt-screen truth.
2. Ensure policy and machine-control paths consume the same authoritative state pipeline rather than side heuristics.
3. Make errors explicit when a capability is unsupported by design instead of letting raw placeholder behavior leak through.
4. Verify that robot-facing semantics stay coherent after the implementation changes.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Client-domain pane lifecycle and alt-screen truth are authoritative in the covered machine-control paths.
2. Policy-sensitive send and wait semantics consume real state rather than hardcoded fallbacks.
3. The covered surfaces no longer expose placeholder-quality capability behavior.
4. Verification evidence covers normal behavior, failure behavior, and safety-sensitive transitions.
5. This bead follows `ft-xbnl0.1.4`'s shared verification contract: comprehensive unit coverage for touched code paths, at least one deterministic integration or E2E script with detailed timestamped logging and artifact capture, and exact `rch exec -- ...` verification commands recorded in the completion evidence.
notes:
This task is the control-plane trust anchor for human and robot actions. It depends on truth, not just UI polish.

Inventory cross-link (`ft-xbnl0.1.2`): this lane owns finish-line machine-control/client truth and builds primarily on `ft-akx00.2.3` (remote `spawn_pane` + authoritative alt-screen) and `ft-akx00.5.4` (stale `PaneCapabilities` stub language). Earlier placeholder beads `ft-akx00.2.1`, `ft-akx00.2.2`, and `ft-akx00.2.4` are already closed and are no longer finish-line blockers.

Scope boundary: non-Rust generated SDK templates in `robot_sdk_contracts.rs` still contain transport placeholders, but they are broader SDK/template debt outside the current `ft-xbnl0` support matrix unless the project explicitly adopts those clients as supported surfaces.

title: Finish live scrollback, pane state, and FTUI surfaces so operator interfaces read real data
description:
# Goal
Make operator-facing state and FTUI surfaces read live, real data rather than null adapters or placeholder views.

This task exists because scrollback visibility and FTUI state are not secondary luxuries in a swarm terminal. They are part of how operators debug agents, recover sessions, and trust what the system is telling them.
design:
# Design
1. Build on the real scrollback wiring and FTUI placeholder-remediation work already underway.
2. Ensure live pane data, historical data, and operator views all share authoritative sources instead of separate placeholder shims.
3. Keep the resulting surface bounded and explicit for large-scrollback future work.
4. Verify both data correctness and operator-visible behavior.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Covered scrollback and FTUI surfaces no longer rely on null adapters or placeholder view bodies.
2. Operator-visible state reflects live and historical data from authoritative sources.
3. The resulting surface is documented well enough that future large-scrollback work can build on it without guesswork.
4. Verification covers data fidelity, empty states, error states, and user-facing behavior.
5. This bead follows `ft-xbnl0.1.4`'s shared verification contract: comprehensive unit coverage for touched code paths, at least one deterministic integration or E2E script with detailed timestamped logging and artifact capture, and exact `rch exec -- ...` verification commands recorded in the completion evidence.
notes:
This task is about making the operator interface honest and useful, not just making a placeholder widget disappear.

Inventory cross-link (`ft-xbnl0.1.2`): this lane owns live scrollback and FTUI truth and is blocked by `ft-akx00.5.1` (real scrollback wiring) and `ft-akx00.5.3` (live FTUI view bodies). `ft-akx00.5.2` is already closed and removed the fake recording delta variants.

Important declassification: `NullPaneScrollbackAccess` in `fleet_scrollback_coordinator.rs` is now `#[cfg(test)]` only, so the live finish-line problem is not a production null adapter surviving in runtime code; it is finishing the real data path and wiring FTUI/operator views onto it.

title: Implement remaining mux-server sessionhandler pane and window operations still marked unimplemented
description:
# Goal
Finish the shared mux-server implementation where sessionhandler operations still bail out as unimplemented.

This task exists because `crates/frankenterm-mux-server-impl/src/sessionhandler.rs` still contains pane or window operations that are part of the supported operational story yet remain unfinished. Those are finish-line blockers even though they were not cleanly captured by the placeholder-remediation program.
design:
# Design
1. Inventory the still-unimplemented sessionhandler operations and classify which ones must be implemented for the supported control-plane contract.
2. Implement real semantics where the operation should exist.
3. Narrow the contract explicitly where the operation truly should not exist, with operator-visible errors instead of generic unimplemented failures.
4. Add tests that exercise the real server-side behavior rather than only local helper logic.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Supported pane and window operations in sessionhandler are no longer left as raw unimplemented branches.
2. The server-side behavior is explicit and test-covered.
3. Callers can distinguish unsupported-by-design from implementation failure.
4. This bead records the exact server methods closed and the evidence attached to each one.
5. This bead follows `ft-xbnl0.1.4`'s shared verification contract: comprehensive unit coverage for touched code paths, at least one deterministic integration or E2E script with detailed timestamped logging and artifact capture, and exact `rch exec -- ...` verification commands recorded in the completion evidence.
notes:
This bead closes a real gap in the mux-server story that would otherwise survive even after the placeholder audit finishes.

Inventory cross-link (`ft-xbnl0.1.2`): this lane is the explicit owner for supported `sessionhandler.rs` pane/window operations that still need real semantics or an explicit unsupported-by-design contract. This gap was not captured cleanly in `ft-akx00` and is therefore finish-line-specific.

Declassification: the nearby `FakePane` `unimplemented!()` methods in `crates/frankenterm-mux-server-impl/src/sessionhandler.rs` live under `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` and should not be treated as shipping-path debt.

title: Finish tmux, detach, SSH, and remote file semantics required for serious swarm operation
description:
# Goal
Complete the remaining operational semantics around tmux-backed panes, detach behavior, SSH config support, and remote file mutation that are required for a serious control plane.

This task exists because these are the kinds of missing semantics that quietly make real workflows brittle. A finished swarm terminal cannot keep saying detach, process lifecycle, and remote metadata are planned ideas rather than supported behavior.
design:
# Design
1. Build directly on the placeholder-remediation tasks for tmux PTY lifecycle, detach, SFTP metadata mutation, and SSH Match Exec behavior.
2. Make domain differences explicit instead of pretending every backend behaves like a local PTY.
3. Ensure safety and policy boundaries are part of the implementation, especially for SSH Match Exec.
4. Verify real operational scenarios rather than only unit-level plumbing.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The covered tmux, detach, SSH, and remote-file semantics are implemented or explicitly narrowed with honest contracts.
2. Domain-specific behavior is documented well enough for operators and future contributors.
3. Tests cover both success cases and principled unsupported or denied cases.
4. Completion evidence shows that the lane is fit for real swarm workflows, not just local unit tests.
5. This bead follows `ft-xbnl0.1.4`'s shared verification contract: comprehensive unit coverage for touched code paths, at least one deterministic integration or E2E script with detailed timestamped logging and artifact capture, and exact `rch exec -- ...` verification commands recorded in the completion evidence.
notes:
This task collects the non-optional operational semantics that make remote and multiplexed workflows credible.

Inventory cross-link (`ft-xbnl0.1.2`): this lane owns the remaining supported tmux/detach/SSH/remote-file placeholder debt and is blocked by `ft-akx00.7.2` (detach semantics), `ft-akx00.7.3` (SFTP metadata mutation), and `ft-akx00.7.4` (SSH `Match Exec`). `ft-akx00.7.1` is already closed and should be treated as satisfied foundational work rather than a remaining placeholder.

title: Finish supported rendering and window-backend capability gaps or narrow support honestly
description:
# Goal
Make renderer and platform-backend support claims match reality.

This task exists because the finish line is not only about control-plane APIs. If supported backends still have placeholder resize, framebuffer, image, glyph, or input paths, the project is still overselling what it supports.
design:
# Design
1. Build on the placeholder-remediation tasks covering backend resize, image rendering, GUI background and glyph behavior, and remaining platform backend gaps.
2. Prefer explicit narrowing over broad but weak support claims.
3. Verify the final behavior with visual or backend-specific evidence where appropriate.
4. Ensure docs and comments match the resulting support matrix.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Supported rendering and backend claims covered by this bead are implemented or narrowed honestly.
2. Placeholder-quality visual or backend paths no longer masquerade as finished features.
3. Verification includes backend-appropriate evidence, not just unit-level assertions.
4. The resulting support matrix is documented and stable enough for release-readiness work.
5. This bead follows `ft-xbnl0.1.4`'s shared verification contract: comprehensive unit coverage for touched code paths, at least one deterministic integration or E2E script with detailed timestamped logging and artifact capture, and exact `rch exec -- ...` verification commands recorded in the completion evidence.
notes:
This task is about honest support, not perfection. A smaller truthful support matrix beats a large misleading one.

Inventory cross-link (`ft-xbnl0.1.2`): this lane owns the remaining finish-line rendering/window-backend placeholder debt and is blocked by `ft-akx00.6.1` (Wayland seat/keyboard), `ft-akx00.6.2` (resize/framebuffer lifecycle), `ft-akx00.6.3` (bitmap/WebGPU readback), and `ft-akx00.6.5` (background sizing/custom glyph placeholder shortcuts). `ft-akx00.6.4` is already closed and no longer a finish-line blocker.
