title: Implement `wa robot state` (live panes + DB enrichment + inferred agent/state)
description:
# Task: `wa robot state`

## Goal
Return a **single canonical JSON view** of all panes so agents can decide what to do next.

## Output fields (v0)
Per-pane (minimum):
- `pane_id`
- `domain`
- `title`
- `cwd` (raw + normalized path)
- `pane_state`:
  - prompt_active
  - command_running
  - alt_screen
  - recent_gap
- `last_activity` timestamp
- `unhandled_event_count`
- `observed` / `ignored` + ignore reason
- **reservation state** (if present):
  - owner_kind / owner_id
  - reason
  - expires_at
- **optional live metadata** (when available from status_update IPC):
  - cursor (row/col)
  - dimensions (cols/rows)
  - is_active

## Data sources
- WezTerm list panes (live)
- DB enrichment for:
  - unhandled events
  - reservation state
  - last detection timestamps
- Optional IPC status updates for cursor/dimensions/active state

## Error behavior
- Stable error codes for:
  - WezTerm unreachable
  - workspace/DB unavailable

## Testing
- Unit tests:
  - deterministic ordering of panes
  - error shape stability
- Integration tests:
  - DB enrichment fields are present and correct
  - reservation fields present when a reservation exists
  - cursor/dimensions appear when status_update events have been received

## Acceptance Criteria
- Robot state is stable, deterministic, and sufficient for agents to select a pane safely.
notes:
Background / Why:
- Robot state is the canonical snapshot for automation; it prevents unsafe guesswork.
- A stable snapshot reduces repeated DB queries and log scraping.

Considerations:
- Keep ordering deterministic and include ignore reasons for privacy.
- Any live-vs-DB mismatches should be surfaced explicitly.

Logging / Observability:
- Log state refresh timings and pane counts (observed/ignored).
- Emit structured warnings when live data and DB differ.

title: Implement `wa robot get-text` (tail/escapes options, robust errors)
description:
# Task: wa robot get-text

## Goal
Fetch pane text for agent decision-making.

This is the primary read primitive for:
- agent reasoning loops
- wait-for verification
- workflow waits (indirectly)

## Requirements
- Supports tail N lines (token-efficient; default should be small).
- Supports --escapes for ANSI parsing use cases (e.g., best-effort alt-screen detection).
- Returns structured error if pane not found.
- Honors global flags:
  - --workspace / WA_WORKSPACE
  - --config (optional)

## Output contract
- Always returns the stable robot envelope.
- Data includes:
  - pane_id
  - requested tail_lines
  - whether escapes were included
  - text payload

## Safety / performance
- Avoid reading excessive scrollback by default.
- Never log pane content.
- Enforce output-size limits (truncate deterministically and report truncation metadata).

## Testing
- Unit/integration tests:
  - output validates against the robot schema (`wa-4vx.7.10`)
  - tail line truncation is deterministic and includes truncation metadata
  - `--escapes` behavior is stable on fixtures
  - error mapping is stable for:
    - pane not found
    - wezterm not running
    - wezterm get-text failures

## Acceptance Criteria
- Works on live panes.
- Errors are stable and actionable (pane not found, wezterm not running, get-text failure).
notes:
Background / Why:
- get-text is the primary read primitive for agents; stability prevents brittle parsing.
- Safe bounds avoid accidental large payloads.

Considerations:
- Enforce size limits with deterministic truncation metadata.
- Preserve a stable escaping policy.

Logging / Observability:
- Log request parameters (pane_id, tail_lines, escapes) but never raw pane text.
- Emit structured errors for missing panes/wezterm failures.
close_reason: Implemented with tail/escapes options, stable error codes, truncation metadata, RobotGetTextData struct. Tests pass.

title: Implement `wa robot send` (PolicyEngine-gated, optional wait-for, timeout)
description:
# Task: wa robot send

## Goal
Send input to a pane safely and optionally wait for a pattern.

This is the highest-risk robot command and must be conservative by default.

## Safety requirements
- Must pass PolicyEngine authorization before sending.
- Must never send into AltScreen or RecentGap panes.
- Must apply rate limiting.
- Must emit an audit record for allow/deny/require-approval outcomes.

## Features
- `--no-newline`
- `--wait-for <pattern>` + `--timeout-secs N` (optional verification)
- `--dry-run` (no injection; return policy decision + redacted preview of what would be sent)

## Workspace/config
- Honors global flags:
  - `--workspace` / `WA_WORKSPACE`
  - `--config` (optional)

## Implementation notes
- Reuse the shared PaneWaiter (`wa-4vx.2.6`) for all wait-for verification logic.
  - Avoid duplicated polling loops.
  - Use shared backoff/timeout/cancellation semantics.
- Output must be stable and validated against robot schemas (`wa-4vx.7.10`).
- When wait-for is requested, include verification outcome details in the audit trail emission layer.

## Testing
- Unit/integration tests validate:
  - allow/deny/require-approval are stable outcomes
  - `--dry-run` never injects input
  - wait-for succeeds/fails deterministically with timeout

## Acceptance Criteria
- Denies sends when policy requires (deny/require-approval are both explicit outcomes).
- `--dry-run` never injects input and returns a stable, redacted preview + policy decision.
- Wait-for succeeds/fails deterministically with timeout.
- Output error codes are stable and actionable.
notes:
Background / Why:
- Send is highest risk; explicit constraints prevent unsafe automation.
- A uniform send API keeps workflows and robots consistent.

Considerations:
- Always go through PolicyEngine and audit; no bypass.
- Wait-for must reuse shared waiter to avoid divergent behavior.

Logging / Observability:
- Audit allow/deny/require-approval with rule_ids and redacted previews.
- Log wait-for timeouts with correlation ids.
close_reason: Implementation complete. Robot send command with PolicyEngine gating, dry-run, wait-for verification, approval integration, and audit trail all working.

title: Quick-start mode (no args) + `wa robot quick-start` output tuned for agents
description:
# Task: Robot quick-start output

## Goal
When invoked with no args (or via explicit command), output a dense, agent-friendly quick start.

This is a critical UX surface for agents:
- it teaches the stable contract (envelope + schemas)
- it reduces “guessing” about workspace/config
- it points to the safest default actions first

## Invocation
Support at least one (either is fine; both is ideal):
- `wa robot` (no subcommand) → quick-start
- `wa robot quick-start` → quick-start

## Output requirements
- Must be **stable JSON** (robot envelope) and validated against schemas (`wa-4vx.7.10`).
- Must be minimal tokens but still actionable.
- Must include:
  - a short description of wa robot mode
  - the canonical global flags:
    - `--workspace` / `WA_WORKSPACE`
    - `--config`
  - the “core loop” for an agent:
    1) `wa robot state`
    2) pick `pane_id`
    3) `wa robot get-text` / `wa robot search`
    4) `wa robot send --dry-run` (safety-first)
    5) `wa robot send` (only when policy allows)
  - references to safety expectations:
    - sends are policy-gated
    - `--dry-run` exists
    - how RequireApproval is surfaced (and how a human can approve)

## Design notes
- Treat this as a *structured help payload*, not a prose wall.
- Prefer a JSON structure like:
  - `commands: [{name, args, summary, examples[]}]`
  - `tips: [...]`
  - `error_handling: { common_codes: [...] }`

## Testing
- Unit tests:
  - output validates against the quick-start schema
  - output includes the required command list and flags
  - output remains “small enough” (token/byte budget) so it’s usable in agent loops
- E2E:
  - runner can invoke the command and capture artifacts (stdout JSON + stderr logs)

## Acceptance Criteria
- `wa robot` (no subcommand) and/or `wa robot quick-start` returns a stable JSON payload that teaches an agent how to use wa safely.
- The output is schema-validated and regression-tested (snapshot or schema validation + key field asserts).

title: Robot mode tests: envelope stability, error codes, command outputs (synthetic)
description:
# Task: Robot mode tests

## Goal
Prevent breaking changes in robot schemas and error codes.

Robot mode is the primary API surface for other tools/agents. A minor formatting change can break automation.

## Coverage

### Envelope stability
- Assert the JSON envelope contains the expected top-level fields (and only intentional additions):
  - ok
  - data (on success)
  - error (on failure)
  - hint (optional)
  - elapsed_ms
  - version
  - now

### Error code stability
- For common error cases, assert:
  - error.code is stable
  - error.message is actionable
  - hint is present when it improves remediation

### Command-level contract tests (incremental)
- **Phase 1 robot commands:**
  - state
  - get-text
  - search
  - events
  - send
  - wait-for

- **Harmonized commands (bd-h1ai):**
  - why (bd-1dnn - implemented)
  - approve (bd-39wn)
  - workflow run/list/status/abort (bd-qvbz tests these)

- **Later phases:**
  - accounts / accounts-refresh
  - rules list/test
  - reservations / reserve / release

## Schema approach
- Validate outputs against versioned JSON schemas (wa-4vx.7.10) in addition to snapshots.
- Snapshots are still useful for human review (especially for error payloads), but schema validation is the real guardrail.

## Testing Requirements

### Robot Why Tests
```rust
#[test]
fn test_robot_why_known_code() {
    let output = execute_robot(&["why", "deny.alt_screen"]);
    assert!(output["ok"].as_bool().unwrap());
    assert!(!output["data"]["explanation"].as_str().unwrap().is_empty());
}

#[test]
fn test_robot_why_unknown_code() {
    let output = execute_robot(&["why", "unknown.code"]);
    assert!(!output["ok"].as_bool().unwrap());
    // Should include list of valid codes
    assert!(output["hint"].as_str().unwrap().contains("available codes"));
}
```

### Robot Approve Tests
See bd-39wn for comprehensive approve testing.

### Workflow Subcommand Tests
See bd-qvbz for comprehensive workflow testing.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Tests fail if:
  - a required field is removed/renamed
  - an error code changes
  - output becomes non-JSON or non-deterministic

## Meta-validation
- Include a "schema + snapshot mismatch" test to ensure both systems are actually running (not silently skipped).
- Add at least one test per command that asserts deterministic field ordering (or explicitly documents if ordering is not guaranteed).
close_reason: done

title: [Robot] `wa robot wait-for` (pattern wait with timeout, robust errors)
description:
# Task: wa robot wait-for

## Goal
Provide a dedicated robot command for waiting until a pane satisfies a condition without sending input.

This is a core building block for:
- agent orchestration loops (avoid sleeping blindly)
- workflows (shared wait logic)
- tests (deterministic sync points)

## Behavior
Command:
- wa robot wait-for <pane_id> "<pattern>" [--timeout-secs N] [--tail N] [--regex]

Semantics:
- Repeatedly poll the pane tail using the same underlying pane text acquisition as wa robot get-text.
- Default matcher is plain substring.
- Optional --regex enables regex matcher (must be explicit).
- Return success when matched.
- Return a stable error when timeout occurs.

## Workspace/config
- Honors global flags:
  - --workspace / WA_WORKSPACE
  - --config (optional)

## Implementation notes
- Use the shared PaneWaiter (wa-4vx.2.6) so robot, workflows, and send verification have identical polling/backoff semantics.
- Avoid logging full pane content.

## Error model (stable)
- WA-ROBOT-PANE-NOT-FOUND
- WA-ROBOT-TIMEOUT
- WA-ROBOT-GET-TEXT-FAILED

## Logging
- Log at INFO when:
  - starting wait (pane_id, timeout)
  - success (elapsed)
  - timeout

## Testing
- Unit tests with a synthetic pane/text source:
  - returns success when the pattern appears
  - returns timeout with stable error envelope
  - regex mode requires explicit flag

## Acceptance Criteria
- With a synthetic fixture, wait-for returns success when the pattern appears.
- Timeout returns a stable error envelope with elapsed_ms and a remediation hint.
close_reason: Implemented wait-for command with PaneWaiter, proper error codes, and JSON response

title: [EPIC] Safety & policy engine (capability gates, rate limits, redaction)
description:
# Safety & policy engine

## Goal
Ensure wa never becomes a liability by enforcing deterministic safety constraints before any action that mutates state.

## Why this is critical
We are automating typing into terminals running powerful tools. A single wrong send can cause data loss.
We therefore treat action authorization as a first-class subsystem.

## Design requirements
- **Capability-based gates** (deterministic):
  - never send into alt-screen
  - require prompt-active for SendText where possible (OSC 133)
  - block SendText if output gap indicates uncertain state
- **Rate limiting** per pane and per action kind
- **Approval modes**:
  - interactive: prompt user for approvals
  - robot/mcp: return `RequireApproval` as an error with a clear reason
- **Secret redaction** for audit logs and outputs

## Deliverables
- `ActionKind` classification (SendText/Spawn/Split/BrowserAuth/WriteFile/ExecuteWorkflow/etc.)
- `PolicyEngine` evaluation:
  - allow/deny/require-approval
  - rule table loaded from config
- `Redactor`:
  - recognize API key patterns, tokens, passwords
  - ensure secrets never appear in logs or robot output
- Integration points:
  - all sends and workflows must call policy authorize

## Acceptance
- Attempting SendText while pane is AltScreen or CommandRunning is denied.
- Policy logs include redacted input.
- Robot mode returns stable error codes for denied actions.



## Success Criteria
- All input injection paths are policy-gated (robot/human/workflow) with safe defaults.
- Policy decisions are explainable (stable reasons + rule ids) and auditable (including denials).
- Secret redaction is applied consistently to logs/audit/export artifacts.
- Approval (allow-once) works with tight scoping and TTL, and is audited.
- Unit/integration tests cover capability gates, rate limiting, redaction, and approval behavior; E2E covers deny/approve flows.


## Testing
- Unit tests:
  - Capability gate matrix: {PromptActive, CommandRunning, AltScreen, RecentGap} × action kinds → expected decision.

title: Command safety gate for SendText: deny/allow/require-approval + optional dcg integration
description:
# Task: Command safety gate for SendText (deny/allow/require-approval)

## Goal
Before `wa` injects text into a pane that *looks like a shell command*, run a safety gate that:
- blocks obvious destructive commands by default
- supports explicit allowlists / require-approval policies
- optionally delegates classification to `dcg` when installed

This implements PLAN.md §14.2 “Command Safety Gate” and strengthens the project’s “do no harm” invariant.

## Why (user value)
Even with correct pane targeting and prompt detection, sending a destructive command at the wrong time can:
- delete work (`rm -rf`, `git clean -fd`)
- rewrite history (`git reset --hard`, force pushes)
- destroy data (`DROP TABLE`, etc.)

We need an explicit last-line-of-defense gate for *what* we send, not only *where/when* we send.

## Scope
This gate applies to **SendText** (human `wa send`, robot `wa robot send`, workflow injection).

Non-goals (for v0.1):
- building a full shell parser
- perfectly classifying every possible dangerous command

We want high-signal, low-false-positive behavior that errs toward safety:
- when uncertain, prefer `RequireApproval` (not silent allow)

## Design
### 1) “Looks like a command” classifier
A lightweight classifier that decides whether the outgoing text should be treated as a command candidate:
- trim leading whitespace
- ignore pure natural-language prompts
- treat as command if it matches common shapes:
  - starts with typical command token (`git`, `rm`, `sudo`, `docker`, `kubectl`, `psql`, `aws`, etc.)
  - contains a shell pipeline/redirection operator (`|`, `>`, `>>`, `;`, `&&`, `||`) in a shell-ish context

This classifier should be conservative: it’s okay if some commands slip through and are handled by the denylist/dcg step, but we want to avoid flagging every English sentence.

### 2) Built-in deny/allow rules (baseline)
Maintain a minimal built-in ruleset for high-risk patterns:
- `rm -rf` variants (especially root/home)
- `git reset --hard`, `git clean -fd`, `git push --force`, `git branch -D`
- obvious SQL destructive operations (Phase-appropriate; optional)

Rules should return one of:
- Allow
- Deny (with stable reason/rule id)
- RequireApproval (with stable reason + allow-once payload)

### 3) Optional dcg integration
If a `dcg` binary is available:
- evaluate the candidate command via dcg’s hook protocol
- if dcg denies, treat as `RequireApproval` (or Deny if configured)
- if dcg allows, continue (still subject to other PolicyEngine capability checks)

If dcg is not installed or errors:
- fall back to built-in rules
- never crash; return a stable, actionable error only if explicitly configured to require dcg

### 4) PolicyEngine integration
The command safety gate should be invoked inside PolicyEngine’s SendText authorization path:
- capability gates (PromptActive, !AltScreen, !RecentGap) still apply
- command safety gate applies to the *text* and can convert Allow → RequireApproval/Deny
- approval flow uses existing allow-once mechanism

## Deliverables
- Command classifier: `is_command_candidate(text) -> bool`
- Command safety evaluator:
  - built-in rule evaluation
  - optional dcg evaluation
  - stable `rule_id` + reason strings
- Config surface (in `wa.toml`):
  - enable/disable gate
  - choose dcg behavior: {disabled, opportunistic, required}
  - policy for dcg deny: {deny, require_approval}
- Wire through:
  - `wa send`
  - `wa robot send`
  - workflows

## Testing
- Unit tests:
  - classifier (command-ish vs prompt-ish)
  - built-in rule matches (positive + near-miss negatives)
  - dcg integration stubbed via fake binary:
    - deny output → RequireApproval/Deny
    - allow output → Allow
    - dcg missing → fallback path

- Integration tests:
  - end-to-end PolicyEngine decision matrix includes command safety results

- E2E:
  - add an E2E scenario that proves destructive-looking sends are blocked/require approval and that safe commands/prompts are allowed (see `wa-4vx.10.25`).

## Acceptance Criteria
- Sending `rm -rf /` (or equivalent) is denied or requires approval (configurable), even when pane is prompt-active.
- The decision is explainable and auditable (stable rule id + reason, redacted).
- dcg integration is optional and cannot break wa if unavailable.
close_reason: Completed

title: Rate limiting: per-pane, per-action-kind (avoid spam / runaway loops)
description:
# Task: Rate limiting

## Goal
Prevent runaway automation by enforcing rate limits such as:
- cap sends per pane per minute
- cap high-risk actions per interval (e.g., browser auth, approvals)

This is a safety primitive: even correct logic can become harmful if it loops.

## Design choices
- Prefer a deterministic, testable algorithm:
  - token bucket (recommended) or fixed-window counters
- Keying should be explicit:
  - per `(pane_id, action_kind)`
  - optionally incorporate `actor_kind` (robot vs human vs workflow) if needed

## Behavior
- On each action, the PolicyEngine consults the limiter.
- When over limit, return either:
  - `RequireApproval` (preferred for recoverability), OR
  - `Deny` for truly dangerous actions

The decision should include:
- the specific limit that triggered
- the retry-after duration (if meaningful)
- remediation hints (wait, reduce concurrency, change config)

## Configuration
- Limits are configurable via wa config with clear defaults.
- Include sensible “safe defaults” so new users don’t get spammed.

## Testing
- Unit tests:
  - limits trigger deterministically
  - counters reset/roll over correctly
  - separate panes do not share budgets
  - separate action kinds do not share budgets
  - `retry_after` is sensible and monotonic

## Acceptance Criteria
- Exceeding a configured limit yields `RequireApproval` or `Deny` with a clear reason.
- Rate limiting behavior is deterministic and test-covered (no timing flakiness).
close_reason: Completed

title: Policy rules loaded from config (allow/deny/require approval) + robot-safe errors
description:
# Task: Policy rules from config

## Goal
Allow operators to tune safety without recompiling:
- allowlist safe actions
- deny known-unsafe actions
- require approval for high-risk patterns

This is a major UX + safety dial:
- lets cautious users run in “require approval” mode initially
- lets advanced users allowlist known-safe panes/actions

## Deliverables
- Config schema for policy rules (via `wa.toml` schema work).
- Rule evaluation order and precedence (must be documented and deterministic).
- In robot/mcp mode, `RequireApproval` must surface as a structured outcome including allow-once metadata.

## Rule model (suggested)
- Match on (at least):
  - action kind (send_text, ctrl_c, workflow_step, mcp_tool)
  - pane_id/domain/title/cwd (where applicable)
  - inferred agent type (optional)
- Decisions:
  - allow
  - deny
  - require_approval

## Precedence
- Hard denies (capability gates, e.g., alt-screen) always win.
- Explicit per-workspace rules override defaults.
- Specific match beats general match (document tie-break rules).

## Testing
- Unit tests (see `wa-4vx.8.6`):
  - precedence rules are deterministic
  - require-approval emits stable allow-once payload
  - deny cannot be overridden by approval
- Integration/E2E:
  - `wa-4vx.10.16` uses a config rule to force `RequireApproval` and validates full approval loop

## Acceptance Criteria
- A sample config rule changes behavior deterministically.
- Robot/human surfaces expose `RequireApproval` with actionable remediation (how to approve).

title: Integrate PolicyEngine into all SendText paths (robot send + workflows)
description:
# Task: Integrate PolicyEngine into input injection paths (SendText / Ctrl-C)

## Goal
Guarantee that **no code path** can inject terminal input without passing policy checks.

## Integration points
- `wa robot send`
- `wa send` (human)
- workflow engine step actions
- any helper utilities that send Ctrl-C / control sequences

## Architecture (avoid duplication)
Implement a single shared helper in core (proposed name):
- `PolicyGatedInjector`

Responsibilities:
1. Build a `PolicyInput` (actor kind, pane id, action kind, redacted summary).
2. Call `PolicyEngine::authorize`.
3. Emit an audit record for allow/deny (redacted summary).
4. If allowed: perform the injection via the WezTerm client.
5. Return a structured outcome suitable for robot/human/workflow logging.

All user-facing send commands and workflow action executors must call this helper. There should be **exactly one** implementation of “send with policy”.

## Testing
- Unit tests:
  - policy deny prevents calling the underlying WezTerm send API
  - RequireApproval returns a stable allow-once payload (when wired)

- Integration tests:
  - smoke test `wa robot send` against a synthetic policy/capability state

## Acceptance Criteria
- Attempting to inject input while pane state is `AltScreen` is denied everywhere.
- There is only one injection implementation shared by robot/human/workflow paths (no duplicated “send-with-policy” logic).

description:
# Task: Policy tests

## Goal
Prevent regressions in safety-critical logic.

Policy regressions are high-impact because they either:
- block safe operations (user-hostile), or
- allow unsafe operations (trust-destroying)

## Testing
Unit tests must cover:
- Capability gates
  - deny SendText in AltScreen
  - deny SendText when recent_gap is true
  - require prompt_active (or RequireApproval if configured)

- Rate limiting
  - per-pane/per-action budgets
  - no runaway loops

- Redaction
  - inputs and secrets never appear in logs/audit summaries

- RequireApproval + allow-once approvals
  - RequireApproval returns a scoped allow-once payload
  - approval enables ONLY the matching action fingerprint
  - TTL expiry works
  - Deny decisions cannot be overridden via approval

- **Reservations**
  - non-owner actions are denied/require-approval per config
  - owner actions are allowed
  - expired reservations are treated as no reservation

description:
# Task: Audit trail emission (core)

## Goal
Ensure the earliest, most safety-relevant actions are auditable from day 1:
- `wa robot send` / `wa send` allow/deny/require-approval decisions
- `wa approve` (approval grants)

This provides user trust and postmortem visibility without waiting for workflows/MCP.

## Actions covered (core)
- `wa robot send` / `wa send`
  - allowed actions
  - denied actions
  - require-approval actions (with allow-once metadata)
- `wa approve` (approval grant)
- **reservation conflicts** (deny/require-approval when a pane is reserved by someone else)

## Requirements
- Audit entries must be written even on denial.
- Audit must include:
  - who initiated (actor kind + actor id)
  - policy decision + reason (+ rule id when relevant)
  - preconditions observed (prompt active, alt-screen, gaps)
  - verification outcomes (wait-for matched, timeout)
- Redaction:
  - never store raw secrets or full inputs
  - store hashes/summaries consistent with the redaction system

## Testing
- Unit tests:
  - an allow/deny decision produces a correctly shaped audit record
  - redaction removes secret-like substrings from summaries
- Integration tests:
  - `wa robot send` denied → audit row exists
  - require-approval → audit row exists and includes allow-once metadata
  - reservation conflict produces an audit row with reservation metadata

## Acceptance Criteria
- Every attempted action (including denials) creates an audit entry.
- Audit records are safe by default (redacted) and sufficient to explain the decision.

title: PaneCapabilities derivation: PromptActive/CommandRunning/AltScreen/RecentGap (deterministic first, safe fallback)
description:
# Task: PaneCapabilities derivation (state → capability gates)

## Goal
Define and maintain a **deterministic** `PaneCapabilities` snapshot for each pane that policy/workflows can trust.

This is the missing link between:
- ingest signals (OSC 133 markers, gap detection, optional status_update IPC)
- safety/policy decisions (whether it is safe to send input)

## Capabilities (v0)
- `prompt_active: bool` (preferred: OSC 133 prompt markers)
- `command_running: bool` (OSC 133 start/end)
- `recent_gap: bool` (true if we emitted a GAP since last verified prompt boundary)
- `alt_screen: Option<bool>`
  - `Some(true)` when confidently detected
  - `Some(false)` when confidently not alt-screen
  - `None` when unknown

## Data sources / precedence
- Deterministic first (preferred):
  - OSC 133 markers
  - explicit GAP events
  - **status_update IPC** (if available) for alt-screen + cursor/dimensions
- Fallback heuristics (careful):
  - only used when deterministic signals are unavailable

## Safety behavior
- If `alt_screen` is unknown, policy should default to deny or require approval for `SendText`.

## Testing
- Unit tests cover state transitions:
  - prompt active ↔ command running
  - gap causes `recent_gap=true`
  - `recent_gap` clears after verified prompt boundary
  - alt-screen transitions when status_update is available

## Acceptance Criteria
- Unit tests cover capability state transitions and gap clearing semantics.
- Policy consumers can rely on these fields being stable and deterministic.

Also fixed heuristic_idle_check bug that caused false positives on '%' ending lines like 'Progress: 50%'.

title: Approval tokens (allow-once): ergonomic override for RequireApproval decisions
description:
# Task: Approval tokens (allow-once)

## Goal
When PolicyEngine returns RequireApproval, provide an ergonomic, safe way for a human to explicitly approve the action without editing config files.

This is essential UX:
- robots/agents can surface a structured error with an "approval code"
- a human can review and grant the approval intentionally
- wa can proceed safely with a minimal blast radius (scoped + expiring)

## Non-goals
- This must NOT override hard Deny decisions.
- This must NOT store secrets in plaintext.

## Design (v0)
### Approval request generation
- On RequireApproval, return a structured payload containing:
  - allow_once_code (short)
  - allow_once_full_hash (long, e.g., sha256:...)
  - expires_at (TTL)
  - human-readable approval summary
  - canonical command the user can run (e.g., `wa approve <code>`)

### Scoping
Approval must be scoped tightly to prevent confused-deputy bugs:
- workspace scope
- action kind (SendText / WorkflowStep / MCP tool)
- pane_id (when applicable)
- action fingerprint (normalized)

### Storage
- Persist approvals in DB (workspace-scoped) with TTL.

### Audit
- Approval grants are audited.

## Testing
- Unit tests:
  - fingerprint determinism
  - TTL expiry works
  - wrong workspace/pane/action_kind does not match
  - RequireApproval never becomes Allow without explicit approval

## Acceptance Criteria
- A RequireApproval result includes a stable allow-once payload suitable for robot and human surfaces.
- Approvals are scoped, expiring, and auditable.
close_reason: Implemented allow-once approval tokens (approval_tokens table, storage APIs, approval service, policy payloads) with scope/TTL + audit + tests

title: [EPIC] Unified configuration (wa.toml + env overrides + validation)
description:
# Unified configuration

## Goal
Implement a single configuration system that controls wa behavior consistently across CLI/daemon/robot/mcp.

## Why this matters
Without a unified config, behavior becomes inconsistent and brittle. Config must be:
- validated (schema + semantic checks)
- overrideable (env vars + CLI flags)
- reloadable (for safe settings)

## Deliverables
- `~/.config/wa/wa.toml` (and data dir under `~/.local/share/wa` by default)
- config loader:
  - merges default + file + env + CLI
  - emits an "effective config" output
- `wa config` commands:
  - init, validate, show --effective, set
- hot reload for non-destructive settings (poll intervals, retention, log level)

## Acceptance
- `wa config validate` catches invalid configs.
- `wa watch --reload-config` updates poll intervals without restart.



## Success Criteria
- A single config loader produces an effective config used consistently across `wa watch`, robot, human CLI, and MCP.
- Workspace resolution yields correct default paths (DB/log/lock/socket) with clear precedence (flags > env > config > defaults).
- Config validation catches invalid settings with actionable errors.
- Pane include/exclude rules are configurable and enforced in ingest to protect privacy and reduce load.
- Tests cover parse/serialize, overrides, validation, and workspace path resolution.


## Testing
- Unit tests:
  - Parse/serialize roundtrip for `wa.toml` (including unknown fields behavior if we allow it).
  - Env + CLI overrides precedence and error messages.
  - Workspace path resolution across OS conventions (XDG, macOS) with deterministic temp dirs.

- Integration tests:
  - “effective config” snapshot tests for representative configs.
  - Hot reload test: mutate config on disk, ensure watcher picks up allowed changes and rejects unsafe ones.

## Acceptance Criteria
- All items in the following sections are satisfied: Success Criteria, Deliverables.
- All Testing requirements pass (unit/integration/E2E) with the logging/artifacts described above.
- Any explicit dependencies for this bead are implemented and validated via tests or E2E artifacts.

title: Filesystem layout & workspace resolution (XDG/macOS conventions, DB/logs/locks/sockets)
description:
# Task: Filesystem layout & workspace resolution

## Goal
Make wa feel predictable, ergonomic, and safe by standardizing where it stores:
- config
- DB/state
- logs
- IPC sockets
- locks/crash reports
- exported artifacts

This directly affects user trust and debuggability.

## Design: workspace vs global config
### Global config (operator defaults)
- Config file location should follow OS conventions:
  - Linux: XDG (e.g., `~/.config/wa/wa.toml`)
  - macOS: standard Application Support paths (or XDG if preferred)
  - Windows: (defer; document if unsupported in v0)

### Workspace (per-project state)
wa needs a workspace root that scopes:
- DB path
- locks
- socket(s)
- crash reports
- diagnostics bundles

Workspace resolution order (v0):
1) explicit CLI flag: `--workspace <path>`
2) env: `WA_WORKSPACE`
3) default: current working directory (or a per-project directory under data dir)

## Path conventions (v0)
Given `workspace_root`:
- DB: `<workspace_root>/.wa/wa.db` (or configurable)
- Lock: `<workspace_root>/.wa/watch.lock`
- IPC socket: `<workspace_root>/.wa/ipc.sock`
- Logs: `<workspace_root>/.wa/logs/wa-watch.log` (optional)
- Crash reports: `<workspace_root>/.wa/crash/<timestamp>.txt`
- Diag bundle: `<workspace_root>/.wa/diag/<timestamp>/`

## Safety requirements
- Never overwrite user files unexpectedly.
- Create directories with restrictive permissions where applicable.
- If `workspace_root` is not writable, fail with a clear error and hint.

## UX requirements
- Provide a single command to print resolved paths:
  - `wa config show --effective` includes all resolved paths
  - `wa doctor` reports them as well

## Testing
- Unit tests for resolution precedence (flag > env > default).
- Cross-platform path tests for path join/normalization.
- Integration-ish tests (temp dirs):
  - workspace not writable produces actionable error
  - lock/socket paths are under `.wa/` and do not collide across workspaces

## Acceptance Criteria
- For a given invocation, wa can print all resolved paths deterministically.
- Locks/sockets/logs/crash reports all live under the workspace scope by default.
- Users can relocate workspace explicitly without editing multiple settings.
notes:
Background / Why:
- Predictable filesystem layout reduces support burden and user confusion.
- Workspace scoping prevents cross-project data bleed.

Considerations:
- Follow OS conventions but keep overrides explicit and documented.
- Never overwrite user files implicitly.
- Prefer restrictive permissions on sensitive paths.

Logging / Observability:
- Log resolved paths at debug level to aid support.
- Emit clear errors for non-writable workspace roots.
close_reason: Completed

title: Pane selection config: include/exclude filters (domain/title/cwd) + privacy defaults
description:
# Task: Pane selection config (include/exclude)

## Goal
Give users control over which panes wa observes and persists.

This improves:
- privacy (avoid capturing sensitive panes)
- performance (reduce ingest load)
- UX (clear boundaries: what wa will and will not touch)

## Config surface (v0)
Add an ingest/panes section that supports include/exclude rules.

Rules should be expressive but safe:
- match by domain name
- match by title (substring/regex)
- match by cwd URI/path prefix

Example shape (illustrative):
- `panes.include: [ ...rules... ]`
- `panes.exclude: [ ...rules... ]`

Precedence:
- exclude wins over include
- if include is empty: default include-all (subject to exclude)

## Safety
- The default should be conservative but not surprising:
  - include-all is fine for early adopters, but wa must strongly nudge users toward configuring excludes for privacy.

## UX requirements
- `wa status` / `wa robot state` must show:
  - observed vs ignored
  - which rule matched (rule id/name) when ignored

## Testing
- Parse/validation tests for rules.
- Matching semantics tests (precedence and edge cases).

## Acceptance Criteria
- Users can configure wa to ignore panes by domain/title/cwd.
- Ignored panes produce no stored segments/events and are clearly labeled in status output.
notes:
Background / Why:
- Pane filtering is essential for privacy and performance.
- Explicit include/exclude rules match user mental models.

Considerations:
- Exclude must win over include.
- Rule ids should be stable so status output is actionable.
- Normalize title/cwd/domain before matching.

Logging / Observability:
- Log match decisions with rule_id and redacted fields.
- Provide aggregate observed/ignored counts per discovery tick.

title: [EPIC] Observability Infrastructure: Structured Logging, Metrics, Health Endpoints
description:
# [EPIC] Observability Infrastructure

## Mission
Make wa **fully observable** with structured logging, metrics export, and health endpoints that enable debugging, monitoring, and alerting.

## Why This Matters
wa runs as a background daemon managing critical automation. When things go wrong:
- Logs must be **structured** (JSON) for parsing by log aggregators
- Metrics must be **exportable** for dashboards and alerts
- Health endpoints must be **queryable** for orchestration

Without observability, debugging is guesswork.

## Components

### 1. Structured Logging Infrastructure
All log output follows a consistent structured format:
```rust
#[derive(Serialize)]
struct LogEntry {
    timestamp: DateTime<Utc>,
    level: Level,
    target: String,
    message: String,
    // Contextual fields
    pane_id: Option<u32>,
    workflow_id: Option<String>,
    event_id: Option<i64>,
    // Performance
    duration_ms: Option<f64>,
    // Error context
    error: Option<ErrorContext>,
}
```

Features:
- JSON output for log aggregators (ELK, Loki, etc.)
- Human-readable output for terminals (default)
- Log levels: trace, debug, info, warn, error
- Contextual fields propagated via tracing spans
- Sensitive data redaction (tokens, passwords)

### 2. Metrics Export
Prometheus-compatible metrics endpoint:
```
# Counters
wa_events_detected_total{type="usage_limit",agent="codex"} 42
wa_workflows_completed_total{workflow="handle_usage_limits",status="success"} 38
wa_policy_decisions_total{decision="allow",action="send"} 1024

# Gauges  
wa_panes_observed 4
wa_panes_ignored 1
wa_queue_depth 0
wa_db_size_bytes 1234567

# Histograms
wa_pattern_match_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.001"} 9500
wa_workflow_step_duration_seconds_bucket{le="1.0"} 450
```

### 3. Health Endpoint
HTTP endpoint for orchestration health checks:
```bash
$ curl localhost:9876/health
{
  "status": "healthy",
  "checks": {
    "wezterm_connection": "ok",
    "database": "ok",
    "pattern_engine": "ok"
  },
  "uptime_seconds": 3600,
  "version": "0.1.0"
}
```

Liveness vs Readiness:
- `/health/live` - process is running
- `/health/ready` - ready to handle requests

### 4. Tracing Integration
Distributed tracing via OpenTelemetry:
- Trace IDs propagated through workflows
- Spans for key operations
- Export to Jaeger/Zipkin (optional)

## Configuration
```toml
[observability]
log_format = "json"  # or "pretty"
log_level = "info"
metrics_enabled = true
metrics_port = 9876
health_port = 9876
tracing_enabled = false
tracing_endpoint = "http://localhost:4317"
```

## Testing
- Unit tests: Log formatting, metrics collection
- Integration tests: Health endpoint responds correctly
- E2E tests: Metrics increment as expected during workflows

## Success Criteria
- All log output is structured and parseable
- Metrics endpoint serves Prometheus-compatible data
- Health endpoint enables orchestration integration
- Sensitive data never appears in logs

## Acceptance Criteria
- Structured logging produces JSON with required fields and redaction applied.
- Metrics endpoint exports Prometheus-compatible counters/gauges/histograms.
- Health endpoints (/health, /health/live, /health/ready) return correct status codes and JSON.
- Observability configuration is documented and validated via tests in `wa-086`.
- No secrets appear in logs or health payloads.
close_reason: Superseded by wa-nu4.3.4 (diagnostics/metrics/bundles) + wa-nu4.3.6 (optional web /health) + wa-4vx.6.5 (structured logging baseline)

# Notification History: Persistent log of sent notifications

## Purpose
Track all sent notifications for debugging, auditing, and user review.

## Implementation

### Database Schema
```sql
CREATE TABLE notification_history (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    timestamp TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now')),

    -- Event reference
    event_id INTEGER REFERENCES events(id),

    -- Notification details
    channel TEXT NOT NULL,  -- 'webhook', 'desktop', 'slack', etc.
    title TEXT NOT NULL,
    body TEXT NOT NULL,
    severity TEXT NOT NULL,  -- 'info', 'warning', 'error', 'critical'

    -- Delivery status
    status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',  -- 'pending', 'sent', 'failed', 'throttled'
    error_message TEXT,

    -- Response tracking
    acknowledged_at TEXT,
    acknowledged_by TEXT,
    action_taken TEXT,

    -- Metadata
    metadata TEXT  -- JSON blob for channel-specific data
);

CREATE INDEX idx_notification_history_timestamp ON notification_history(timestamp);
CREATE INDEX idx_notification_history_status ON notification_history(status);
CREATE INDEX idx_notification_history_event ON notification_history(event_id);
```

title: Phase 3: Replace tokio network I/O with asupersync
description:
# Phase 3: Replace tokio network I/O

## Goal
Replace all tokio network I/O (Unix sockets, TCP, TLS) with asupersync networking primitives.

## Scope
- tokio::net::UnixStream/UnixListener → asupersync::net equivalents
- tokio::net::TcpListener/TcpStream → asupersync::net::TcpListener/TcpStream
- tokio-rustls → asupersync TLS (rustls-based)
- tokio::io::{AsyncReadExt, AsyncWriteExt, BufReader} → asupersync I/O traits
- reqwest → asupersync::http client

## Key architectural note
asupersync provides its own networking stack that does NOT depend on tokio. The I/O reactor abstracts over epoll/kqueue/io_uring. All network ops go through Cx capability context.

## Affected modules
- mux_client.rs — UnixStream (997 LOC, most critical)
- ipc.rs — UnixListener + UnixStream (~400 LOC)
- native_events.rs — UnixListener (~400 LOC)
- web.rs — TcpListener (feature-gated)
- distributed.rs — TLS/mTLS (feature-gated)

## Migration risk: HIGH
Network I/O is where most subtle bugs hide. The mux_client.rs PDU framing protocol over Unix sockets is especially delicate.
close_reason: Flattened: Phase 3 was a pure bottleneck with no concrete work. Its children (wa-q8vj3 Unix sockets, wa-1u55z TCP/TLS) now depend directly on their prerequisites (wa-2abzy channels, wa-1yz79 time). Network I/O summary preserved in wa-e34d9 epic.

# [EPIC] Rollback Log Visualization

## Mission
Provide visibility into what actions wa has taken and what could be undone, building trust through transparency.

Users fear automation because they don't know:

- Whether actions can be undone
- How to recover from mistakes

Rollback visualization addresses:

- **Debugging**: Trace action sequences

- Timeline of all wa actions
- Grouped by workflow/pane

- `wa history --pane 0` - pane-specific history
- `wa history --undo-able` - only undoable actions

### Undo Capabilities
- Send actions: show what was sent (can't undo)
- Workflow states: can abort/resume
- File changes (if any): can restore

### Integration
- Works with audit trail
- Links to workflow step logs
- Shows in TUI

## Success Criteria
- Users can see full action history
- Undo status is clear
- Recovery paths documented

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] wa history shows action timeline
- [ ] Undo status displayed per action
- [ ] Grouping by workflow works
- [ ] Integration with audit trail
- [ ] Tests cover visualization

## Testing

- E2E scenario captures history output and logs.

title: Action history data model: audit_actions + action_undo + view
description:
# Action history data model: audit_actions + undo metadata + view

## Purpose
Define a **single source of truth** for action history without duplicating writes:
- reuse `audit_actions` as the canonical action record
- store undo metadata separately
- expose a read‑optimized view for UI/CLI

This avoids maintaining two action logs and keeps retention/redaction rules centralized.

## Data model
### 1) Canonical actions
Use existing `audit_actions` as the base record (see `wa-4vx.3.8`).

### 2) Undo metadata table
Add a small companion table for undoability + undo state:
```sql
CREATE TABLE action_undo (
  audit_action_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  undoable BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  undo_strategy TEXT NOT NULL,         -- none|manual|workflow_abort|pane_close|custom
  undo_hint TEXT,                      -- redacted guidance for humans
  undo_payload TEXT,                   -- JSON for executor (redacted)
  undone_at TEXT,
  undone_by TEXT,
  FOREIGN KEY (audit_action_id) REFERENCES audit_actions(id)
);

CREATE INDEX idx_action_undo_undoable ON action_undo(undoable) WHERE undoable = 1;
```

### 3) History view
Expose a read‑optimized view that joins:
- `audit_actions`
- `workflow_step_log` / `workflow_executions`
- `action_undo`

```sql
CREATE VIEW action_history AS
SELECT a.*, u.undoable, u.undo_strategy, u.undo_hint, u.undone_at, u.undone_by,
       w.workflow_id, w.step_name
FROM audit_actions a
LEFT JOIN action_undo u ON u.audit_action_id = a.id
LEFT JOIN workflow_step_log w ON w.audit_action_id = a.id;
```

## Why this design
- **No duplicate writes**: audit is already required for safety
- **Consistent redaction**: all actions share the same redaction rules
- **Flexible**: undo metadata can evolve without altering core audit schema

## Testing
- Schema creation tests (action_undo + view)
- Join correctness tests (audit + workflow + undo)
- Undo metadata validation tests
- Query performance tests (indexes used)

## Acceptance Criteria
- `action_history` view returns stable, ordered records.
- Undo metadata is stored without duplicating action content.
- Queries for `wa history` are indexed and fast.
close_reason: Data model fully implemented: audit_actions table, action_undo table with undo strategy/hint/payload, action_history view joining audit+undo+workflow_step_log. Tests pass: action_history_view_exists_after_init, action_history_includes_undo_metadata. Schema migration in v006. CLI command (wa history) would be a separate task.

title: Action recording service: capture all wa actions in audit log
description:
# Task: Action recording service (audit_actions + action_undo)

## Purpose
Capture all wa actions for history/visualization and potential undo **without duplicating writes**:
- `audit_actions` is the canonical record (see `wa-4vx.3.8`).
- `action_undo` stores undo metadata and undo state (see `wa-5em.5`).

This service is the single integration point where “something happened” becomes queryable and explainable to users.

## Recording points (must be covered)

### 1) SendText
Record a SendText action whenever wa injects text (human/robot/mcp/workflow), including:
- pane/domain identifiers
- actor (human/robot/mcp/workflow)
- policy decision + rule ids (allow/deny/require-approval)

**Redaction is mandatory.** Never store the raw text.
Store only a safe summary:
- `text_length`
- `text_preview_redacted` (apply redactor; consider truncation)
- `text_hash` (stable hash for correlation without revealing content)
- `command_candidate: bool` (if the command-safety gate classified it)

Example (pseudocode):
```rust
pub async fn record_send_text(&self, pane_id: u64, text: &str, ctx: &SendContext) -> Result<ActionId> {
    let redacted = self.redactor.redact(text);
    let preview = redacted.chars().take(80).collect::<String>();

    self.storage.insert_audit_action(AuditAction {
        action_type: ActionType::SendText,
        pane_id,
        description: format!("Sent {} chars to pane", text.len()),
        details: json!({
            "text_length": text.len(),
            "text_preview_redacted": preview,
            "text_hash": stable_hash(text),
            "triggered_by": ctx.triggered_by,
            "policy": ctx.policy_summary,
        }),
        ..Default::default()
    }).await
}
```

### 2) Workflow actions
Record workflow start/step/complete/fail as actions so `wa history` can render a tree:
- WorkflowStart: undoable via `undo_strategy=workflow_abort` while running.
- WorkflowStep: parent_action_id points at WorkflowStart.
- WorkflowCompleted/Failed: not undoable (but may include manual remediation hints).

### 3) Pane operations
Record pane lifecycle operations that wa performs (spawn/split/activate), including:
- undo_strategy where applicable (e.g., close pane) **but always require confirmation at the CLI layer**.

## Service design constraints
- Recording must not block hot paths:
  - use the same single-writer DB channel model as storage
  - or buffer with bounded queue
- If buffering is used:
  - buffer size + flush policy must be bounded
  - flush on shutdown must be explicit and tested
  - tests must not depend on wall-clock sleeps; provide a `flush_now()` hook

## Testing
- Unit tests:
  - redaction invariants (raw secret never appears in stored details)
  - correct undo_strategy assignment per action type
  - parent/child linkage for workflow steps

- Integration tests:
  - a synthetic workflow run produces:
    - audit_actions rows
    - action_undo rows
    - action_history view rows
  - denial paths are recorded (attempted action logged, no SendText recorded as “executed”)

## Acceptance Criteria
- All send_text calls (human/robot/mcp/workflow) produce a redacted audit action.
- Workflow starts/steps/completions are recorded and linkable as a tree.
- Undo metadata is present only when appropriate and is itself redacted.
- Recording is performant and never blocks the watcher/event hot path.
close_reason: Completed audit action recording lane; fixed robot send to propagate persisted audit_action_id and revalidated gates (check/fmt pass, clippy fails on unrelated pre-existing warnings).

description:
# History CLI

## Purpose
Provide CLI commands for viewing and filtering the action history.

## Commands

### wa history
Default view showing recent actions:
```bash
wa history

# Output
╭────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ Action History (Last 24 hours)                                             │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Time       Pane  Action              Description                    Undo   │
│ ─────────  ────  ─────────────────   ────────────────────────────  ─────  │
│ 14:32:05   0     workflow_complete   handle_usage_limits           -      │
│ 14:32:04   0     send_text          Sent 12 chars                  -      │
│ 14:32:02   0     workflow_step      wait_for_stable                -      │
│ 14:31:58   0     workflow_start     handle_usage_limits            ✓      │
│ 14:31:55   0     detection          codex.usage_limit_warning      -      │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

Showing 5 of 127 actions. Use --limit to see more.
Undoable actions: 12
```

### wa history --pane <id>
Filter by pane:
```bash
wa history --pane 0 --limit 20
```

### wa history --workflow <id>
Filter by workflow execution:
```bash
wa history --workflow wf-abc123

# Output shows workflow tree
╭────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ Workflow: handle_usage_limits (wf-abc123)                                  │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ├── 14:31:58 workflow_start    Started handle_usage_limits                 │
│ │   ├── 14:32:02 workflow_step wait_for_stable (5.2s)                     │
│ │   ├── 14:32:04 send_text     Sent account switch command                │
│ │   └── 14:32:05 workflow_step verify_switched (1.1s)                     │
│ └── 14:32:05 workflow_complete Success                                     │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

### wa history --undoable
Show only undoable actions:
```bash
wa history --undoable

# Output
12 undoable actions found:
ID      Time       Pane  Action           Undo Available
10234   14:31:58   0     workflow_start   Abort workflow
10201   14:25:12   1     pane_spawn       Close pane
...
```

### wa history --since/--until
Time-based filtering:
```bash
wa history --since "1 hour ago"
wa history --since "2026-01-18T12:00:00" --until "2026-01-18T14:00:00"
```

### wa history --export
Export to file:
```bash
wa history --export json > history.json
wa history --export csv > history.csv
```

## Testing
- CLI argument parsing tests
- Output formatting golden tests
- Filter combination tests
- Export format validation tests

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] wa history shows recent actions
- [ ] --pane filter works correctly
- [ ] --workflow shows tree view
- [ ] --undoable filter works
- [ ] Time-based filters work
- [ ] Export produces valid JSON/CSV
- [ ] Robot mode outputs valid JSON
- [ ] Tests cover all command variations

title: Rollback visualization tests: data model, recording, CLI, undo, E2E
description:
# Task: Rollback visualization tests (audit_actions + action_undo + history + undo)

## Goal
Provide comprehensive, regression-resistant test coverage for the rollback visualization system (`wa-5em`):
- the **action history data model** (`audit_actions` + `action_undo` + `action_history` view)
- the **action recording service** (what gets recorded, when, and how it is redacted)
- the **human CLI surfaces** (`wa history`, `wa undo`) and their stable outputs
- the **undo engine semantics** (what is undoable, what happens when undo runs)

This bead is intentionally “deep” because rollback/undo is trust-critical UX: if it lies, leaks secrets, or flakes, users will stop trusting wa.

## Scope

### 1) Data model + query tests (unit/integration)
Validate the design from `wa-5em.5`:
- Schema correctness:
  - `action_undo` exists and references `audit_actions`
  - `action_history` view exists and joins correctly
  - indexes exist for common queries (`undoable`, recent actions, pane/workflow filters)

- Ordering and filtering semantics:
  - “recent actions” ordering is deterministic
  - filters by pane/workflow/action_type behave correctly

- Redaction invariants:
  - stored previews are redacted consistently with audit policy (`wa-4vx.8.3`)
  - secret-looking strings never round-trip in clear

### 2) Recording tests (unit/integration)
Cover each recording point from `wa-5em.6`:
- SendText
- WorkflowStart / WorkflowStep / WorkflowCompleted
- Pane operations (spawn/split/activate) where applicable

Assertions:
- parent/child linkage is correct for workflow steps
- undoable/undo_strategy/undo_payload are correct (and *absent* for non-undoables)
- “triggered_by” metadata is recorded (human/robot/mcp/workflow)

### 3) CLI output tests (unit + contract)
- Snapshot tests (plain mode):
  - `wa history` output is stable and contains **no ANSI escapes**
  - stable truncation rules and stable ordering

- JSON mode tests:
  - stable schema and error codes
  - redaction invariants hold

### 4) Undo engine tests (unit/integration)
- Undo success paths:
  - abort a running workflow (supported undo type)
  - mark an action as undone with timestamp + actor

- Undo not-applicable paths:
  - non-undoable action -> clear structured error + remediation hints
  - already-undone -> idempotent “no-op” outcome

### 5) E2E coverage (via standard harness)
Implement an E2E case that follows the shared E2E contract and produces excellent artifacts.

Requirements:
- Use the standard runner (`wa-4vx.10.11`) and registry (`wa-4vx.10.20`).
- Follow the harness contract (`wa-4vx.10.6`) and structured logging baseline (`wa-4vx.6.5`).
- Avoid wall-clock sleeps where possible:
  - prefer explicit wait conditions (`wa robot wait-for`, health checks, step-log / action-history queries)
  - if a bounded sleep is truly unavoidable, justify it and keep it small

**E2E scenario (deterministic intent):**
1. Start a watcher/workflow execution in a dedicated test workspace.
2. Trigger a synthetic workflow that generates a predictable action tree (workflow start + steps + at least one send).
3. Assert `wa history` contains:
   - the workflow action tree
   - at least one undoable action surfaced in `wa undo --list`
4. Run `wa undo <action-id> --yes` and verify:
   - action is marked undone
   - the underlying target (e.g., workflow) is aborted/cancelled as appropriate
5. Collect artifacts:
   - watcher logs
   - `action_history` slice/export (redacted)
   - audit slice (redacted)
   - a human-readable summary file describing what happened

## Testing
- Unit tests for:
  - schema/query invariants
  - redaction invariants
  - recording coverage per action type

- Integration tests for:
  - end-to-end action recording + history query on a temp workspace DB
  - undo success + undo not-applicable cases

- E2E tests:
  - one case registered in `./scripts/e2e_test.sh` that validates history + undo with artifacts

## Registry
- Register this case in the E2E case registry (`wa-4vx.10.20`), including prerequisites and default inclusion status.
- Ensure `./scripts/e2e_test.sh --all` includes this case (or mark non-default with justification).

## Acceptance Criteria
- Data model tests validate schema + indexes + deterministic ordering.
- Recording tests cover all relevant action types and parent/child linkage.
- `wa history` and `wa undo` outputs are stable in plain + JSON modes and never leak secrets.
- E2E case runs deterministically under the standard runner and produces actionable artifacts on failure.
notes: Resolved clippy (environment.rs updated by CobaltGlen). Added workflow abort audit test in workflows.rs; full checks rerun: cargo fmt --check, cargo check --all-targets, cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings, cargo test (all pass).
close_reason: Completed coverage: data-model/recording/CLI/undo + E2E history_undo_workflow scenario

title: Audit and enhance ingest loop to provide all status metadata without Lua
description:
## Overview

Verify that wa's existing ingest/polling loop already provides all the metadata that STATUS_UPDATE_LUA was sending, and enhance it if needed. The goal is to confirm we lose nothing by removing the Lua hook.

## Current STATUS_UPDATE_LUA Payload

The Lua snippet sends this JSON to \`wa event --from-status\`:
\`\`\`json
{
  "schema_version": 0,
  "pane_id": 123,
  "domain": "local",
  "title": "zsh",
  "cursor": {"row": 10, "col": 5},
  "dimensions": {"rows": 24, "cols": 80},
  "is_alt_screen": false,
  "ts": 1706123456789
}
\`\`\`

## What Ingest Loop Already Provides

wa's ingest loop (crates/wa-core/src/ingest.rs) polls \`wezterm cli list --format json\`:

\`\`\`json
[
  {
    "window_id": 0,
    "tab_id": 0,
    "pane_id": 0,
    "workspace": "default",
    "size": "80x24",        // ✅ dimensions available
    "title": "zsh",         // ✅ title available  
    "cwd": "/home/user",    // ✅ cwd available (bonus!)
    "domain": "local",      // ✅ domain available (new in WezTerm)
    "is_active": true       // ✅ active state available
  }
]
\`\`\`

## Gap Analysis

| Field | Lua Provides | CLI Provides | Action Needed |
|-------|-------------|--------------|---------------|
| pane_id | ✅ | ✅ | None |
| domain | ✅ | ✅ | None |
| title | ✅ | ✅ | None |
| dimensions | ✅ (rows/cols) | ✅ (80x24 string) | Parse "80x24" → (80, 24) |
| cursor position | ✅ | ❌ | See notes below |
| is_alt_screen | ✅ | ❌ | Handled by wa-mw44 (escape sequence detection) |
| cwd | ❌ | ✅ | Bonus - we get MORE data |

### Cursor Position

The cursor position was rarely used by wa. Options:
1. **Remove dependency**: Confirm no wa code actually needs cursor position
2. **On-demand query**: If ever needed, \`wezterm cli get-text --pane-id X\` includes cursor info
3. **Escape sequence parsing**: Could track cursor from CSI sequences (complex, probably overkill)

**Recommendation**: Audit wa codebase to confirm cursor position is unused, document as unavailable in polling mode.

## Implementation Tasks

### 1. Parse Dimensions String
\`\`\`rust
fn parse_dimensions(size: &str) -> Option<(u16, u16)> {
    let parts: Vec<&str> = size.split('x').collect();
    if parts.len() == 2 {
        let cols = parts[0].parse().ok()?;
        let rows = parts[1].parse().ok()?;
        Some((cols, rows))
    } else {
        None
    }
}
\`\`\`

### 2. Verify Domain Field Available
Check WezTerm version requirements — \`domain\` field was added in WezTerm 20230712+.
Add fallback for older versions (default to "local").

### 3. Audit Cursor Usage
Search codebase for any dependency on cursor position:
\`\`\`bash
rg "cursor" crates/wa-core/src/
\`\`\`

### 4. Update PaneInfo Struct
Ensure ingest.rs PaneInfo struct includes all fields:
\`\`\`rust
pub struct PaneInfo {
    pub pane_id: u64,
    pub title: String,
    pub domain: String,
    pub cwd: Option<String>,
    pub dimensions: (u16, u16),  // (cols, rows)
    pub is_active: bool,
    pub is_alt_screen: bool,  // From ScreenStateTracker
}
\`\`\`

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] All STATUS_UPDATE_LUA fields available without Lua (except cursor if unused)
- [ ] Dimensions parsed from "WxH" string format
- [ ] Domain field handled with fallback for old WezTerm
- [ ] Cursor position usage audited and documented
- [ ] PaneInfo struct updated
- [ ] Unit tests for dimension parsing
- [ ] Integration test: ingest loop provides complete metadata

## Dependencies

- Depends on: wa-mw44 (alt-screen detection) for is_alt_screen field

## Files to Modify

- crates/wa-core/src/ingest.rs — PaneInfo struct and parsing
- crates/wa-core/src/wezterm.rs — CLI output parsing

## References

- wezterm cli list: https://wezfurlong.org/wezterm/cli/cli/list.html
- Current ingest.rs: crates/wa-core/src/ingest.rs

title: Watchdog/heartbeat system: deadlock detection and auto-recovery
description:
# Watchdog/Heartbeat System

## Purpose
Monitor wa's own health and recover from hangs or deadlocks.

## How It Works
1. Main loop updates heartbeat timestamp each iteration
2. Watchdog thread checks heartbeat every N seconds
3. If heartbeat stale > threshold, trigger recovery

## Implementation
```rust
pub struct Watchdog {
    heartbeat: Arc<AtomicU64>,  // Unix timestamp
    stale_threshold: Duration,
    recovery_action: RecoveryAction,
}

pub enum RecoveryAction {
    LogWarning,
    DumpDiagnostics,
    ForceRestart,
}
```

## Recovery Sequence
1. Log warning with stack traces
2. Dump diagnostic state (queue depths, lock holders)
3. If still stale after N seconds: force restart
4. Generate crash report with diagnostics

## Diagnostic Dump
When watchdog triggers:
- Thread states
- Queue depths
- Lock holder info (if available)
- Recent event log
- Memory usage

## Status Reporting
```
$ wa status --health

Watchdog:
  Main loop: healthy (last heartbeat 0.1s ago)
  DB writer: healthy (queue: 3 items)
  Ingest: healthy (lag: 15ms)
```

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Heartbeat updated each main loop iteration
- [ ] Watchdog thread monitors heartbeat
- [ ] Recovery actions trigger at configurable threshold
- [ ] Diagnostic dump provides useful context
- [ ] Crash report generated on force restart

## Testing
- Unit tests for breaker/backoff logic and state transitions.
- Integration tests simulating IO failures and recovery paths.
- Chaos harness scenarios with verbose logs and recovery assertions.

title: Environment detection: detect WezTerm, agents, config state for contextual exercises
description:
# Environment detection for tutorial

## Purpose
Detect the user's environment to provide contextual exercises and skip irrelevant steps. A user without WezTerm running shouldn't do "start watching" exercises.

## Background
Different users have different setups:
- WezTerm running vs not
- Agents present vs empty panes
- wa configured vs fresh install
- Existing DB vs first time

The tutorial should adapt to each situation.

## Implementation Details

### Environment Checks
```rust
pub struct TutorialEnvironment {
    wezterm_running: bool,
    wezterm_version: Option<String>,
    pane_count: usize,
    agent_panes: Vec<AgentInfo>, // Panes with detected agents
    wa_configured: bool,         // wa.toml exists
    db_has_data: bool,           // Segments/events exist
    shell_integration: bool,     // OSC 133 markers detected
}

impl TutorialEnvironment {
    pub async fn detect() -> Self { ... }
    
    pub fn can_run_exercise(&self, exercise: &Exercise) -> CanRun {
        match exercise.requirements {
            Requires::WeztermRunning if !self.wezterm_running => 
                CanRun::No("Start WezTerm first"),
            Requires::AgentPresent if self.agent_panes.is_empty() => 
                CanRun::Simulation("No agents detected, using simulation"),
            _ => CanRun::Yes,
        }
    }
}
```

### Exercise Requirements
Each exercise declares its requirements:
```rust
pub struct Exercise {
    id: ExerciseId,
    title: String,
    requirements: Vec<Requirement>,
    can_simulate: bool,  // True if exercise works in sandbox mode
}
```

### Adaptive Flow
1. User starts track
2. Detect environment
3. For each exercise:
   - Check requirements
   - If met: run exercise
   - If not met but can_simulate: run in sandbox
   - If not met and can't simulate: skip with explanation

## Testing
- Unit tests for each detection check
- Mock tests for different environment states
- Integration tests with real WezTerm (optional, CI skip)

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] TutorialEnvironment struct with all detection fields
- [ ] detect() function checks all conditions
- [ ] can_run_exercise() returns appropriate guidance
- [ ] Clear user messaging for skipped exercises
- [ ] Tests for all detection paths

title: Rollback visualization tests: data model, recording, CLI, undo, E2E
description:
# Task: Rollback visualization tests (audit_actions + action_undo + history + undo)

## Goal
Provide comprehensive, regression-resistant test coverage for the rollback visualization system (`wa-5em`):
- the **action history data model** (`audit_actions` + `action_undo` + `action_history` view)
- the **action recording service** (what gets recorded, when, and how it is redacted)
- the **human CLI surfaces** (`wa history`, `wa undo`) and their stable outputs
- the **undo engine semantics** (what is undoable, what happens when undo runs)

This bead is intentionally “deep” because rollback/undo is trust-critical UX: if it lies, leaks secrets, or flakes, users will stop trusting wa.

## Scope

### 1) Data model + query tests (unit/integration)
Validate the design from `wa-5em.5`:
- Schema correctness:
  - `action_undo` exists and references `audit_actions`
  - `action_history` view exists and joins correctly
  - indexes exist for common queries (`undoable`, recent actions, pane/workflow filters)

- Ordering and filtering semantics:
  - “recent actions” ordering is deterministic
  - filters by pane/workflow/action_type behave correctly

- Redaction invariants:
  - stored previews are redacted consistently with audit policy (`wa-4vx.8.3`)
  - secret-looking strings never round-trip in clear

### 2) Recording tests (unit/integration)
Cover each recording point from `wa-5em.6`:
- SendText
- WorkflowStart / WorkflowStep / WorkflowCompleted
- Pane operations (spawn/split/activate) where applicable

Assertions:
- parent/child linkage is correct for workflow steps
- undoable/undo_strategy/undo_payload are correct (and *absent* for non-undoables)
- “triggered_by” metadata is recorded (human/robot/mcp/workflow)

### 3) CLI output tests (unit + contract)
- Snapshot tests (plain mode):
  - `wa history` output is stable and contains **no ANSI escapes**
  - stable truncation rules and stable ordering

- JSON mode tests:
  - stable schema and error codes
  - redaction invariants hold

### 4) Undo engine tests (unit/integration)
- Undo success paths:
  - abort a running workflow (supported undo type)
  - mark an action as undone with timestamp + actor

- Undo not-applicable paths:
  - non-undoable action -> clear structured error + remediation hints
  - already-undone -> idempotent “no-op” outcome

### 5) E2E coverage (via standard harness)
Implement an E2E case that follows the shared E2E contract and produces excellent artifacts.

Requirements:
- Use the standard runner (`wa-4vx.10.11`) and registry (`wa-4vx.10.20`).
- Follow the harness contract (`wa-4vx.10.6`) and structured logging baseline (`wa-4vx.6.5`).
- Avoid wall-clock sleeps where possible:
  - prefer explicit wait conditions (`wa robot wait-for`, health checks, step-log / action-history queries)
  - if a bounded sleep is truly unavoidable, justify it and keep it small

**E2E scenario (deterministic intent):**
1. Start a watcher/workflow execution in a dedicated test workspace.
2. Trigger a synthetic workflow that generates a predictable action tree (workflow start + steps + at least one send).
3. Assert `wa history` contains:
   - the workflow action tree
   - at least one undoable action surfaced in `wa undo --list`
4. Run `wa undo <action-id> --yes` and verify:
   - action is marked undone
   - the underlying target (e.g., workflow) is aborted/cancelled as appropriate
5. Collect artifacts:
   - watcher logs
   - `action_history` slice/export (redacted)
   - audit slice (redacted)
   - a human-readable summary file describing what happened

## Testing
- Unit tests for:
  - schema/query invariants
  - redaction invariants
  - recording coverage per action type

- Integration tests for:
  - end-to-end action recording + history query on a temp workspace DB
  - undo success + undo not-applicable cases

- E2E tests:
  - one case registered in `./scripts/e2e_test.sh` that validates history + undo with artifacts

## Registry
- Register this case in the E2E case registry (`wa-4vx.10.20`), including prerequisites and default inclusion status.
- Ensure `./scripts/e2e_test.sh --all` includes this case (or mark non-default with justification).

## Acceptance Criteria
- Data model tests validate schema + indexes + deterministic ordering.
- Recording tests cover all relevant action types and parent/child linkage.
- `wa history` and `wa undo` outputs are stable in plain + JSON modes and never leak secrets.
- E2E case runs deterministically under the standard runner and produces actionable artifacts on failure.

title: Watch-and-notify mode: wa watch --notify-only for alert-only monitoring
description:
# Watch-and-Notify Mode: Continuous monitoring with alert delivery

## Purpose
Enable wa to run in notification-only mode, alerting on events without auto-handling.

## Use Case
Some users want to be notified of events but handle them manually:
- Learning the system behavior
- High-stakes environments requiring human review
- Debugging automation issues

## Implementation

### CLI Command
```bash
# Watch and notify on all events
$ wa watch --notify-only

# Watch and notify only on specific events
$ wa watch --notify-only --notify-filter "usage_limit,compaction"

# Watch with specific notification channels
$ wa watch --notify-only --notify-via webhook,desktop
```

### Configuration
```toml
[notifications]
# Enable watch-and-notify mode
notify_only = true

# Which events trigger notifications
notify_filter = ["*.usage_limit*", "*.compaction", "*.error"]

# Notification channels
channels = ["webhook", "desktop"]

# Throttling
min_interval_seconds = 60
max_per_hour = 30
```

### NotifyOnlyMode Implementation
```rust
pub struct NotifyOnlyWatcher {
    event_bus: EventBus,
    notifier: Notifier,
    filter: EventFilter,
    throttle: ThrottleState,
}

impl NotifyOnlyWatcher {
    pub async fn run(&mut self) -> Result<()> {
        loop {
            let event = self.event_bus.recv().await?;

            if !self.filter.matches(&event) {
                continue;
            }

            if !self.throttle.allow(&event) {
                tracing::debug!("Throttled notification for {:?}", event.rule_id);
                continue;
            }

            // Log event without handling
            tracing::info!(
                event_id = %event.id,
                rule_id = %event.rule_id,
                pane_id = %event.pane_id,
                "Event detected (notify-only mode)"
            );

            // Send notification
            self.notifier.send(Notification {
                title: format!("wa: {}", event.rule_id),
                body: event.to_notification_body(),
                severity: event.severity(),
                actions: event.suggested_actions(),
            }).await?;
        }
    }
}
```

### Notification Body Generation
```rust
impl Event {
    pub fn to_notification_body(&self) -> String {
        format!(
            "Detected: {}\nPane: {} ({})\nTime: {}\n\nSuggested action:\n  {}",
            self.rule_id,
            self.pane_id,
            self.pane_title,
            self.timestamp.format("%H:%M:%S"),
            self.suggested_action().unwrap_or("No action suggested"),
        )
    }
}
```

### Desktop Notification Example
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 🔔 wa: codex.usage_limit_reached    │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Pane 9 (codex @ /project)           │
│ Detected: 14:30:15                  │
│                                     │
│ Run: wa workflow run handle_usage.. │
│                                     │
│ [Dismiss]  [Handle]  [View Details] │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Testing
- Notify-only mode does not auto-handle events
- Notifications delivered to configured channels
- Throttling works correctly
- Filter patterns match expected events

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] wa watch --notify-only implemented
- [ ] Event filtering via --notify-filter
- [ ] Throttling prevents notification spam
- [ ] Desktop and webhook channels supported
- [ ] Notification includes suggested actions
notes: Implemented notify-only mode for wa watch: CLI flags --notify-only/--notify-filter/--notify-via, config.notifications.notify_only, and channel/filter overrides in watcher startup; notify-only disables auto-handling while leaving notifications pipeline + cooldown/dedup in place. Added config field default + tests updated. cargo fmt/check/clippy/test passed.

title: CLI command timeout hardening — kill_on_drop and orphan reaper
description:
# CLI Command Timeout Hardening — kill_on_drop and Orphan Reaper

## Goal
Add aggressive timeout enforcement and orphan process cleanup to wa CLI subprocess spawning, preventing stuck wezterm cli process accumulation.

## Background
WezTerm CLI commands can hang indefinitely due to lock contention, no socket read timeout, notification feedback loops. We observed 60+ stuck processes on production servers.

## kill_on_drop Wrapper
Modify run_cli() in wezterm.rs:
- tokio::Command with kill_on_drop(true)
- Enforce configurable timeout (default 15s)
- On timeout: child is dropped → killed → Error::CliTimeout returned

## Orphan Reaper
Periodic background task in wa watch:
- Scan for wezterm cli processes older than threshold (default 30s)
- **Linux**: pgrep + /proc/<pid>/stat for process age
- **macOS**: pgrep + ps -o etime= for process age
- Kill orphans with SIGKILL after age threshold
- Log reap report: scanned count, killed count

## Configuration
```toml
[cli]
timeout_seconds = 15
orphan_reap_interval = 60
orphan_age_seconds = 30
```

## Tests
- CLI command respects timeout (mock slow command)
- kill_on_drop cleanly terminates timed-out processes
- Orphan reaper identifies and kills old processes
- Reap report logged with correct counts
- No FD or resource leaks from killed processes
- **Test on both Linux and macOS** (process age detection differs)
- **Criterion benchmarks**: reaper scan <10ms for 1000 processes

## Acceptance criteria
- CLI commands timeout after configured seconds
- kill_on_drop ensures cleanup even on wa crash/panic
- Orphan reaper runs periodically
- Works correctly on Linux and macOS
- No resource leaks from killed processes

title: [EPIC] Event Timeline with Cross-Pane Correlation
description:
# [EPIC] Event Timeline with Cross-Pane Correlation

## Mission
Provide a **unified temporal view** of events across all panes, with correlation highlighting to show relationships between events.

## Why This Matters
When managing agent swarms, the question is often: "What happened across all my agents?"

Individual event logs are:
- Per-pane (hard to see the big picture)
- Chronologically disjoint
- Missing correlation context

A unified timeline shows:
- All events on a shared time axis
- Correlations across panes (failover triggered by usage limit)
- Patterns over time (compaction always happens 10 min in)

## How It Works

### CLI Mode
```bash
$ wa timeline --last 30m

Timeline: 2026-01-18 14:00 - 14:30 (4 panes, 12 events)

14:02:15 ─┬─ Pane 1 (codex): session.started
          │
14:05:32 ─┼─ Pane 3 (claude): session.started  
          │
14:12:01 ─┼─ Pane 1 (codex): session.compaction ──→ handled (14:12:08)
          │
14:28:03 ─┼─ Pane 1 (codex): codex.usage_limit_reached
          ├──→ workflow: handle_usage_limits (in progress)
          │
14:28:45 ─┴─ Pane 7 (codex-backup): session.started [CORRELATED: failover]

Legend: ──→ workflow action  [CORRELATED] cross-pane relationship
```

### TUI Mode
Interactive scrollable timeline with:
- Zoom in/out on time ranges
- Click events to see details
- Filter by pane, event type, severity
- Correlation lines connecting related events

### Robot Mode
```json
{
  "timeline": {
    "start": "2026-01-18T14:00:00Z",
    "end": "2026-01-18T14:30:00Z",
    "events": [...],
    "correlations": [
      {"events": [123, 456], "type": "failover", "confidence": 0.95}
    ]
  }
}
```

## Correlation Detection
Simple heuristics for v1:
- **Temporal**: Events within N seconds
- **Causal**: Usage limit → failover session start
- **Agent-related**: Same agent type, different panes
- **Workflow-related**: Events handled by same workflow run

## Key Design Decisions
- Timeline is **read-only** (query, not mutation)
- Correlations are **heuristic** (may be wrong, show confidence)
- Timeline is **bounded** (default last 1h, configurable)
- Output supports **JSON** for automation

## Testing
- Unit tests: correlation detection produces expected results
- Integration tests: timeline aggregates events correctly
- Visual tests: ASCII output renders correctly for various scenarios

## Success Criteria
- `wa timeline` shows events across all panes on unified axis
- Correlations are highlighted with relationship type
- TUI timeline is interactive and responsive
- Timeline query is fast (<100ms for typical time ranges)

## Acceptance Criteria
- Timeline aggregates events across panes with correlation markers.
- wa timeline produces a stable ASCII view.
- TUI timeline view works when enabled.
- wa-6sk.5 tests pass.

title: Timeline data model: unified event view with cross-pane aggregation
description:
# Timeline Data Model

## Purpose
Define the data structures and queries for aggregating events across panes into a unified timeline.

## Data Structures
```rust
pub struct TimelineEvent {
    pub id: EventId,
    pub timestamp: DateTime<Utc>,
    pub pane_id: PaneId,

pub struct Timeline {

    pub end: DateTime<Utc>,
    pub events: Vec<TimelineEvent>,
```
