title: [EPIC] Actionable Quick-Fix Suggestions for Events and Errors
description:
# [EPIC] Actionable Quick-Fix Suggestions

## Mission
Every detected event and every error includes an **explicit, copy-pasteable command** to fix or handle it. No ambiguity about what to do next.

## Why This Matters
When something happens—an event is detected, an error occurs—users face a "now what?" moment:
- "Which command handles this event?"
- "How do I fix this error?"
- "What are my options?"

Quick-fix suggestions eliminate this friction:
- Copy-paste the suggested command
- See alternative approaches
- Learn the correct workflow

## How It Works

### For Events
```bash
$ wa events --unhandled

Unhandled Events (2):

1. codex.usage_limit_reached (Pane 9, 2 min ago)
   Codex hit its usage limit and needs account rotation.
   
   Quick fix: wa workflow run handle_usage_limits --pane 9
   Preview:   wa workflow run handle_usage_limits --pane 9 --dry-run
   Manual:    Exit Codex (Ctrl-C), log in with different account

2. session.compaction (Pane 3, 5 min ago)
   Claude Code compacted context and may have lost project state.
   
   Quick fix: wa workflow run handle_compaction --pane 3
   Preview:   wa workflow run handle_compaction --pane 3 --dry-run
   Manual:    Ask Claude to re-read AGENTS.md and key project files
```

### For Errors
```bash
$ wa watch
Error: WezTerm CLI not found

Quick fix: brew install wezterm  # macOS
           apt install wezterm   # Ubuntu
           See: https://wezfurlong.org/wezterm/install

Then retry: wa watch
```

```bash
$ wa send --pane 99 "hello"
Error: Pane 99 not found

Available panes: 1, 3, 7, 9
Did you mean:   wa send --pane 9 "hello"  (closest match)
List all:       wa status
```

### For Policy Denials
```bash
$ wa send --pane 3 "continue"
Error: Send denied - AltScreen active

Quick fix: Exit AltScreen (close vim/less/etc.) and retry
Why:       wa why denied --pane 3
```

## Implementation Components

### 1. Event Suggestion Templates
Each rule definition includes `suggested_action`:
```rust
RuleDef {
    id: "codex.usage_limit_reached",
    suggested_workflow: Some("handle_usage_limits"),
    manual_fix: "Exit Codex (Ctrl-C), log in with different account",
    // ...
}
```

### 2. Error Remediation System
Error types carry remediation hints:
```rust
enum WaError {
    WezTermNotFound {
        remediation: vec![
            Remediation::Command("brew install wezterm"),
            Remediation::Url("https://wezfurlong.org/wezterm/install"),
        ]
    },
    // ...
}
```

### 3. Context-Aware Suggestions
Use current state to generate relevant commands:
- Typo detection ("Did you mean pane 9?")
- Available resources ("Available panes: 1, 3, 7, 9")
- Environment-specific hints (macOS vs Linux)

## Design Principles
1. **Always show the command**: Not "run the workflow" but `wa workflow run X`
2. **Copy-friendly**: Commands can be copy-pasted directly
3. **Show alternatives**: Quick fix, preview, manual
4. **Progressive detail**: Brief first, expand on request

## Testing
- Unit tests: Each rule has valid suggestion templates
- Integration tests: Suggestions are generated for known scenarios
- UX tests: Suggestions are understandable and accurate

## Success Criteria
- All unhandled events include suggested commands
- All errors include "Quick fix:" with specific steps
- Suggestions are context-aware (show available panes, etc.)
- Users can copy-paste suggestions directly

## Acceptance Criteria
- Actionable suggestions appear for common error and event types.
- Suggestions are context-aware, redacted, and non-spammy.
- Suggested actions include stable IDs and references to fixes.
- All child tasks are complete and wa-bnm.4 tests pass.

description:
# Error Remediation System

## Purpose
Make every error in wa self-documenting with specific, actionable remediation steps.

## Implementation

### Remediation Struct
```rust
pub struct Remediation {
    pub summary: String,           // One-line fix
    pub commands: Vec<RemediationCommand>,
    pub alternatives: Vec<String>,
    pub learn_more: Option<String>,
}

pub struct RemediationCommand {
    pub label: String,        // "Quick fix", "Preview", "Override"
    pub command: String,      // Actual command
    pub platform: Option<String>, // "macOS", "Linux", etc.
}
```

### Error Types with Remediation
```rust
pub enum WaError {
    WezTermNotFound(Remediation),
    PaneNotFound { pane_id: PaneId, available: Vec<PaneId>, remediation: Remediation },
    PolicyDenied { reason: PolicyReason, remediation: Remediation },
    ConfigInvalid { field: String, remediation: Remediation },
    // ...
}
```

### Platform Detection
Detect OS to provide platform-specific commands:
```
macOS: brew install wezterm
Ubuntu: apt install wezterm
Arch: pacman -S wezterm
```

## Display Format
```
Error: WezTerm CLI not found

Quick fix:
  macOS:  brew install wezterm
  Ubuntu: apt install wezterm
  Other:  https://wezfurlong.org/wezterm/install

Then retry: wa watch
```

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All WaError variants include remediation
- [ ] Platform-specific commands where relevant

- [ ] Error display includes remediation by default

title: Context-aware suggestions: typo detection, fuzzy matching, available resources
description:
# Context-Aware Suggestions

## Purpose
Use current system state to provide smart, contextual suggestions in error messages.

## Features

### 1. Typo Detection
When user specifies non-existent resource, suggest closest match:
```
$ wa send --pane 99 "hello"
Error: Pane 99 not found

Did you mean: wa send --pane 9 "hello"  (closest match)
Available:    1, 3, 7, 9
```

Uses Levenshtein distance for string matching.

### 2. Available Resources
Always show what's available when something is not found:
```
Available panes: 1 (codex), 3 (claude), 7 (local)
Available workflows: handle_compaction, handle_usage_limits
Available rules: codex.*, claude.*, core.*
```

### 3. Environment-Aware Commands
Detect environment and tailor suggestions:
- macOS: homebrew commands
- Linux: apt/dnf/pacman commands
- Container: different paths

### 4. Recent State Hints
```
$ wa send --pane 3 "continue"
Error: Pane 3 is in AltScreen (vim)

Hint: Pane 3 entered AltScreen 2 minutes ago
Wait for: vim to exit, or use a different pane
```

## Implementation
```rust
pub struct SuggestionContext {
    pub available_panes: Vec<PaneInfo>,
    pub available_workflows: Vec<String>,
    pub platform: Platform,
    pub recent_state: Vec<StateChange>,
}

pub fn suggest_closest<T>(input: &str, candidates: &[T]) -> Option<T>;
pub fn format_available(items: &[T]) -> String;
```

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Typo suggestions for pane IDs
- [ ] Available resources shown on not-found errors
- [ ] Platform-specific commands detected automatically
- [ ] Recent state provides temporal context

## Testing
- Unit tests for template rendering and suggested_action interpolation.
- Integration tests: fixture errors/events produce actionable suggestions.
- E2E: extend an events/error scenario to assert suggestions and rule-id logs.

title: Custom workflows: YAML/TOML definitions with step sequences
description:
# Custom workflows

## Purpose
Allow users to define custom workflows in YAML/TOML without writing Rust code.

## Workflow Definition Format
```yaml
# ~/.config/wa/workflows/my_custom_workflow.yaml
name: my_custom_workflow
description: "Handle our custom agent's restart prompt"
triggers:
  - event_type: "my-org.restart_prompt"
    agent_types: ["custom-agent"]

steps:
  - name: wait_for_stable
    action: wait
    condition:
      type: pane_idle
      timeout: 5s
  
  - name: send_restart_command
    action: send_text
    text: "/restart\n"
    policy: require_approval  # or allow, deny
  
  - name: verify_restart
    action: wait
    condition:
      type: pattern
      pattern: "Agent restarted successfully"
      timeout: 30s

on_failure:
  action: notify
  message: "Custom workflow failed at step: ${failed_step}"
```

## Step Actions
```yaml
# Available actions
actions:
  - send_text      # Send keystrokes to pane
  - wait           # Wait for condition
  - notify         # Send notification
  - log            # Write to audit log
  - abort          # Stop workflow
  - conditional    # If/else branching
  - loop           # Repeat steps
```

## Implementation
```rust
pub struct YamlWorkflow {
    name: String,
    description: String,
    triggers: Vec<WorkflowTrigger>,
    steps: Vec<WorkflowStep>,
    on_failure: Option<FailureHandler>,
}

impl Workflow for YamlWorkflow {
    async fn execute(&self, ctx: &mut WorkflowContext) -> Result<WorkflowResult> {
        for step in &self.steps {
            match self.execute_step(step, ctx).await {
                Ok(StepResult::Continue) => continue,
                Ok(StepResult::Abort) => break,
                Err(e) => {
                    if let Some(handler) = &self.on_failure {
                        handler.execute(ctx, &e).await?;
                    }
                    return Err(e);
                }
            }
        }
        Ok(WorkflowResult::Success)
    }
}
```

## Testing
- Unit tests for YAML parsing
- Step action tests
- Conditional and loop tests
- Failure handling tests

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] YAML format supports all required actions
- [ ] Workflows load from user directory
- [ ] Steps execute in sequence
- [ ] Conditions work correctly
- [ ] Failure handlers execute
- [ ] Documentation covers workflow authoring
- [ ] Tests cover all step types

title: [EPIC] asupersync Migration in FrankenTerm Crates — Replace smol/async-io/tokio
description:
# [EPIC] asupersync Migration in FrankenTerm Crates

## Why
FrankenTerm crates currently use smol (promise, mux, config) and async-io (async_ossl, wezterm-uds) for async. The project-wide strategy is to replace ALL async runtimes with asupersync (wa-e34d9). This epic covers the FrankenTerm-specific crate migrations.

## Context
- smol is used in: promise (core), mux (spawning), config (async config reload), codec (async PDU I/O)
- async-io is used in: async_ossl (OpenSSL async wrapper), wezterm-uds (Unix domain sockets)
- wezterm-ssh uses tokio via libssh2-sys — this is the hardest migration since libssh2 is C
- asupersync provides: Cx (capability context), structured concurrency, backpressure, cancellation

## Migration order
1. promise crate (foundation — other crates depend on it)
2. codec crate (PDU I/O — used by mux)
3. async_ossl + wezterm-uds (I/O primitives)
4. config crate (async config reload)
5. mux crate (spawning, domain management)
6. wezterm-ssh (hardest — C library async integration)

## Depends on
- wa-e34d9: asupersync must be ready (foundation + Cx infrastructure)
- wa-2umk2: FrankenTerm must be in-tree (we're modifying these crates)

## Strategy: feature-flagged dual-runtime
Like the Lua strategy, use feature flags during migration:
- `async-smol` (default initially): existing smol code
- `async-asupersync`: new asupersync code
- Once all crates migrated and tested, flip default and eventually remove smol

# Replace smol with asupersync in FrankenTerm promise crate

## Why
The promise crate (frankenterm/promise/) is the async foundation for all FrankenTerm crates. It provides `SpawnFunc`, `Promise<T>`, and async task spawning. Currently uses smol's block_on and spawn. Must be migrated first because mux, config, and codec depend on it.

## Current state
- frankenterm/promise/Cargo.toml: depends on smol
- frankenterm/promise/src/lib.rs: uses smol::block_on, smol::spawn
- frankenterm/promise/src/spawn.rs: SpawnFunc wraps smol executor

## What to change
1. Replace `smol::block_on` with `asupersync::block_on` (or Cx-based equivalent)
2. Replace `smol::spawn` with asupersync structured concurrency
3. Replace `smol::Timer` with asupersync timer
4. Feature flag: `async-smol` (default) vs `async-asupersync`
5. Both paths must produce identical behavior

## Key consideration
The promise crate's API must remain stable — it's used by every other FrankenTerm crate. The migration is internal implementation, not API change.

## Testing
- All existing promise tests pass with both feature flags
- Promise resolution works correctly with asupersync executor
- Cancellation behavior is preserved
- No leaked tasks after scope exit

## Test framework requirements

### LabRuntime DPOR — concurrent promise resolution
Use LabRuntime with DPOR exploration to verify:
- Concurrent resolution of multiple promises never produces lost wakeups
- Promise::poll from multiple threads is linearizable (only one thread sees Ready)
- Cancellation of a promise while another thread resolves it never panics or leaks
- SpawnFunc task completion is visible to all waiters in bounded time

### criterion benchmarks — promise creation/resolution
Benchmark with criterion:
- Promise<T> creation time (target: <100ns per promise)
- Promise resolution (set value + wake) latency (target: <100ns)
- SpawnFunc overhead vs raw executor spawn (target: <2x overhead)
- Throughput: promises created and resolved per second (target: >10M/sec)

### proptest — promise state machine transitions
Use proptest to generate arbitrary sequences of promise operations (create, poll, resolve, cancel, drop) and verify:
- A promise is resolved at most once (no double-resolution)
- Polling a resolved promise always returns Ready with the correct value
- Dropping a promise before resolution does not leak the pending task
- State transitions follow the expected FSM: Pending -> {Resolved, Cancelled}

description:
# Replace async-io in async_ossl and wezterm-uds

## Why
These two crates provide async I/O primitives used by the mux and SSH systems:
- async_ossl: Async OpenSSL wrapper (TLS for mux connections)
- wezterm-uds: Async Unix domain socket handling

## Current state
- async_ossl/src/lib.rs: Uses async-io for polling OpenSSL BIO
- wezterm-uds/src/lib.rs: Uses async-io for Unix socket polling

## What to change
1. Replace async-io polling with asupersync I/O polling (Cx-based)
2. OpenSSL BIO integration: map SSL_read/SSL_write to asupersync futures
3. Unix socket: map connect/accept/read/write to asupersync
4. Feature flag both crates: `async-io` vs `async-asupersync`

## Key consideration
These crates deal with raw file descriptors and system calls. The asupersync I/O reactor must support registering arbitrary FDs for read/write readiness, similar to what async-io provides via Async<T>.

## macOS platform note
On macOS, the I/O notification backend must use **kqueue** instead of Linux's epoll. The asupersync I/O reactor should abstract over this via a platform-specific poller:
- Linux: epoll_create1 / epoll_ctl / epoll_wait
- macOS/BSD: kqueue / kevent
- Both async_ossl and wezterm-uds must be tested on macOS to ensure kqueue-based FD registration works correctly for OpenSSL BIOs and Unix domain sockets
- Note: macOS Unix domain socket paths are limited to 104 bytes (vs 108 on Linux)

## Testing
- TLS handshake works with asupersync
- Unix socket connection and data transfer works
- Verify no FD leaks after connection close
- Test with real mux server connection

## Test framework requirements

### criterion benchmarks — I/O throughput
Benchmark with criterion:
- TLS handshake latency with asupersync vs async-io baseline (target: <5ms)
- Unix domain socket throughput (target: >1GB/s for local IPC)
- OpenSSL BIO read/write throughput through async wrapper (target: >500MB/s)
- FD registration/deregistration overhead in the I/O reactor

### LabRuntime DPOR — concurrent I/O operations
Use LabRuntime with DPOR exploration to verify:
- Concurrent TLS connections never deadlock on BIO polling
- Concurrent Unix socket accept + read/write is linearizable
- FD close during pending read/write produces clean errors, no use-after-close
- Multiple tasks sharing an I/O reactor do not starve each other

title: Extension sandboxing: WASM or Lua runtime for safe custom code execution
description:
# Extension Sandboxing

## Purpose
Run custom extension code safely without risking system security.

## Options Evaluated

### 1. WASM (Recommended)
- Pros: Strong isolation, multi-language, proven
- Cons: Larger binary, more complex
- Libraries: wasmtime, wasmer

### 2. Lua
- Pros: Simple, fast, battle-tested (Neovim/WezTerm)
- Cons: Single language, needs careful sandboxing
- Libraries: rlua, mlua

## Recommendation: WASM via wasmtime
- Better isolation guarantees
- Supports Rust, Go, C, AssemblyScript
- WASI for controlled system access

## Sandbox Capabilities
```rust
pub struct ExtensionSandbox {
    engine: wasmtime::Engine,
    linker: wasmtime::Linker<SandboxState>,
    capabilities: SandboxCapabilities,
}

pub struct SandboxCapabilities {
    pub read_pane_output: bool,
    pub send_notifications: bool,
    pub http_requests: bool,
    pub file_access: FileAccessScope,
}
```

## Capability Levels
- Level 1: Read-only (patterns only)
- Level 2: Read + notify (most workflows)
- Level 3: Read + notify + HTTP (integrations)
- Level 4: Full (admin extensions)

## Extension Manifest
```toml
[extension]
name = "my-patterns"
capabilities = ["read_pane_output"]
```

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] WASM runtime integrated
- [ ] Capability-based permissions
- [ ] Extensions cannot access system without permission
- [ ] Untrusted extension cannot crash wa

## Testing
- Unit tests for sandbox policy enforcement and resource limits.
- Integration tests running a restricted extension in a sandbox.
- Security checks: verify no filesystem/network escape.

title: E2E script: workspace isolation (no cross-project DB leakage; --workspace honored)
description:
# Task: E2E script — workspace isolation

## Goal
Prove that wa honors workspace scoping and does not leak data across projects.

This is a critical UX property:
- users run multiple projects in parallel
- agents should not read/write the wrong DB
- debugging depends on knowing which workspace you are looking at

## Scenario
- Spawn a dummy pane that prints a unique token: WORKSPACE_TOKEN.

Steps
1) Start wa watch with --workspace <A>.
2) Wait until WORKSPACE_TOKEN is persisted (wa robot search --workspace <A>).
3) Run wa robot search --workspace <B> for WORKSPACE_TOKEN.

Assertions
- In workspace A: the token is found.
- In workspace B: the token is NOT found.

Optional extension
- Start wa watch in workspace B and ensure it creates a distinct DB.

## Artifacts
- effective config for both workspaces
- wa watch logs
- wa robot search outputs for A and B

## Registry
- Register this case in the E2E case registry (`wa-4vx.10.20`), including prerequisites and default inclusion status.
- Ensure `./scripts/e2e_test.sh --all` includes this case (or mark non-default with justification).

## Logging
- Follow the standard E2E harness logging contract (`wa-4vx.10.6`) and runner (`wa-4vx.10.11`).
- Emit per-step start/end markers with timestamps + durations.
- Include case name and pane ids in every log line.
- Redact secrets (device codes, tokens) in logs and artifacts.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Test is deterministic.
- Failures make it obvious whether the bug is:
  - workspace resolution
  - DB path derivation
  - CLI flag propagation


## Testing
- Meta-validation:
  - Assert the two workspaces produce distinct DB/log paths (not just search behavior).
  - Add a control assertion that workspace B can find a different token once it has ingested something.

- Artifact validation:
  - Artifacts must include the derived paths (workspace root, db path, log path) to make mis-scoping diagnosable.

# Phase 2: Workflow Engine & Automation

## Overview
This epic builds the workflow automation system that responds to detected patterns. The workflow engine is what makes wa "active" rather than just a passive monitor - it can take corrective actions when agents hit limits, experience compaction, need authentication, etc.

## Strategic Importance
The workflow system transforms wa from a "monitoring tool" into an "automation platform". This is where the real value emerges:
- Automatic context recovery after compaction
- Automatic account rotation on usage limits
- Automatic authentication renewal
- Foundation for more sophisticated multi-agent coordination

## Key Components

### 1. Workflow Engine Architecture
- Trait-based workflow definition: \`Workflow\` trait with name, description, handles, steps, execute_step
- Step results: Continue, Done, Retry, Abort, WaitFor
- WaitCondition: Pattern, PaneIdle, External
- Per-pane workflow locking (prevent conflicting workflows)
- Idempotent, recoverable, audited execution

### 2. Handle Usage Limits Workflow (Codex First)
Steps:
1. Exit current session gracefully (Ctrl-C twice for Codex)
2. Parse session info for resume (session ID, token usage)
3. Select next available account
4. Perform account authentication
5. Resume previous session
6. Send continue prompt

This is the most complex workflow and proves out the architecture.

### 3. Handle Compaction Workflow
Steps:
1. Wait for compaction to complete (stabilization window)
2. Send agent-specific context refresh prompt
   - Claude Code: "Reread AGENTS.md so it's still fresh in your mind."
   - Codex: "Please re-read AGENTS.md and any key project context files."
   - Gemini: "Please re-examine AGENTS.md and project context."

### 4. Browser Automation Skeleton
- Playwright integration structure
- Browser profile persistence
- OpenAI device auth flow (skeleton)
- Anthropic OAuth flow (skeleton)
- Google auth flow (skeleton)
- Semi-automated fallback (open browser for human when automation fails)

### 5. CAUT Integration
- Shell out to \`caut\` for usage tracking
- get_usage(service) - current usage for OpenAI/Anthropic/Google
- refresh_usage(service) - refresh from APIs
- Account selection logic based on percent_remaining

## Workflow Design Constraints
Every workflow must be:
- **Idempotent**: Re-running doesn't make a mess
- **Recoverable**: Can resume after a crash
- **Audited**: Every step recorded (what was observed, what was sent)
- **Guarded**: Each step validates state before action

## Workflow Execution Model
Each step follows: Observe → Decide → Act → Verify

Step can return:
- \`Continue\` - proceed to next step
- \`WaitFor(condition)\` - pause until condition met
- \`Retry(after)\` - retry same step after delay
- \`Abort(reason)\` - stop workflow with error
- \`Done(result)\` - workflow completed successfully

## Data-Driven Workflow Descriptors
In addition to compiled Rust workflows, support YAML/TOML descriptors for simple prompt injection sequences:

\`\`\`yaml
# ~/.config/wa/workflows/custom_compaction.yaml
name: custom_compaction_prompt
trigger:
  event: session.compaction
  agent: claude_code
steps:
  - wait_stable: 2s
  - send: |
      Please re-read AGENTS.md and the project's README.md.
  - wait_for: "❯"
\`\`\`

## Success Criteria
- [ ] Workflow engine can execute multi-step workflows
- [ ] handle_compaction workflow works end-to-end for Claude Code
- [ ] handle_usage_limits workflow works end-to-end for Codex (at least skeleton)
- [ ] Browser automation structure is in place (can be extended in Phase 3)
- [ ] CAUT integration returns account usage data
- [ ] Workflows are audited and recoverable

## Dependencies
- Depends on Phase 1 (Foundation) - needs pattern engine, storage, watcher

## Technical Notes

### Why Codex First for Usage Limits?
- Codex has the clearest device auth flow
- Resume mechanism is well-documented
- Good test case for the complexity

### Semi-Automated Browser Auth
If Playwright can't complete auth (MFA, CAPTCHA, password):
1. Open non-headless browser
2. Request human to complete auth
3. Persist browser profile for future sessions
4. Notify when auth complete

This provides graceful degradation.

title: User pattern packs: load custom rules from ~/.config/wa/patterns/
description:
# User pattern packs

## Purpose
Allow users to define custom pattern packs that load alongside built-in packs.

## User Pack Location
```
~/.config/wa/patterns/
├── my-org-patterns/
│   ├── pack.toml        # Pack metadata
│   └── rules.toml       # Rule definitions
└── custom-agent/
    ├── pack.toml
    └── rules.toml
```

## Pack Format
```toml
# pack.toml
[pack]
name = "my-org-patterns"
version = "1.0.0"
description = "Custom patterns for internal agents"
extends = "core.codex"  # Optional: inherit from built-in

# rules.toml
[[rules]]
id = "my-org.custom_warning"
name = "Custom Warning Pattern"
pattern = "\\[INTERNAL\\] Warning: (.+)"
severity = "warning"
extract = { message = "$1" }
agent_types = ["codex", "custom-agent"]
```

## Loading Priority
1. Built-in packs (highest priority)
2. User packs in order found
3. Workspace-local packs (.wa/patterns/)

For conflicts, later packs override earlier ones unless `extends` is used.

## Implementation
```rust
pub fn load_all_packs(config: &Config) -> Result<Vec<PatternPack>> {
    let mut packs = vec![];
    
    // Load built-in
    packs.extend(load_builtin_packs()?);
    
    // Load user packs
    let user_dir = config.patterns_dir();
    if user_dir.exists() {
        for entry in fs::read_dir(user_dir)? {
            let pack = PatternPack::load(entry?.path())?;
            packs.push(pack);
        }
    }
    
    // Load workspace packs
    if let Some(workspace_dir) = config.workspace_patterns_dir() {
        // Similar loading
    }
    
    // Resolve inheritance and conflicts
    resolve_pack_inheritance(&mut packs)?;
    
    Ok(packs)
}
```

## Validation
User packs are validated on load:
- Valid TOML syntax
- Required fields present
- Regex patterns compile
- No duplicate rule IDs (within pack)

## Testing
- Unit tests for pack loading
- Tests for inheritance resolution
- Tests for conflict handling
- Tests for invalid pack rejection

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] User packs load from ~/.config/wa/patterns/
- [ ] Pack format documented
- [ ] Inheritance (extends) works
- [ ] Conflict resolution is predictable
- [ ] Invalid packs rejected with clear errors
- [ ] Tests cover all scenarios

title: [Human command] wa undo (undo supported actions with confirmation)
description:
# Task: [Human command] `wa undo` (undo supported actions with confirmation)

## Goal
Provide a safe, human‑friendly CLI for undoing **supported** action types, using the undo engine from wa‑5em.

## Command Surface
- `wa undo --list` (list undoable actions)
- `wa undo <action-id>` (undo specific action)
- `wa undo --all-in-workflow <workflow_id>` (bulk undo)
- `--yes` to skip confirmation
- `--format json|plain` for automation

## Safety
- Show explicit summary before undo:
  - action type, pane/workflow, time, undoability reason
- Require confirmation unless `--yes`.
- If not undoable, return structured error with manual guidance.

## Output
- TTY: rich panel with action summary and result
- Non‑TTY: structured JSON with stable codes

## Testing
- Unit/integration tests:
  - list output includes undoable actions only
  - undo success path updates action log
  - undo not‑applicable returns clear error
- E2E:
  - extend rollback visualization E2E (`wa-5em.9`) to call `wa undo` and verify state + logs

## Acceptance Criteria
- `wa undo` is safe by default (confirmation required).
- Structured output includes action ids + undo results.
- Errors include remediation hints when undo is not applicable.
notes: 2026-02-08: Claimed after bd-5em.8 closure. Implementing wa undo CLI surface using new wa-core undo executor (list/single-action/workflow-scope, confirmation, plain/json outputs).

title: Criterion benchmarks + budgets (pattern detect, delta extraction, FTS query)
description:
# Task: Benchmarks + budgets

## Goal
Prevent performance regressions on hot paths.

This is the “performance test suite” complement to unit/E2E tests: it ensures wa stays fast enough to run continuously.

## Bench targets (must exist)
- Overlap/delta extraction (hot ingest path)
- Pattern engine quick reject (typical no-match)
- Pattern detection on “typical pane output”
- FTS query latency for common queries on representative DB size
- Watcher loop overhead when idle (per-pane check cost)

## Initial budgets (PLAN §13.4 + Appendix G.7)
These are v0 targets; we can tune later, but they must be explicitly recorded so regressions are real failures, not vibes.

- Quick reject no-match: **< 1µs** for typical non-matching text.
- Pattern detection (typical corpus): **p50 < 1ms**, **p99 < 5ms**.
- FTS query common patterns (DB ~100k captures):
  - **p50 < 10ms**, **p99 < 50ms** (hard cap: < 50ms for common queries).
- Watcher loop overhead (idle): **< 100µs per pane check**.

Notes:
- Budgets should be reported with machine metadata (OS/CPU/rustc/features).
- CI should enforce budgets in a non-flaky way (relative threshold vs baseline, or dedicated perf runners).

## CI integration
- Local-only initially is acceptable if CI is too noisy, but the harness must produce machine-readable artifacts.
- Once stable, integrate into CI (tracked by `wa-nu4.3.4.4`) with:
  - clear pass/fail thresholds
  - artifact upload of benchmark results on failure

## Artifacts & logging
Bench runs must produce debuggable artifacts:
- raw Criterion JSON output
- a short summary (top regressions, top slowest benches)
- build/machine metadata:
  - OS, CPU model, rustc version, enabled features
  - git commit hash when available

## Testing
- Bench harness self-check:
  - Add a small “sanity bench” guaranteed to run so the harness failing to execute is caught early.

- Budget enforcement tests:
  - If budget checks are implemented as code, include a unit test that feeds a fake benchmark JSON and asserts:
    - regression triggers failure
    - outputs include which benchmark regressed and by how much

## Acceptance Criteria
- Bench suite runs locally and produces a baseline.
- Budgets above are documented and emitted in summaries.
- CI enforcement can come later if early CI is too noisy, but the artifacts/logging are in place.
notes: Progress (2026-01-21): added bench metadata/budget emission (JSONL) via benches/bench_common.rs; each bench now emits budgets + machine metadata and writes target/criterion/wa-bench-meta.jsonl.

title: Design MuxSnapshot schema for full mux state serialization
description:
## Goal
Design and implement the core data structures that represent a complete, serializable snapshot of the WezTerm mux server state. This is the foundational data model for the entire session persistence feature.

## Background & Motivation
When the wezterm-mux-server process dies or needs to be restarted (e.g., due to memory leaks, protocol corruption after extended runtime, or upgrades), ALL running processes in all panes are killed because the mux server owns the PTY file descriptors. The kernel sends SIGHUP to all child processes. There is currently no way to save and restore session state across restarts.

WezTerm's Lua API provides building blocks (get_lines_as_escapes, inject_output, process/directory introspection, mux hierarchy enumeration) but no native serialization. The resurrect.wezterm plugin does this via Lua but is approximate and limited.

wa (wezterm_automata) already has: SQLite storage with WAL mode, pane tracking (PaneRecord), delta extraction, agent session correlation (AgentSessionRecord), and a vendored mux client. We can leverage all of this.

## Design Requirements
1. Define MuxSnapshot struct containing:
   - snapshot_id: String (UUID)
   - created_at: i64 (epoch ms)
   - mux_server_pid: Option<u32>
   - wezterm_version: String
   - wa_version: String
   - windows: Vec<WindowSnapshot>
   - workspaces: Vec<WorkspaceSnapshot>
   - active_workspace: Option<String>

2. Define WindowSnapshot containing:
   - window_id: u64
   - workspace: String
   - title: Option<String>
   - tabs: Vec<TabSnapshot>
   - active_tab_index: usize

3. Define TabSnapshot containing:
   - tab_id: u64
   - title: Option<String>
   - pane_tree: PaneNode (recursive tree for splits)
   - active_pane_id: u64

4. Define PaneNode enum:
   - Leaf(PaneSnapshot) for single panes
   - VSplit { left: Box<PaneNode>, right: Box<PaneNode>, ratio: f64 } for vertical splits
   - HSplit { top: Box<PaneNode>, bottom: Box<PaneNode>, ratio: f64 } for horizontal splits

5. Define PaneSnapshot containing:
   - pane_id: u64
   - domain: String
   - title: Option<String>
   - cwd: Option<String> (working directory)
   - foreground_process: Option<ProcessInfo>
   - dimensions: PaneDimensions (rows, cols, scrollback_rows)
   - cursor_position: Option<CursorPosition>
   - is_alt_screen: bool
   - user_vars: HashMap<String, String>
   - scrollback_hash: Option<String> (hash of scrollback content, for dedup)
   - agent_session: Option<AgentSessionRef> (link to wa's agent session tracking)

6. Define ProcessInfo:
   - name: String
   - argv: Option<Vec<String>>
   - pid: Option<u32>
   - is_whitelisted_for_restore: bool

7. Define AgentSessionRef:
   - agent_type: String (claude_code, codex, gemini)
   - session_id: Option<String>
   - wa_agent_session_id: Option<i64>

8. All structs must derive Serialize, Deserialize, Clone, Debug
9. All structs must be roundtrip-safe through JSON and potentially TOON format
10. Include schema version field for forward compatibility

## Implementation Location
New file: crates/wa-core/src/snapshot_schema.rs
Re-export from crates/wa-core/src/lib.rs

## Acceptance Criteria
- All structs compile and pass serde roundtrip tests
- Schema can represent arbitrary pane split topologies via recursive PaneNode
- JSON serialization produces human-readable output
- Schema version is included for migration support
- Integration with existing PaneRecord and AgentSessionRecord types

## Property Testing Requirements

### Proptest
Add `tests/proptest_snapshot_schema.rs`:
- **schema_versioning_compatibility**: For any MuxSnapshot with schema_version N (proptest generates versions 1..=current), assert that a deserializer for version current can read it (forward compatibility). For any MuxSnapshot with schema_version current, assert that fields not present in version N-1 are handled gracefully with defaults (backward compatibility). This ensures that snapshots created by older wa versions can always be read by newer wa versions.
- **pane_node_roundtrip**: For any arbitrary PaneNode tree (proptest generates random trees with 1-50 leaves), assert JSON roundtrip produces identical trees.
- **snapshot_completeness**: For any arbitrary MuxSnapshot (proptest generates), assert that every pane_id referenced in the PaneNode trees appears exactly once (no orphans, no duplicates).
- **optional_fields_resilience**: For any MuxSnapshot, randomly set optional fields to None (proptest generates a bitmask), serialize to JSON, deserialize, and assert all non-optional fields survive and optional fields are correctly None.

## Cross-References
- **wa-29k1** (SnapshotEngine orchestrator): wa-29k1 is the primary consumer of the MuxSnapshot schema. It populates the structs defined here during the capture pipeline. Any schema changes must be coordinated with the SnapshotEngine's capture logic.
- **bd-nz6** (SQLite tables for snapshot storage): wa-nz6 stores MuxSnapshot as JSON in the snapshot_json column. The schema must remain JSON-serializable, and any schema version bumps must be accompanied by migration logic in bd-nz6's storage layer. The snapshot_size_bytes column in wa-nz6 depends on the serialized size of the structs defined here.

title: Implement cass CLI wrapper (query/search JSON, timeouts, errors)
description:
# Task: Implement cass CLI wrapper

## Goal
Treat `cass` (coding_agent_session_search) as an external "truth source" and expose a small internal API for:
- querying a known session id
- searching sessions by path/agent
- extracting useful summary fields (token counts, timestamps)

## Why
Claude Code may not expose stable terminal session identifiers, and token accounting is frequently only available out-of-band.
`cass` already has domain logic and history storage; wa should reuse it rather than reinvent it.

## Requirements
- Robust process execution:
  - handle `cass` not installed (actionable error)
  - handle non-zero exit codes
  - enforce timeouts (avoid hanging workflows)
- JSON parsing with serde:
  - version-tolerant (ignore unknown fields)
  - clear error mapping for invalid JSON
- Safety:
  - never log full transcripts by default
  - avoid storing raw message content unless explicitly requested

## Deliverables
- `cass::query(session_id)` and `cass::search(path, agent)` wrappers.
- Data models for the JSON we rely on.
- Error enum that distinguishes: missing tool / timeout / parse error / cass returned no match.

## Testing
- Covered by `wa-nu4.2.4.4` (fixtures + missing-tool + ambiguity cases).

## Acceptance Criteria
- Given a captured JSON fixture, parsing succeeds.
- When `cass` binary is missing, wa produces a clear error + next steps.

title: Define Outcome<T,E> error handling strategy
description:
# Define Outcome<T,E> error handling strategy

## Background
Asupersync uses Outcome<T,E> instead of Result<T,E>. Outcome has four variants:
- Ok(T) — success
- Err(E) — application error
- Cancelled(CancelReason) — task was cancelled (user, timeout, fail-fast, race-loss, parent, shutdown)
- Panicked(PanicPayload) — task panicked

The severity lattice for composition: Ok < Err < Cancelled < Panicked (worst wins in joins).

## What needs to happen
1. Decide whether to adopt Outcome throughout the codebase or create adapter layers
2. If adapting: create From<Outcome<T,E>> for Result<T,E> and vice versa
3. If adopting: plan the gradual migration of return types
4. Handle the ? operator — Outcome implements Try trait differently than Result

## Recommendation
Start with adapter layer approach:
- Internal async code uses Outcome natively
- Public API boundaries convert to/from Result
- This minimizes blast radius while gaining cancel-correctness internally

## Key patterns to establish
- How to convert existing anyhow::Result → Outcome
- How to handle Cancelled at module boundaries
- How to propagate CancelReason through the call stack
- How to use cx.checkpoint()? for explicit cancellation points

## Acceptance criteria
- Error handling strategy document/module with conversion utilities
- Outcome adapter traits implemented
- Example migration of one simple async function showing the pattern

## Property-based testing
- **Proptest for Outcome composition laws**: Verify that Outcome's monadic operations obey algebraic laws:
  - `map`: identity law (`outcome.map(|x| x) == outcome`), composition law (`outcome.map(f).map(g) == outcome.map(|x| g(f(x)))`)
  - `and_then`: left identity, right identity, associativity
  - `or_else`: error recovery ordering, Cancelled vs Err priority respects severity lattice
  - Use `proptest!` with `prop::sample::Index` to generate arbitrary Outcome variants and verify laws hold across all variant combinations.

## Benchmark requirements
- **Criterion benchmarks for Outcome vs Result overhead**: Measure that Outcome operations (map, and_then, or_else, ?) have zero-cost overhead compared to equivalent Result operations. Add `benches/outcome_vs_result.rs` comparing: construction, pattern matching, chaining 10 operations, and error propagation with ?. Target: identical codegen (verify with `--emit=asm` if needed).
close_reason: Implemented: outcome adapter layer, tests, and benchmarks already present in-tree

title: Integrate streaming tailers: prefer subscription when available; fallback to polling
description:
# Task: Integrate streaming tailers

## Goal
Teach the ingest system to choose between:
- polling tailers (CLI get-text)
- streaming tailers (vendored subscribe)

The objective is reduced CPU/latency without changing downstream semantics.

## Capability detection
At runtime, decide per workspace/domain:
- if subscription is supported and healthy → use streaming
- otherwise → use polling

The decision should be:
- deterministic
- observable in logs/health snapshot

## Semantics must match polling mode
Regardless of tailer type:
- segments are written with seq
- gaps are emitted on discontinuity
- pattern detection and workflows behave the same

## Failure & fallback behavior
- If streaming connection drops:
  - record a diagnostic event
  - fall back to polling with backoff

- If polling is too slow or misses data:
  - record explicit GAP events (existing invariant)

## Performance expectations

title: Sync exported DB snapshots (immutable artifacts, versioned filenames)
description:
# Task: Sync exported DB snapshots (immutable artifacts)

## Goal
Make it easy to move **database snapshots** between machines for debugging or continuity, without ever touching the live DB file.

## Safety model
- Only sync snapshots created via `wa export` / `wa diag bundle` (explicit export paths).
- Never sync the live DB file or WAL/SHM.
- Treat snapshots as immutable artifacts:
  - versioned filenames
  - no in-place overwrite
  - optional compression (if/when supported by export)

## Naming & versioning
- Filenames should encode enough metadata to be self-describing:
  - wa version
  - created timestamp (UTC)
  - workspace key (hashed/short)
  - optional host

## Push/pull behavior
- `push` uploads snapshot(s) to the target under an artifacts directory.
- `pull` downloads snapshots and places them under a local artifacts directory.
- Default behavior is additive (no overwrites).

## UX expectations
- Plans should clearly distinguish:
  - “syncing snapshots” (safe)
  - “syncing live DB” (forbidden; should never appear)

## Testing
- Covered by `wa-nu4.3.8.5` (sync tests):
  - live DB paths are rejected
  - snapshot filenames are stable and never overwritten
  - push/pull round-trips via local-directory backend

## Acceptance Criteria
- `wa sync push` can push an exported snapshot to a target without overwriting existing files.
- `wa sync pull` can pull the same snapshot back and preserves the filename.
- Attempts to sync live DB paths are rejected by the planner.

title: Phase 4: Fix clippy errors in FrankenTerm crates
description:
Fix 8 clippy deny-by-default errors across FrankenTerm crates to achieve zero clippy errors workspace-wide.

## Fixes applied
1. wezterm-dynamic/src/error.rs: for-return → .into_iter().next() (never_loop)
2. wezterm-ssh/src/host.rs: for-break → .split_whitespace().next() (never_loop)
3. wezterm-ssh/src/sessioninner.rs: for-break → .split_whitespace().next() (never_loop)
4. config/src/lua.rs (2x): for-return → .sequence_values().next() (never_loop)
5. mux/src/tab.rs: for-return → .into_iter().next() (never_loop)
6. termwiz/src/caps/probed.rs (2x): .read() → .read_exact() (unused_io_amount)
7. termwiz/src/terminal/unix.rs: .write() → .write_all() (unused_io_amount)
8. wezterm-input-types/src/lib.rs: n >= 13 && n <= 35 → (13..=35).contains(&n) (manual_range_contains)
9. term/src/lib.rs: Added #![allow(clippy::unused_io_amount)] for 8 intentional write-discard patterns

## Why these aren't just warnings
FrankenTerm crates don't inherit workspace lints (no [lints] workspace = true). These are clippy's own deny-by-default lints (never_loop, unused_io_amount) which are treated as errors by cargo clippy.

# [EPIC] Smart Environment Detection

## Mission
Automatically detect the user's environment and configure wa optimally, reducing setup friction.

## Why This Matters
Users struggle with configuration:
- "Which settings do I need?"
- "Why isn't it detecting my agents?"
- "What's the right poll interval?"

Smart detection provides:
- **Zero-config start**: Works out of the box
- **Optimal defaults**: Tuned for detected environment
- **Guided setup**: Suggests improvements

### Environment Detection
- WezTerm version and capabilities
- Shell type (bash, zsh, fish)
- OSC 133 support
- Agent presence and types
- Remote panes (SSH)
- System resources (CPU, RAM)

### Auto-configuration

- Pattern packs based on detected agents
- Storage paths based on OS conventions
- Safety defaults based on environment

```rust
pub struct DetectedEnvironment {

    osc_133_support: bool,
    agents: Vec<DetectedAgent>,
    remotes: Vec<RemoteHost>,
    system: SystemInfo,
}
```

### CLI Integration
- `wa doctor` shows detection results
- `wa setup` uses detection for suggestions
- Config shows effective settings with sources

## Success Criteria
- New users need no configuration to start
- Detection is accurate for common setups
- Suggestions improve user experience

```rust
pub struct SetupWizard {
    env: DetectedEnvironment,
    term: Terminal,
}

impl SetupWizard {
    pub async fn run(&mut self) -> Result<Config> {
        self.show_welcome().await?;
        self.show_detection().await?;
        
        let config = match self.prompt_config_choice().await? {
            Choice::Accept => self.auto_config(),
            Choice::Customize => self.run_customization().await?,

        }
        
        self.save_config(&config).await?;
        self.show_complete().await?;
        
        Ok(config)
    }
}
```

# [EPIC] E2E Test Harness

## Mission
Provide a **comprehensive E2E testing framework** with scripted scenarios, detailed logging, and CI integration that validates wa works correctly in real-world conditions.

## Why This Matters
Unit tests validate components in isolation. E2E tests validate **the whole system works together**:
- WezTerm integration actually works
- Patterns detect real agent output
- Workflows execute correctly end-to-end
- Error recovery handles real failures

Without E2E tests, we ship bugs that only manifest in production.

## E2E Test Architecture

### Test Harness
```
tests/e2e/
├── harness/
│   ├── mod.rs           # Test harness library
│   ├── fixtures.rs      # Test fixtures and setup
│   ├── assertions.rs    # Custom assertions
│   └── logging.rs       # Detailed test logging
├── scenarios/
│   ├── basic_ingest.rs  # Basic text capture
│   ├── pattern_detection.rs
│   ├── workflow_execution.rs
│   ├── policy_enforcement.rs
│   └── error_recovery.rs
├── scripts/
│   ├── run_all.sh       # Run all E2E tests
│   ├── setup_wezterm.sh # Setup test WezTerm instance
│   └── cleanup.sh       # Cleanup after tests
└── fixtures/
    ├── codex_session.txt
    ├── claude_session.txt
```

Every E2E test produces detailed logs:

### Test Scenarios

#### 2. Pattern Detection

### CI Integration
```yaml

  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  services:
    wezterm:
      image: wezterm/wezterm:latest
```

- E2E tests cover all major user journeys

title: Epic: Replace tokio async runtime with asupersync
description:
# Epic: Replace tokio async runtime with asupersync

## Background
FrankenTerm currently uses tokio 1.49.0 (full features) as its async runtime, with ~1,090 async patterns across 61 files. The asupersync library (https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/asupersync) is a spec-first, cancel-correct, capability-secure Rust async runtime that replaces tokio entirely.

## Why asupersync?
1. **Structured concurrency** - Every spawned task belongs to a Scope; no orphan tasks possible
2. **Cancel-correctness** - Multi-phase cancellation protocol (Request→Drain→Finalize) vs tokio's silent drop
3. **Capability security** - All effects gated through Cx context token; no ambient authority
4. **Four-valued Outcome<T,E>** - Ok/Err/Cancelled/Panicked vs Result's Ok/Err
5. **Two-phase channel ops** - Reserve/Commit pattern eliminates "message lost on cancellation" bugs
6. **Deterministic testing** - LabRuntime with virtual time, seed-controlled scheduling, DPOR exploration
7. **Built-in networking** - TCP/UDP/TLS/HTTP/gRPC without tokio transitive deps

## Scope
Replace ALL tokio usage across the codebase:
- Core runtime and task spawning → asupersync Scope/Cx
- Sync primitives (Mutex, RwLock, Semaphore) → asupersync sync
- Channels (mpsc, watch, broadcast) → asupersync channels
- Network I/O (UnixStream, TcpListener) → asupersync net
- Time (sleep, timeout) → asupersync via Cx
- select! macro → asupersync combinators
- tokio-rustls → asupersync TLS
- reqwest → asupersync HTTP client
- Test infrastructure → LabRuntime

## Key Migration Patterns
| Tokio | Asupersync |
|-------|------------|
| #[tokio::main] | RuntimeBuilder::new().build()?.block_on(...) |
| tokio::spawn(fut) | scope.spawn(fut) inside cx.region() |
| tokio::select! | asupersync::combinator::select/race |
| tokio::time::sleep | cx.sleep(duration) |
| tokio::sync::mpsc | asupersync::channel::mpsc (reserve/commit) |
| tokio::sync::Mutex | asupersync::sync::Mutex (guard obligation) |
| Result<T,E> | Outcome<T,E> (four-valued) |
| Drop cancellation | cx.checkpoint() explicit cancellation points |

## Critical Consideration
All async functions gain a `cx: &mut Cx` parameter. This is the most pervasive change - it threads through the entire call graph. Plan function signature changes carefully to minimize churn.

## Estimated Scale
- 61 files with async code
- ~1,090 async pattern instances
- ~586 network I/O instances
- Core modules: pool.rs (554 LOC), mux_pool.rs (583 LOC), mux_client.rs (997 LOC), runtime.rs (~500 LOC), ipc.rs (~400 LOC), tailer.rs (~600 LOC), native_events.rs (~400 LOC)
notes: LavenderHorizon taking a bounded non-conflicting slice: replace remaining direct tokio runtime-builder usage in clean frankenterm-core modules/tests with runtime_compat equivalents, avoiding files already active in the current worktree.

title: Layout restoration engine — recreate window/tab/split topology from snapshot
description:
## Goal
Implement the layout restoration engine that recreates the exact window/tab/pane split topology from a MuxSnapshot, positioning panes in the same arrangement they had before the mux server restart.

## Background & Motivation
After a mux server restart, all windows, tabs, and split panes are gone. The restoration engine must recreate the exact same layout using WezTerm CLI commands (wezterm cli spawn, wezterm cli split-pane). This is the visual foundation — users should see the same window arrangement they had before.

WezTerm's resurrect.wezterm plugin does approximate layout restoration via Lua but has limitations: it can't restore exact split ratios, and it struggles with complex nested splits. Our approach uses the vendored mux client and exact pane geometry data captured in the MuxSnapshot.

## Technical Design

### Struct Definition
```rust
// Location: crates/wa-core/src/snapshot/restore_layout.rs
pub struct LayoutRestorer {
    mux_client: Arc<DirectMuxClient>,
    config: RestoreConfig,
}

pub struct RestoreConfig {
    pub restore_working_dirs: bool,  // default: true
    pub restore_split_ratios: bool,  // default: true
    pub restore_window_positions: bool, // default: false (OS may differ)
}

// Maps old pane IDs to new pane IDs after restoration
pub type PaneIdMap = HashMap<PaneId, PaneId>;
```

### Core Algorithm
1. For each window in the snapshot:
   a. Create a new window (wezterm cli spawn --new-window)
   b. Record the new window_id
2. For each tab in the window:
   a. If not the first tab, create new tab (wezterm cli spawn-tab)
   b. Record the new tab_id
3. For the pane tree within each tab:
   a. Use recursive descent on the PaneNode tree
   b. For Split nodes: create split-pane with correct direction (horizontal/vertical)
   c. For Leaf nodes: record the pane_id mapping (old -> new)
   d. Adjust split ratios using resize commands

### Recursive Split Restoration
```rust
async fn restore_pane_tree(
    &self,
    node: &PaneNode,
    parent_pane_id: PaneId,
    id_map: &mut PaneIdMap,
) -> Result<PaneId> {
    match node {
        PaneNode::Leaf { pane_id, cwd, .. } => {
            id_map.insert(*pane_id, parent_pane_id);
            if self.config.restore_working_dirs {
                // Set working directory via shell command
                self.set_cwd(parent_pane_id, cwd).await?;
            }
            Ok(parent_pane_id)
        }
        PaneNode::Split { direction, children, ratio, .. } => {
            // First child uses the existing pane
            let first = self.restore_pane_tree(&children[0], parent_pane_id, id_map).await?;
            // Second child gets a new split pane
            let new_pane = self.create_split(parent_pane_id, *direction).await?;
            let second = self.restore_pane_tree(&children[1], new_pane, id_map).await?;
            // Adjust split ratio
            if self.config.restore_split_ratios {
                self.adjust_ratio(first, second, *ratio).await?;
            }
            Ok(first)
        }
    }
}
```

## Integration Points
- **MuxSnapshot schema** (bd-cuz): Reads PaneNode tree structure
- **DirectMuxClient**: Uses spawn, split-pane, and resize PDUs
- **WeztermClient** (wezterm.rs): Fallback to CLI for operations not in mux protocol
- **PaneIdMap**: Returned to caller for use by scrollback injection and process re-launch

## Key Files to Create/Modify
- CREATE: crates/wa-core/src/snapshot/restore_layout.rs
- MODIFY: crates/wa-core/src/snapshot/mod.rs (add module)
- MODIFY: crates/wa-core/src/vendored/mux_client.rs (may need spawn/split PDU support)

## Edge Cases
- Window manager may not honor exact window positions (especially across restarts)
- Split ratios may need multiple resize iterations to converge
- If mux server has existing panes, restoration should create in addition (not replace)
- Tab titles should be restored from snapshot metadata

## Dependencies
- bd-cuz: MuxSnapshot schema (PaneNode tree definition)

## Acceptance Criteria
- Single window with multiple tabs restores correctly
- Horizontal and vertical splits restore with correct topology
- Nested splits (3+ levels deep) restore correctly
- Split ratios are approximately correct (within 5% of original)
- Working directories are set correctly for each pane
- PaneIdMap correctly maps all old pane IDs to new ones
- Handles graceful errors (e.g., if a split fails, continues with remaining)

## Estimated Effort
2-3 hours implementation, 1 hour testing

## Test Requirements

### Property-Based Testing (proptest)
Add proptest cases in `crates/wa-core/tests/proptest_layout_restore.rs`:
- **Layout roundtrip invariant**: For any arbitrary layout tree, `save(restore(save(layout))) == save(layout)` — saving a restored layout must produce an identical snapshot to the original. This is the fundamental correctness property. Strategy: `arb_layout_tree()` generates random PaneNode trees with 1-50 panes, random split directions, and random ratios in [0.1, 0.9].
- **PaneIdMap completeness**: For any layout tree, after restoration the PaneIdMap must contain exactly one entry for every leaf pane in the original tree (no missing mappings, no extra mappings).
- **Topology preservation**: For any layout tree, the structural shape (split directions, nesting depth, child ordering) of the restored layout must exactly match the original, regardless of specific pane IDs.
- **Split ratio fidelity**: For any layout tree with split ratios, restored ratios must be within 5% of originals. Strategy: `arb_ratio()` generates f64 in [0.1, 0.9].

### Criterion Benchmarks
Add benchmarks in `crates/wa-core/benches/layout_restore.rs`:
- `bench_restore_50_pane_layout`: Restore a 50-pane complex layout (10 tabs, mixed splits), target <500ms
- `bench_restore_single_tab_deep_splits`: Restore a single tab with 10-level deep nested splits
- `bench_pane_id_map_construction`: PaneIdMap construction for 200 panes, target <1ms

## Cross-References
- **wa-2dd4s.3** (Zellij swap layouts): Zellij-style swap layouts provide named layout presets that can be toggled. The layout restoration engine should be aware of swap layout metadata in snapshots so that restored sessions can resume swap-layout cycling from where the user left off.
- **wa-2dd4s.2** (Floating panes): Floating (overlay) panes are not part of the split tree — they exist as separate overlay layers. The layout restoration engine must handle floating pane metadata separately from the recursive split restoration, restoring them as overlays at their original positions and sizes.

description:
# wa send --dry-run Implementation

## Purpose
Allow users to preview exactly what `wa send` would do before executing.

## Output Format
```
DRY RUN - No changes will be made

Target Resolution:
  Pane: 3 (claude_code @ /home/user/project)
  Domain: local

Policy Evaluation:
  ✓ Rate limit: 2/10 sends in last minute (within budget)
  ✓ Pane state: PromptActive (safe to send)
  ✓ No recent gaps (continuity OK)
  ✓ Command safety: text appears safe

Expected Action:
  - Inject 18 characters via wezterm cli send-text --pane-id 3
  - Wait for: prompt boundary (timeout: 30s)

To execute for real:
  wa send --pane 3 "Reread AGENTS.md"
```

## Implementation Steps
1. Parse and validate all send arguments
2. Resolve target pane (same as real execution)
3. Call PolicyEngine.evaluate() without executing
4. Build PlannedAction with character count and target
5. Format and display report

- Multiple targets: show all resolved panes
- Policy denial: show what would block and why
- Ambiguous target: show all candidates and how to narrow

title: Implement Playwright auth flow for Google (Gemini CLI /auth)
description:
# Task: Implement Playwright auth flow for Google (Gemini CLI `/auth`)

## Goal
Implement `BrowserAutomation::complete_google_auth(...)` that establishes an authenticated Google session suitable for Gemini CLI.

## Context / why this is hard
- Google sign-in is complex (SSO, MFA, device prompts).
- Automation can be rate-limited or challenged.
- Our priority is **robustness and safety**, not full automation at any cost.

## Expected workflow integration
Gemini usage-limit workflow will:
1. send `/auth` into the Gemini CLI pane
2. parse any printed instructions (URL/code) if present
3. call this Playwright flow
4. return to the pane and resume/restart session as appropriate

## Implementation outline
### Happy path (already authenticated)
- Load profile for `(service=google, account_key)`.
- Navigate to a stable page (`https://accounts.google.com/`).
- Detect a "signed-in" selector (account avatar / profile) and return `Success`.

### Login path
- If not signed in, proceed through:
  - email entry
  - account selection
  - (potentially) password/MFA — which we do NOT automate

### Password/MFA/SSO handling
- If any step requires password/MFA/SSO confirmation:
  - return `NeedsHuman` with URL and instructions (redacted)
  - keep the browser visible (non-headless) for manual completion
  - after completion, persist profile storage state

## Safety requirements
- Strict timeouts for waits.
- Redact sensitive URL parameters.
- Do not store secrets in DB.

## Testing
- Integration tests (offline):
  - Playwright against local HTML fixtures representing:
    - already-authenticated state
    - needs-human state (password/MFA)
  - validate structured outcomes and redaction
- Manual smoke tests:
  - validate on a real machine with a pre-authenticated profile

## Deliverables
- Google auth flow implementation using persistent profiles.
- A clear "manual completion" fallback path.

## Acceptance Criteria
- With a pre-authenticated profile, flow returns `Success` reliably.
- Without a profile, flow returns `NeedsHuman` with actionable instructions (no secrets leaked).

title: User pattern packs: load custom rules from ~/.config/wa/patterns/
description:
# User pattern packs

## Purpose
Allow users to define custom pattern packs that load alongside built-in packs.

## User Pack Location
```
~/.config/wa/patterns/
├── my-org-patterns/
│   ├── pack.toml        # Pack metadata
│   └── rules.toml       # Rule definitions
└── custom-agent/
    ├── pack.toml
    └── rules.toml
```

## Pack Format
```toml
# pack.toml
[pack]
name = "my-org-patterns"
version = "1.0.0"
description = "Custom patterns for internal agents"
extends = "core.codex"  # Optional: inherit from built-in

# rules.toml
[[rules]]
id = "my-org.custom_warning"
name = "Custom Warning Pattern"
pattern = "\\[INTERNAL\\] Warning: (.+)"
severity = "warning"
extract = { message = "$1" }
agent_types = ["codex", "custom-agent"]
```

## Loading Priority
1. Built-in packs (highest priority)
2. User packs in order found
3. Workspace-local packs (.wa/patterns/)

For conflicts, later packs override earlier ones unless `extends` is used.

## Implementation
```rust
pub fn load_all_packs(config: &Config) -> Result<Vec<PatternPack>> {
    let mut packs = vec![];
    
    // Load built-in
    packs.extend(load_builtin_packs()?);
    
    // Load user packs
    let user_dir = config.patterns_dir();
    if user_dir.exists() {
        for entry in fs::read_dir(user_dir)? {
            let pack = PatternPack::load(entry?.path())?;
            packs.push(pack);
        }
    }
    
    // Load workspace packs
    if let Some(workspace_dir) = config.workspace_patterns_dir() {
        // Similar loading
    }
    
    // Resolve inheritance and conflicts
    resolve_pack_inheritance(&mut packs)?;
    
    Ok(packs)
}
```

## Validation
User packs are validated on load:
- Valid TOML syntax
- Required fields present
- Regex patterns compile
- No duplicate rule IDs (within pack)

## Testing
- Unit tests for pack loading
- Tests for inheritance resolution
- Tests for conflict handling
- Tests for invalid pack rejection

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] User packs load from ~/.config/wa/patterns/
- [ ] Pack format documented
- [ ] Inheritance (extends) works
- [ ] Conflict resolution is predictable
- [ ] Invalid packs rejected with clear errors
- [ ] Tests cover all scenarios

title: Custom workflows: YAML/TOML definitions with step sequences
description:
# Custom workflows

## Purpose
Allow users to define custom workflows in YAML/TOML without writing Rust code.

## Workflow Definition Format
```yaml
# ~/.config/wa/workflows/my_custom_workflow.yaml
name: my_custom_workflow
description: "Handle our custom agent's restart prompt"
triggers:
  - event_type: "my-org.restart_prompt"
    agent_types: ["custom-agent"]

steps:
  - name: wait_for_stable
    action: wait
    condition:
      type: pane_idle
      timeout: 5s
  
  - name: send_restart_command
    action: send_text
    text: "/restart\n"
    policy: require_approval  # or allow, deny
  
  - name: verify_restart
    action: wait
    condition:
      type: pattern
      pattern: "Agent restarted successfully"
      timeout: 30s

on_failure:
  action: notify
  message: "Custom workflow failed at step: ${failed_step}"
```

## Step Actions
```yaml
# Available actions
actions:
  - send_text      # Send keystrokes to pane
  - wait           # Wait for condition
  - notify         # Send notification
  - log            # Write to audit log
  - abort          # Stop workflow
  - conditional    # If/else branching
  - loop           # Repeat steps
```

## Implementation
```rust
pub struct YamlWorkflow {
    name: String,
    description: String,
    triggers: Vec<WorkflowTrigger>,
    steps: Vec<WorkflowStep>,
    on_failure: Option<FailureHandler>,
}

impl Workflow for YamlWorkflow {
    async fn execute(&self, ctx: &mut WorkflowContext) -> Result<WorkflowResult> {
        for step in &self.steps {
            match self.execute_step(step, ctx).await {
                Ok(StepResult::Continue) => continue,
                Ok(StepResult::Abort) => break,
                Err(e) => {
                    if let Some(handler) = &self.on_failure {
                        handler.execute(ctx, &e).await?;
                    }
                    return Err(e);
                }
            }
        }
        Ok(WorkflowResult::Success)
    }
}
```

## Testing
- Unit tests for YAML parsing
- Step action tests
- Conditional and loop tests
- Failure handling tests

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] YAML format supports all required actions
- [ ] Workflows load from user directory
- [ ] Steps execute in sequence
- [ ] Conditions work correctly
- [ ] Failure handlers execute
- [ ] Documentation covers workflow authoring
- [ ] Tests cover all step types

title: Extension sandboxing: WASM or Lua runtime for safe custom code execution
description:
# Extension Sandboxing

## Purpose
Run custom extension code safely without risking system security.

## Options Evaluated

### 1. WASM (Recommended)
- Pros: Strong isolation, multi-language, proven
- Cons: Larger binary, more complex
- Libraries: wasmtime, wasmer

### 2. Lua
- Pros: Simple, fast, battle-tested (Neovim/WezTerm)
- Cons: Single language, needs careful sandboxing
- Libraries: rlua, mlua

## Recommendation: WASM via wasmtime
- Better isolation guarantees
- Supports Rust, Go, C, AssemblyScript
- WASI for controlled system access

## Sandbox Capabilities
```rust
pub struct ExtensionSandbox {
    engine: wasmtime::Engine,
    linker: wasmtime::Linker<SandboxState>,
    capabilities: SandboxCapabilities,
}

pub struct SandboxCapabilities {
    pub read_pane_output: bool,
    pub send_notifications: bool,
    pub http_requests: bool,
    pub file_access: FileAccessScope,
}
```

## Capability Levels
- Level 1: Read-only (patterns only)
- Level 2: Read + notify (most workflows)
- Level 3: Read + notify + HTTP (integrations)
- Level 4: Full (admin extensions)

## Extension Manifest
```toml
[extension]
name = "my-patterns"
capabilities = ["read_pane_output"]
```

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] WASM runtime integrated
- [ ] Capability-based permissions
- [ ] Extensions cannot access system without permission
- [ ] Untrusted extension cannot crash wa

## Testing
- Unit tests for sandbox policy enforcement and resource limits.
- Integration tests running a restricted extension in a sandbox.
- Security checks: verify no filesystem/network escape.

title: Explanation templates: reusable reason patterns for wa why and errors
description:
# Explanation Templates: Reusable reason patterns for wa why

## Purpose
Provide consistent, helpful explanations for common scenarios via template system.

## Implementation

### Template Structure
```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct ExplanationTemplate {
    pub id: &'static str,
    pub scenario: &'static str,
    pub brief: &'static str,
    pub detailed: &'static str,
    pub suggestions: Vec<&'static str>,
    pub see_also: Vec<&'static str>,
}
```

### Built-in Templates

#### Policy Denials
```rust
pub static DENY_ALT_SCREEN: ExplanationTemplate = ExplanationTemplate {
    id: "deny.alt_screen",
    scenario: "Send denied because alt-screen is active",
    brief: "Pane is in full-screen mode (vim, less, etc.)",
    detailed: r#"
The pane is currently displaying an alternate screen buffer, which typically
means a full-screen application like vim, less, htop, or similar is running.

Sending text while alt-screen is active could:
- Corrupt the application state
- Cause unintended keystrokes
- Interfere with user interaction

The safety policy blocks sends to alt-screen panes by default.
"#,
    suggestions: vec![
        "Exit the full-screen application first",
        "Use --force if you're certain this is safe",
        "Configure policy to allow specific alt-screen apps",
    ],
    see_also: vec!["wa policy", "wa status --pane <id>"],
};

pub static DENY_COMMAND_RUNNING: ExplanationTemplate = ExplanationTemplate {
    id: "deny.command_running",
    scenario: "Send denied because a command is running",
    brief: "Another command is currently executing in the pane",
    detailed: r#"
The pane has an active command running (detected via OSC 133 markers or
heuristics). Sending text while a command runs could:

- Interrupt the running command
- Queue input for later (confusing)
- Cause the shell to misinterpret input

wa waits for command completion before sending unless overridden.
"#,
    suggestions: vec![
        "Wait for the current command to finish",
        "Use Ctrl-C to cancel the running command first",
        "Use --wait-for to send after a specific pattern",
    ],
    see_also: vec!["wa status", "wa send --wait-for"],
};

pub static DENY_RECENT_GAP: ExplanationTemplate = ExplanationTemplate {
    id: "deny.recent_gap",
    scenario: "Send denied due to recent output gap",
    brief: "Pane had no output recently, possibly waiting for input",
    detailed: r#"
wa detected a gap in pane output that suggests the pane might be:
- Waiting for user input at a prompt
- Displaying a confirmation dialog
- In an unknown state

The policy requires a prompt marker (OSC 133) or manual confirmation.
"#,
    suggestions: vec![
        "Check the pane manually to see its state",
        "Use --force if you've verified the pane is ready",
        "Enable OSC 133 support in your shell for better detection",
    ],
    see_also: vec!["wa capabilities --pane <id>"],
};
```

#### Workflow Explanations
```rust
pub static WORKFLOW_USAGE_LIMIT: ExplanationTemplate = ExplanationTemplate {
    id: "workflow.usage_limit",
    scenario: "Why handle_usage_limits workflow was triggered",
    brief: "Codex hit its daily token usage limit",
    detailed: r#"
The Codex agent reported it has reached its usage limit. This typically
happens when:

- Daily token quota exceeded
- Account-level rate limiting triggered

The handle_usage_limits workflow will:
1. Gracefully exit the current Codex session
2. Parse the session summary for resume ID
3. Select an alternate OpenAI account
4. Complete device auth flow
5. Resume the session with new credentials
"#,
    suggestions: vec![
        "Let the workflow complete automatically",
        "Check account status with: caut status",
        "Configure account pool in wa.toml",
    ],
    see_also: vec!["wa workflow status", "caut"],
};
```

### Template Registry
```rust
lazy_static! {
    pub static ref EXPLANATION_TEMPLATES: HashMap<&'static str, &'static ExplanationTemplate> = {
        let mut m = HashMap::new();
        m.insert("deny.alt_screen", &DENY_ALT_SCREEN);
        m.insert("deny.command_running", &DENY_COMMAND_RUNNING);
        m.insert("deny.recent_gap", &DENY_RECENT_GAP);
        m.insert("workflow.usage_limit", &WORKFLOW_USAGE_LIMIT);
        // ... more templates
        m
    };
}

pub fn get_explanation(id: &str) -> Option<&'static ExplanationTemplate> {
    EXPLANATION_TEMPLATES.get(id).copied()
}
```

### Template Interpolation
```rust
pub fn render_explanation(
    template: &ExplanationTemplate,
    context: &HashMap<String, String>,
) -> String {
    let mut output = template.detailed.to_string();
    for (key, value) in context {
        output = output.replace(&format!("{{{}}}", key), value);
    }
    output
}
```

## Testing
- All templates have valid structure
- Interpolation works correctly
- No broken cross-references

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Templates for all common denial reasons
- [ ] Templates for all workflow triggers
- [ ] wa why uses templates consistently
- [ ] Templates documented in help

This epic focuses on user experience, external integrations, and robustness. After Phase 3, wa works - now we make it delightful to use and integrate with the broader ecosystem.

## Strategic Importance
Phase 4 transforms wa from "working prototype" to "production-ready tool":
- MCP server enables AI agents to control wa
- rich_rust output makes CLI pleasant for humans
- Setup automation reduces friction for new users
- CASS integration enables session archaeology
- Comprehensive testing ensures reliability

## Key Components

### 1. MCP Server with fastmcp_rust
Tools:
- wa.state - Get current pane states
- wa.get_text - Get text from pane
- wa.send - Send text to pane
- wa.wait_for - Wait for pattern
- wa.search - FTS search
- wa.events - Get events
- wa.workflow_run - Execute workflow
- wa.accounts - List accounts
- wa.accounts_refresh - Refresh account usage
- wa.rules_list - List detection rules
- wa.rules_test - Test pattern matching

Resources:
- wa://panes - Current pane registry
- wa://events - Event feed
- wa://accounts - Account status
- wa://workflows - Available workflows
- wa://rules - Pattern rules

### 2. rich_rust CLI Output
- render_pane_table() - Tables for pane listings
- render_event_panel() - Panels for events with severity colors
- Progress indicators for long operations
- Consistent styling across all commands

### 3. Setup Automation

#### SSH Config Parser
- Parse ~/.ssh/config
- Extract hosts, hostnames, users, ports, identity files
- Filter out wildcards

#### Automated Remote Setup
1. Check if wezterm is installed
2. Install WezTerm if needed (apt/dnf)
3. Create systemd service for wezterm-mux-server
4. Enable lingering for service persistence
5. Optionally install wa binary
6. Verify service is running

#### WezTerm Config Generator
- Generate ssh_domains with WezTerm multiplexing
- Domain-specific colors (optional)
- wa integration hooks (user-var-changed forwarding)
- Idempotent patching (WA-BEGIN/WA-END markers)

### 4. CASS Integration (coding_agent_session_search)
- find_session(session_id) - Correlate wa session with cass data
- search_sessions(path, agent) - Find sessions in a directory
- Session archaeology for context recovery
- Token usage correlation

### 5. Comprehensive Testing

#### Unit Tests
- Delta extraction correctness (overlap cases, wrap cases)
- Pattern rules per agent (positive + negative fixtures)
- Workflow step guards (prompt detection, alt-screen checks)
- DB schema migration tests
- Policy engine capability checks

#### Integration Tests
- Simulate wezterm cli outputs via fixtures
- Run workflow engine against fake panes
- Test StorageHandle async operations

#### Golden Corpus Regression Tests
Directory structure:
\`\`\`
tests/corpus/
├── codex/
│   ├── usage_limit_v1.txt
│   ├── usage_limit_v1.expect.json
├── claude_code/
│   ├── session_end.txt
│   └── session_end.expect.json
└── gaps/
    ├── scrollback_truncation.txt
    └── scrollback_truncation.expect.json
\`\`\`

#### Property-Based Tests (proptest)
- Segment sequence monotonicity
- FTS finds inserted text
- Delta extraction completeness

#### Performance Budgets (Criterion)
- pattern_detection_typical: p50 < 1ms, p99 < 5ms
- fts_query_common: p50 < 10ms, p99 < 50ms
- CI enforcement with baseline comparison

## Success Criteria
- [ ] MCP server exposes all robot mode functionality
- [ ] CLI output is beautiful with rich_rust
- [ ] \`wa setup\` configures local and remote hosts
- [ ] CASS integration works for session correlation
- [ ] Test coverage > 70% overall
- [ ] All performance budgets met
- [ ] Documentation sufficient for contributors

## Dependencies
- Depends on Phase 1-3 (all core functionality)

## Configuration
At this point, wa.toml should be fully functional:

log_level = "info"

[safety]

[metrics]

title: Human CLI tests: output layer snapshots + no-ANSI guarantees
description:
# Task: Human CLI tests for output layer

## Goal
Make the human CLI output layer trustworthy and regression-resistant.

Humans will pipe wa output into files, paste it into issues, and rely on it under stress. Output regressions are user-hostile.

## Scope

### Renderer-level snapshot tests (core renderers)
Renderer-level tests (no subprocess) for the **Phase 4 baseline** human CLI:
- status/panes table renderer
- events list/panel renderer (**raw/technical** event fields)
- query/search results renderer
- workflow summary renderer
- audit feed renderer

### Explicit non-scope (covered elsewhere)
To keep priorities and dependencies sane, this bead intentionally does **not** block on Phase 4 “UX excellence extras”. Those renderers/overlays must still be tested, but they are covered by their own beads:
- Natural-language event descriptions in event rendering: `wa-0go.7`
- History timeline / rollback visualization output: `wa-5em.9`
- Suggestion overlays in status/events/errors: `wa-tp4.8`

This separation keeps the **core CLI output layer** stable early, while allowing optional overlays to evolve without blocking core ship readiness.

## Format selection behavior
- auto mode chooses rich only when explicitly told "tty" (injectable in tests)
- plain mode is stable and contains no ANSI escape sequences
- json mode is stable and uses a documented schema (may share the robot envelope)

## Key requirements
- Snapshot tests for plain output (golden text). The exact formatting should be intentional.
- Snapshot tests for json output (stable fields, stable error codes).
- Redaction expectations:
  - never print secrets in plain/rich output
  - when showing inputs, use a redacted summary consistent with audit rules

## Implementation notes
- Keep renderers pure: typed input -> String.
- Avoid dependence on real TTY detection in tests. Inject a bool or OutputMode instead.

## Acceptance Criteria
- A deliberate formatting change requires updating snapshots.
- Piped output contains no ANSI sequences by default.
- Errors follow the same structure across commands (message + hint + code).

## Testing
- Meta-validation:
  - Add an explicit assertion that plain-mode output contains no `\x1b[` ANSI escapes.
  - Add a fake secret string in inputs and assert it never appears in renderer output.

- Snapshot discipline:
  - Snapshots should be per-renderer and small enough to review; avoid one mega-snapshot that is hard to update.

title: Make Lua optional in FrankenTerm config crate (feature-flag)
description:
# Make Lua Optional in FrankenTerm Config Crate

## Context
The config crate (frankenterm/config/) hard-depends on mlua with features=[vendored, lua54, async, send, serialize]. Under the new dual-runtime strategy (Option C), Lua becomes optional — users can choose Lua, WASM, or both.

## What changes
1. Make mlua dependency optional behind `lua` feature
2. Make luahelper dependency optional behind `lua` feature  
3. Gate all Lua-related code in config/src/ behind `#[cfg(feature = "lua")]`
4. Default features INCLUDE `lua` for backward compat
5. `no-lua` feature excludes it (for minimal/headless builds)
6. Ensure config crate compiles and provides basic config loading even without Lua

## Feature flag design
```toml
[features]
default = ["lua"]
lua = ["dep:mlua", "dep:luahelper"]
no-lua = []  # Explicit opt-out
```

## Files affected
- frankenterm/config/Cargo.toml (feature flags, optional deps)
- frankenterm/config/src/lua.rs (gate behind #[cfg(feature = "lua")])
- frankenterm/config/src/lib.rs (conditional module inclusion)
- Any file in config/src/ that imports from lua.rs

## Why keep Lua as default
Existing WezTerm users have wezterm.lua configs. Breaking them by default would be hostile. The `lua` feature is default-on, `no-lua` is opt-in for minimal builds.

## Testing
- `cargo check -p config` — must work (default, with Lua)
- `cargo check -p config --no-default-features` — must compile (no Lua)
- `cargo check -p config --features lua` — explicit Lua, must work
- `cargo test -p config` — existing tests pass

## Cross-References
- **wa-3k2g1** (luahelper optional): Once config gates its luahelper dep behind `lua`, the luahelper crate becomes truly optional at the workspace level. This bead is a prerequisite for wa-3k2g1.
- **wa-2ufom** (Mux Lua optional): The mux crate depends on config. Mux's Lua optionality depends on config's Lua optionality being done first — otherwise mux inherits a transitive hard dependency on mlua through config.
- Together with wa-3k2g1 and wa-2ufom, this forms the "Lua-optional triad" — all three must land for a clean no-Lua build path.
notes: Landed on origin/main (commit 54226a1). Added lua feature (default-on) + optional mlua/luahelper deps; cfg-gated Lua modules + conversion macros; added no-lua stubs so --no-default-features builds. Verified: cargo check -p config --all-targets; cargo check -p config --all-targets --no-default-features; cargo test (workspace) passes with TMPDIR=/Users/jemanuel/tmp-ft. cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings currently fails in multiple workspace crates (pre-existing).
