title: [EPIC] Phase 5: Advanced Features
description:
# Phase 5: Advanced Features

## Overview
This epic covers advanced capabilities that provide significant value but aren't strictly necessary for v0.1.0. These features differentiate wa from simpler monitoring tools and lay groundwork for future multi-machine orchestration.

## Strategic Importance
Phase 5 features enable:
- Higher performance through selective vendoring
- Real-time responsiveness through output streaming
- Fleet-scale coordination through multi-agent features
- Long-term maintainability through optimization and documentation

## Key Components

### 1. Selective WezTerm Vendoring

#### Analysis
| Approach | Pros | Cons |
|----------|------|------|
| CLI Only | Simple, stable | Limited capabilities, subprocess overhead |
| Lua IPC | Event-driven, rich data | Requires user config modification |
| Full Vendor | Maximum capability | Maintenance burden, version tracking |
| Selective Vendor | Best of both worlds | Careful design required |

#### Implementation
\`\`\`toml
[dependencies]
wezterm-mux-proto = { git = "https://github.com/wez/wezterm", optional = true }
wezterm-term = { git = "https://github.com/wez/wezterm", optional = true }

[features]
default = []
vendored = ["wezterm-mux-proto", "wezterm-term"]
\`\`\`

DirectMuxClient for zero-copy scrollback access
UnifiedClient that uses best available method
Version compatibility checking

### 2. Real-Time Output Streaming
With vendoring enabled:
- Subscribe to pane output events
- Eliminate polling latency entirely
- Lower CPU usage
- Foundation for responsive UIs

### 3. Multi-Agent Coordination Features

#### Cross-Session Communication
- Pane-to-pane messaging primitives
- Shared state for coordinated workflows
- Dependency-aware task distribution

#### Distributed Mode (Optional)
Mode A (Single-node): wa runs on workstation, connects to all domains
Mode B (Distributed): wa-agent runs near each mux server

\`\`\`
┌─────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────┐
│   Workstation   │     │   dev-server    │
│  wa-aggregator  │◄────│    wa-agent     │
│  (central)      │     │   (local tail)  │
└─────────────────┘     └─────────────────┘
\`\`\`

Benefits:
- Lower latency (local capture)
- Fewer bytes (only deltas over wire)
- Isolation (one domain failing doesn't stall all)

### 4. Performance Optimization Pass

#### Targets
- Quick reject: < 1μs for typical non-matching text
- Pattern engine: < 1ms for full detection
- FTS query: < 50ms for common queries
- Watcher loop: < 100μs per pane check when idle

#### Benchmarks
\`\`\`rust
#[bench]
fn bench_quick_reject_no_match(b: &mut Bencher) {
    let engine = PatternEngine::new();
    let boring = "ls -la\ndrwxr-xr-x...".repeat(100);
    b.iter(|| black_box(engine.detect(&boring)));
}
\`\`\`

#### Memory Optimization
- LRU cache for output hashes
- Rolling hashes per pane
- Prune old entries

### 5. Documentation and skills.md
- Complete README with architecture overview
- CONTRIBUTING.md for new contributors
- API documentation for all public interfaces
- skills.md for AI agent integration
- Workflow specification docs

### 6. Observability Enhancements

#### Health Model
\`wa status --health --format json\` reports:
- wezterm: cli_ok, mux_ok, vendored_ok
- ingest: lag_max_ms, lag_avg_ms, panes_tracked
- event_bus: queue depths
- storage: db_writable, wal_pages, last_checkpoint
- workflows: active count, oldest_running_ms

#### Prometheus Metrics (optional)
\`wa watch --metrics :9464\`
- wa_ingest_deltas_total
- wa_ingest_lag_ms_bucket
- wa_pattern_detections_total
- wa_workflow_runs_total
- wa_db_write_latency_ms_bucket

#### Diagnostic Bundle
\`wa diag bundle --last 15m\` produces tarball with:
- Config (redacted)
- Version matrix
- Recent events
- Gap summary
- Health snapshot

### 7. Fuzzing
cargo-fuzz targets:
- Pattern pack parsing (malformed TOML)
- Regex extractors (pathological patterns)
- OSC marker parsing (invalid escapes)
- FTS queries (malformed queries)

## Success Criteria
- [ ] Vendored build provides real-time streaming
- [ ] Performance benchmarks meet budgets
- [ ] Multi-agent coordination works for 2+ agents
- [ ] Documentation is complete and accurate
- [ ] Observability provides full visibility
- [ ] Fuzzing finds no crashes

## Dependencies
- Depends on Phase 1-4 (all prior work)

## Definition of Done for v0.1.0
wa is "meaningfully real" when:
- [ ] It continuously captures pane output and can search it with FTS
- [ ] It detects at least the primary patterns reliably
- [ ] It can run handle_compaction safely end-to-end
- [ ] It can run handle_usage_limits for Codex end-to-end
- [ ] It exposes robot mode + MCP so an agent can operate it
- [ ] It has documentation sufficient for another developer
- [ ] It passes CI (lint, test, build) on every commit

- “Which pane is my agent running in?”

This is the TUI equivalent of `wa status` + quick drill-down.

Back the view via the shared query layer / robot state model:

title: Design MuxSnapshot schema for full mux state serialization
description:
## Goal
Design and implement the core data structures that represent a complete, serializable snapshot of the WezTerm mux server state. This is the foundational data model for the entire session persistence feature.

## Background & Motivation
When the wezterm-mux-server process dies or needs to be restarted (e.g., due to memory leaks, protocol corruption after extended runtime, or upgrades), ALL running processes in all panes are killed because the mux server owns the PTY file descriptors. The kernel sends SIGHUP to all child processes. There is currently no way to save and restore session state across restarts.

WezTerm's Lua API provides building blocks (get_lines_as_escapes, inject_output, process/directory introspection, mux hierarchy enumeration) but no native serialization. The resurrect.wezterm plugin does this via Lua but is approximate and limited.

wa (wezterm_automata) already has: SQLite storage with WAL mode, pane tracking (PaneRecord), delta extraction, agent session correlation (AgentSessionRecord), and a vendored mux client. We can leverage all of this.

## Design Requirements
1. Define MuxSnapshot struct containing:
   - snapshot_id: String (UUID)
   - created_at: i64 (epoch ms)
   - mux_server_pid: Option<u32>
   - wezterm_version: String
   - wa_version: String
   - windows: Vec<WindowSnapshot>
   - workspaces: Vec<WorkspaceSnapshot>
   - active_workspace: Option<String>

2. Define WindowSnapshot containing:
   - window_id: u64
   - workspace: String
   - title: Option<String>
   - tabs: Vec<TabSnapshot>
   - active_tab_index: usize

3. Define TabSnapshot containing:
   - tab_id: u64
   - title: Option<String>
   - pane_tree: PaneNode (recursive tree for splits)
   - active_pane_id: u64

4. Define PaneNode enum:
   - Leaf(PaneSnapshot) for single panes
   - VSplit { left: Box<PaneNode>, right: Box<PaneNode>, ratio: f64 } for vertical splits
   - HSplit { top: Box<PaneNode>, bottom: Box<PaneNode>, ratio: f64 } for horizontal splits

5. Define PaneSnapshot containing:
   - pane_id: u64
   - domain: String
   - title: Option<String>
   - cwd: Option<String> (working directory)
   - foreground_process: Option<ProcessInfo>
   - dimensions: PaneDimensions (rows, cols, scrollback_rows)
   - cursor_position: Option<CursorPosition>
   - is_alt_screen: bool
   - user_vars: HashMap<String, String>
   - scrollback_hash: Option<String> (hash of scrollback content, for dedup)
   - agent_session: Option<AgentSessionRef> (link to wa's agent session tracking)

6. Define ProcessInfo:
   - name: String
   - argv: Option<Vec<String>>
   - pid: Option<u32>
   - is_whitelisted_for_restore: bool

7. Define AgentSessionRef:
   - agent_type: String (claude_code, codex, gemini)
   - session_id: Option<String>
   - wa_agent_session_id: Option<i64>

8. All structs must derive Serialize, Deserialize, Clone, Debug
9. All structs must be roundtrip-safe through JSON and potentially TOON format
10. Include schema version field for forward compatibility

## Implementation Location
New file: crates/wa-core/src/snapshot_schema.rs
Re-export from crates/wa-core/src/lib.rs

## Acceptance Criteria
- All structs compile and pass serde roundtrip tests
- Schema can represent arbitrary pane split topologies via recursive PaneNode
- JSON serialization produces human-readable output
- Schema version is included for migration support
- Integration with existing PaneRecord and AgentSessionRecord types

## Property Testing Requirements

### Proptest
Add `tests/proptest_snapshot_schema.rs`:
- **schema_versioning_compatibility**: For any MuxSnapshot with schema_version N (proptest generates versions 1..=current), assert that a deserializer for version current can read it (forward compatibility). For any MuxSnapshot with schema_version current, assert that fields not present in version N-1 are handled gracefully with defaults (backward compatibility). This ensures that snapshots created by older wa versions can always be read by newer wa versions.
- **pane_node_roundtrip**: For any arbitrary PaneNode tree (proptest generates random trees with 1-50 leaves), assert JSON roundtrip produces identical trees.
- **snapshot_completeness**: For any arbitrary MuxSnapshot (proptest generates), assert that every pane_id referenced in the PaneNode trees appears exactly once (no orphans, no duplicates).
- **optional_fields_resilience**: For any MuxSnapshot, randomly set optional fields to None (proptest generates a bitmask), serialize to JSON, deserialize, and assert all non-optional fields survive and optional fields are correctly None.

## Cross-References
- **wa-29k1** (SnapshotEngine orchestrator): wa-29k1 is the primary consumer of the MuxSnapshot schema. It populates the structs defined here during the capture pipeline. Any schema changes must be coordinated with the SnapshotEngine's capture logic.
- **wa-3q7q** (SQLite tables for snapshot storage): wa-3q7q stores MuxSnapshot as JSON in the snapshot_json column. The schema must remain JSON-serializable, and any schema version bumps must be accompanied by migration logic in wa-3q7q's storage layer. The snapshot_size_bytes column in wa-3q7q depends on the serialized size of the structs defined here.
close_reason: Implemented: session_topology.rs (TopologySnapshot, WindowSnapshot, TabSnapshot, PaneNode) and session_pane_state.rs (PaneStateSnapshot, ProcessInfo, TerminalState, ScrollbackRef, AgentMetadata). All required types present with serde roundtrip tests.

title: Doctor tests: fixture-based checks + output stability (JSON/TTY)
description:
# Task: `wa doctor` tests

## Goal
Make `wa doctor` a **trustworthy** and **regression-resistant** diagnostic surface.

`wa doctor` is how users decide whether to trust the tool. If it flakes, lies, or leaks secrets, we lose users.

## Test scope

### Unit tests
- Path resolution rendering (workspace root, DB/log/lock paths) is correct and deterministic.
- JSON output shape is stable (fields present, naming stable, no secret leakage).
- Redaction is applied to any potentially sensitive field (even on error paths).

### Integration tests (fixture-driven; no real WezTerm required)
Run `wa doctor` in a hermetic test environment that simulates:
- A healthy system.
- Missing `wezterm` binary / `wezterm cli list` failure.
- Workspace not writable.
- DB unreadable / schema mismatch.
- Watcher not running / lock held / stale lock.
- Optional feature checks present/absent (mcp/browser/web/tui) without forcing those deps.

## Test strategy / harness design
- Prefer dependency injection where feasible (traits) so we can simulate:
  - `wezterm` CLI calls
  - storage open/migration version
  - watcher health snapshot
- If process-based stubbing is simpler, use a test harness that:
  - writes a small “fake wezterm” executable to a temp dir
  - prepends that temp dir to `PATH`
  - feeds deterministic stdout/stderr for specific subcommands

## Output stability requirements
- Non-TTY mode:
  - `wa doctor --format json` must be strictly machine-parseable and stable.
  - Tests validate JSON against a versioned schema (if/when we add a schema for doctor output).
- TTY mode:
  - Tests validate key content (not exact ANSI art); either strip ANSI or snapshot a normalized rendering.

## Logging & debuggability
- Tests must capture logs on failure and print them (bounded) to make failures diagnosable.
- Ensure logs do not leak secrets (redaction applied to any dynamic content).

## Deliverables
- Unit test module(s) for doctor output + redaction.
- Integration test harness utilities for stubbing wezterm/storage/watcher.
- A small set of golden fixtures covering the major failure modes.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `wa doctor` has coverage for each major check and for each major failure mode.
- Tests do not require:
  - network access
  - a real WezTerm instance
  - a real user home directory
- Adding a new doctor check requires adding at least one test covering both success and failure paths.

## Testing
- Meta-validation:
  - Ensure the integration harness actually uses the fake `wezterm` binary (assert invocation).
  - Add an explicit assertion that `--format json` output contains no ANSI escapes and validates against schema (once added).

## Goal
Define and enforce basic performance budgets so wa stays fast as features accrete.

## Key hot paths

title: [EPIC] CLI Polish: Shell Completions, Aliases, Progressive Disclosure
description:
# [EPIC] CLI Polish

## Mission
Make the wa CLI feel **polished and professional**—the kind of tool where attention to detail builds trust.

## Why This Matters
CLI UX is cumulative. Many small improvements add up to a tool that feels delightful:
- Tab completion → fewer typos, faster navigation
- Smart aliases → muscle memory efficiency
- Progressive disclosure → clean by default, detailed on request
- Consistent patterns → predictable behavior

## Components

### 1. Shell Completions
Full tab completion for all commands:
```bash
$ wa <TAB>
watch    status   events   send     workflow   ...

$ wa send --pane <TAB>
1 (codex @ /home/user/project)
3 (claude @ /home/user/other)

$ wa workflow run <TAB>
handle_compaction    handle_usage_limits    handle_auth_required
```

Implementation:
- clap derives completions for bash/zsh/fish/powershell
- Dynamic completions for pane IDs, workflow names
- `wa completions bash > ~/.bash_completion.d/wa`

### 2. Smart Aliases
Built-in short forms for common operations:
```bash
was     → wa status
wae     → wa events --unhandled
waq     → wa query
waw     → wa watch
wat     → wa timeline
```

Also support user-defined aliases in config.

### 3. Progressive Disclosure
Output verbosity levels:
- Default: Essential info only
- `-v`: Additional context
- `-vv`: Debug details
- `--format json`: Machine-readable (stable schema; intended for scripts/automation)

Notes:
- `-v/-vv` controls *how much* information we include.
- `--format {auto|plain|json}` controls *how* we render it (TTY-rich vs stable plain vs machine JSON).

Example:
```bash
$ wa status
Panes: 4 observed, 1 ignored
Events: 2 unhandled

$ wa status -v
Panes:
  1: codex [PromptActive] /home/user/project (last: 2m ago)
  3: claude [CommandRunning] /home/user/other (last: 5s ago)
  ...

Events (unhandled):
  - codex.usage_limit_reached (Pane 1, 2m ago)
  - session.compaction (Pane 3, 5m ago)
```

### 4. Consistent Help Patterns
Every command has:
- `--help`: Usage and options
- `-h`: Brief usage
- Examples in help text
- Cross-references to related commands

```bash
$ wa send --help
wa send - Send text to a pane

USAGE:
    wa send --pane <ID> [OPTIONS] <TEXT>

OPTIONS:
    --pane <ID>      Target pane ID (required)
    --dry-run        Preview without executing
    --wait-for <PAT> Wait for pattern after send
    --timeout <SEC>  Wait timeout (default: 30)

EXAMPLES:
    wa send --pane 3 "hello"
    wa send --pane 3 --dry-run "hello"
    wa send --pane 3 --wait-for ">>>" "continue"

SEE ALSO:
    wa status       List available panes
    wa why          Explain send failures
```

### 5. Output Consistency
All commands follow the same patterns:
- Success: Clean output, exit 0
- Error: Error message with remediation, exit 1
- JSON mode: Structured output with envelope
- No ANSI when piped

## Testing
- Completion tests: Verify completions are generated correctly
- Alias tests: Aliases resolve to correct commands
- Output tests: Progressive disclosure works as expected
- Help tests: All commands have valid help text

## Success Criteria
- Tab completion works for all commands and dynamic values
- Aliases are documented and work as expected
- Output verbosity is consistent across all commands
- Help text is comprehensive and includes examples

## Acceptance Criteria
- Shell completions are generated and kept in sync with CLI.
- Aliases and verbosity levels behave consistently.
- Help output follows a unified style across commands.
- wa-rnf.5 tests pass.


## Testing
- Unit: clap completion generation + alias expansion + verbosity routing.
- Snapshot/contract: help output + non-TTY no-ANSI checks; JSON output schema validation.
- CI: smoke tests ensure generated completions and help text remain in sync.

```toml
[aliases]
```

```rust
fn resolve_alias(args: &[String], config: &Config) -> Vec<String> {
    if let Some(alias) = config.aliases.get(&args[0]) {
        let expanded = shell_words::split(alias)?;
        [expanded, args[1..].to_vec()].concat()
    } else {
        args.to_vec()

}
```

title: Progressive disclosure: default/verbose/debug output levels
description:
# Progressive disclosure (verbosity)

## Goal
Show essential information by default, with increasing detail available on request, without sacrificing scriptability.

## Key design rule
- `-v/-vv` controls **how much** information we include.
- `--format {auto|plain|json}` controls **how** we render it.

This keeps CLI behavior consistent and avoids a proliferation of ad-hoc `--json` flags.

## Verbosity levels
- Default (no flag): Essential info only
- `-v`: Additional context
- `-vv`: Debug details

## JSON mode
- Use `--format json` for machine-readable output.
- JSON output must be schema-stable and compatible with non-TTY usage.

## Example: `wa status`
```bash
# Default
$ wa status
Panes: 4 observed, 1 ignored
Events: 2 unhandled

# Verbose
$ wa status -v
Panes:
  1: codex [PromptActive] /home/user/project (last: 2m ago)
  3: claude [CommandRunning] /home/user/other (last: 5s ago)
  5: local [Ignored] (exclude rule: title=htop)
  7: gemini [PromptActive] /home/user/gemini (last: 30s ago)

Events (unhandled):
  - codex.usage_limit_reached (Pane 1, 2m ago)
  - session.compaction (Pane 3, 5m ago)

# Debug
$ wa status -vv
[as above, plus:]
Health:
  Queue depth: 0
  Ingest lag: 12ms
  DB size: 1.2GB
  Circuit breakers: all closed

# Machine
$ wa status --format json | jq .
```

## Implementation sketch
```rust
#[derive(Parser)]
struct Cli {
    #[arg(short, long, action = ArgAction::Count)]
    verbose: u8,
}

fn format_status(status: &Status, verbosity: u8) -> String {
    match verbosity {
        0 => format_status_brief(status),
        1 => format_status_verbose(status),
        _ => format_status_debug(status),
    }
}
```

## Consistency rules
- All human commands support `-v` and `-vv`.
- Default shows what the user needs to know.
- Verbose adds context for understanding.
- Debug adds internal state for troubleshooting.
- `--format json` output must not contain ANSI escapes and must be schema-stable.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All commands support `-v/-vv`.
- [ ] Default output is clean and minimal.
- [ ] Verbose adds useful context.
- [ ] Debug shows internal state.
- [ ] Consistent pattern across all commands.

## Testing
- Unit tests for verbosity routing (brief/verbose/debug paths).
- Contract tests:
  - `--format json` schema validation
  - no ANSI escapes in non-TTY/plain/json
- Help/output snapshot tests where appropriate (normalized).

title: [EPIC] Session State Persistence — Safe Mux Server Restarts
description:
## Goal
Enable safe WezTerm mux server restarts by snapshotting and restoring complete session state — layout, scrollback, process info, and agent session metadata — so that 50+ AI agent sessions can survive a mux server restart with minimal disruption.

## Background & Motivation
The WezTerm mux server (wezterm-mux-server) accumulates memory leaks over time — we observed 76GB RSS after 23 days of running 50+ AI agent panes on a 256GB RAM server. The only fix is restarting the mux server, but this kills ALL agent sessions (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini) running inside those panes.

This epic adds a "snapshot-restart-restore" workflow to wa (WezTerm Automata) so we can:
1. Capture complete mux state to SQLite before restart
2. Restart the mux server (clearing leaked memory)
3. Restore the visual layout, scrollback history, and re-launch agent processes

This is a wa-native solution (not a WezTerm fork change) that leverages wa's existing vendored mux client, SQLite storage, and async runtime.

## Architecture Overview
```
wa snapshot save → MuxSnapshot → SQLite
                     ├── PaneNode tree (layout)
                     ├── ScrollbackData (per-pane content)
                     ├── ProcessInfo (shell/agent commands)
                     └── AgentSessionRef (wa session metadata)

wa snapshot restore → Read SQLite → Reconstruct
                       ├── Create windows/tabs/splits
                       ├── Inject scrollback content
                       └── Re-launch processes
```

## Sub-beads
1. SnapshotEngine orchestrator (coordinates capture)
2. Layout restoration engine (recreates window/tab/split topology)
3. Scrollback injection engine (restores visual content)
4. Process re-launch engine (restarts shells and agents)
5. CLI commands (wa snapshot save/restore/list/diff)
6. Safe-restart workflow (atomic snapshot-restart-restore cycle)
7. E2E tests (roundtrip verification)
8. Documentation (user guide and architecture)

## Dependencies
Requires: bd-cuz (schema), bd-nz6 (SQLite tables), bd-ybq (scrollback capture), bd-2t2 (layout capture)

## Acceptance Criteria
- `wa snapshot save` captures full mux state in <5 seconds for 50 panes
- `wa snapshot restore` recreates layout with correct split topology
- Scrollback content visible in restored panes
- Agent processes re-launched with correct working directories
- Safe-restart workflow is atomic (rollback on failure)
- E2E tests pass with roundtrip verification

description:
# Workflow: handle_gemini_quota

## Purpose
Handle Gemini-specific quota and rate limit scenarios:
- Daily API quota limits
- Requests-per-minute rate limits
- Model-specific token limits

## Detection Patterns
```
# Quota exhausted
"Resource has been exhausted"
"quota exceeded"
"RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED"

# Rate limit
"Too many requests"
"Please slow down"
"429 Too Many Requests"

# Token limit
"maximum token limit"
"context length exceeded"
```

## Workflow Steps

### Step 1: Detect and classify
- Parse error code/message
- Determine: quota vs rate vs token limit
- Extract reset time if available

### Step 2: Quota exhaustion handling
1. Check if alternate API key available
2. If yes: rotate to new key
3. If no: notify user with reset time
4. Persist state for resume at reset

### Step 3: Rate limit handling
1. Extract retry-after header/message
2. Implement exponential backoff
3. Resume when safe

### Step 4: Token limit handling
1. Similar to Claude Code context handling
2. Suggest conversation restart
3. Save state for continuity

## Safety Constraints
- Don't spam retries
- Respect API terms of service
- Preserve conversation state

## Configuration
```toml
[workflows.handle_gemini_quota]
api_key_rotation = false  # Require explicit enable
max_retries = 3
backoff_base_seconds = 60
```

## Testing
- Fixture: quota error patterns
- Fixture: rate limit error patterns
- Unit: backoff calculation
- E2E: quota → notification flow

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Rate limits handled with backoff
- [ ] API key rotation works when enabled
- [ ] User notified with reset times

title: Watch-and-notify mode: wa watch --notify-only for alert-only monitoring
description:
# Watch-and-Notify Mode: Continuous monitoring with alert delivery

## Purpose
Enable wa to run in notification-only mode, alerting on events without auto-handling.

## Use Case
Some users want to be notified of events but handle them manually:
- Learning the system behavior
- High-stakes environments requiring human review
- Debugging automation issues

## Implementation

### CLI Command
```bash
# Watch and notify on all events
$ wa watch --notify-only

# Watch and notify only on specific events
$ wa watch --notify-only --notify-filter "usage_limit,compaction"

# Watch with specific notification channels
$ wa watch --notify-only --notify-via webhook,desktop
```

### Configuration
```toml
[notifications]
# Enable watch-and-notify mode
notify_only = true

# Which events trigger notifications
notify_filter = ["*.usage_limit*", "*.compaction", "*.error"]

# Notification channels
channels = ["webhook", "desktop"]

# Throttling
min_interval_seconds = 60
max_per_hour = 30
```

### NotifyOnlyMode Implementation
```rust
pub struct NotifyOnlyWatcher {
    event_bus: EventBus,
    notifier: Notifier,
    filter: EventFilter,
    throttle: ThrottleState,
}

impl NotifyOnlyWatcher {
    pub async fn run(&mut self) -> Result<()> {
        loop {
            let event = self.event_bus.recv().await?;

            if !self.filter.matches(&event) {
                continue;
            }

            if !self.throttle.allow(&event) {
                tracing::debug!("Throttled notification for {:?}", event.rule_id);
                continue;
            }

            // Log event without handling
            tracing::info!(
                event_id = %event.id,
                rule_id = %event.rule_id,
                pane_id = %event.pane_id,
                "Event detected (notify-only mode)"
            );

            // Send notification
            self.notifier.send(Notification {
                title: format!("wa: {}", event.rule_id),
                body: event.to_notification_body(),
                severity: event.severity(),
                actions: event.suggested_actions(),
            }).await?;
        }
    }
}
```

### Notification Body Generation
```rust
impl Event {
    pub fn to_notification_body(&self) -> String {
        format!(
            "Detected: {}\nPane: {} ({})\nTime: {}\n\nSuggested action:\n  {}",
            self.rule_id,
            self.pane_id,
            self.pane_title,
            self.timestamp.format("%H:%M:%S"),
            self.suggested_action().unwrap_or("No action suggested"),
        )
    }
}
```

### Desktop Notification Example
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 🔔 wa: codex.usage_limit_reached    │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Pane 9 (codex @ /project)           │
│ Detected: 14:30:15                  │
│                                     │
│ Run: wa workflow run handle_usage.. │
│                                     │
│ [Dismiss]  [Handle]  [View Details] │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Testing
- Notify-only mode does not auto-handle events
- Notifications delivered to configured channels
- Throttling works correctly
- Filter patterns match expected events

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] wa watch --notify-only implemented
- [ ] Event filtering via --notify-filter
- [ ] Throttling prevents notification spam
- [ ] Desktop and webhook channels supported
- [ ] Notification includes suggested actions
notes: Implemented notify-only mode for wa watch: CLI flags --notify-only/--notify-filter/--notify-via, config.notifications.notify_only, and channel/filter overrides in watcher startup; notify-only disables auto-handling while leaving notifications pipeline + cooldown/dedup in place. Added config field default + tests updated. cargo fmt/check/clippy/test passed.

title: Proactive alerts: threshold monitoring and notification triggers
description:
# Proactive alerts

## Purpose
Alert users before they hit limits or exceed budgets, preventing surprises and enabling proactive optimization.

## Alert Types

### 1. Cost Threshold Alerts
```rust
pub struct CostAlert {
    id: AlertId,
    threshold: Decimal,      // e.g., $50.00
    period: AlertPeriod,     // Day, Week, Month
    current_value: Decimal,
    percent_of_threshold: f32,
}

pub enum AlertLevel {
    Info,      // 50% of threshold
    Warning,   // 75% of threshold
    Critical,  // 90% of threshold
    Exceeded,  // 100%+ of threshold
}
```

### 2. Token Usage Alerts
```rust
pub struct TokenAlert {
    threshold: u64,
    period: AlertPeriod,
    per_agent: Option<AgentType>,
}
```

### 3. Rate Limit Frequency Alerts
```rust
pub struct RateLimitAlert {
    max_hits: u32,     // e.g., 5 per hour
    period: Duration,
}
```

### 4. Account Balance Alerts
```rust
pub struct AccountBalanceAlert {
    account_id: String,
    min_percent_remaining: f32,  // e.g., 15%
}
```

## Alert Configuration
```toml
# wa.toml
[analytics.alerts]
enabled = true

[[analytics.alerts.rules]]
metric = "cost"
threshold = 50.0
period = "day"
notify = ["terminal"]  # or "webhook", "email"

[[analytics.alerts.rules]]
metric = "account_balance"
threshold = 15  # percent
account = "*"   # all accounts
notify = ["terminal", "webhook"]
```

## Alert Monitoring Service
```rust
pub struct AlertMonitor {
    rules: Vec<AlertRule>,
    storage: StorageHandle,
    notifiers: Vec<Box<dyn Notifier>>,
}

impl AlertMonitor {
    pub async fn check_alerts(&self) -> Vec<TriggeredAlert> {
        let mut triggered = vec![];
        
        for rule in &self.rules {
            let current = self.get_current_value(&rule).await?;
            if let Some(alert) = rule.check(current) {
                triggered.push(alert);
            }
        }
        
        triggered
    }
    
    pub async fn notify_triggered(&self, alerts: &[TriggeredAlert]) -> Result<()> {
        for alert in alerts {
            for notifier in &self.notifiers {
                notifier.notify(alert).await?;
            }
        }
        Ok(())
    }
}
```

## Notification Channels

### Terminal (CLI output)
```
⚠️  ALERT: Daily cost threshold approaching
    Current: $42.50 / $50.00 (85%)
    Recommendation: Consider pausing non-critical workflows
```

### Status Command Integration
```bash
wa status

# Shows alerts at top
⚠️  1 active alert: Daily cost at 85% of $50 limit

Panes: 3 active...
```

## Testing
- Unit tests for threshold calculations
- Integration tests with mock metrics
- Tests for each notification channel

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Cost alerts trigger at configured thresholds
- [ ] Token alerts work per-agent and global
- [ ] Rate limit frequency tracked and alerted
- [ ] Account balance alerts work
- [ ] Terminal notifications clear and visible
- [ ] wa status shows active alerts
- [ ] Tests cover all alert types

title: Auto-Tuning Configuration Parameters
description:
## Goal
Implement automatic tuning of WezTerm/FrankenTerm configuration parameters based on observed system load, replacing static config with adaptive parameters that respond to actual conditions.

## Background & Motivation
WezTerm has dozens of tunable parameters (scrollback size, polling intervals, connection timeouts, etc.) that are currently static. Optimal values depend on runtime conditions:
- 5 panes: aggressive polling, large scrollback → great responsiveness
- 50 panes: same settings → mux server overwhelmed, memory bloated
- High memory pressure: need reduced scrollback, less frequent snapshots
- Idle periods: can afford more expensive operations (garbage collection, snapshots)

Currently users must manually tune these, and static values can't adapt as conditions change throughout the day.

## Technical Design

### Parameter Space
```rust
pub struct TunableParams {
    /// Polling interval for pane state (ms)
    pub poll_interval_ms: u64,          // range: 100-10000
    /// Scrollback lines per pane
    pub scrollback_lines: usize,        // range: 500-10000
    /// Snapshot interval (seconds)
    pub snapshot_interval_secs: u64,    // range: 60-1800
    /// Connection pool size
    pub pool_size: usize,               // range: 1-16
    /// Backpressure threshold
    pub backpressure_threshold: f64,    // range: 0.3-0.9
}
```

### Control Loop
Simple proportional control (not PID — KISS principle):
```rust
pub struct AutoTuner {
    params: TunableParams,
    targets: TuningTargets,
    history: VecDeque<SystemMetrics>,
}

pub struct TuningTargets {
    /// Target RSS as fraction of available memory
    pub target_rss_fraction: f64,       // default: 0.5
    /// Target mux response latency (ms)
    pub target_latency_ms: f64,         // default: 10.0
    /// Target CPU utilization fraction
    pub target_cpu_fraction: f64,       // default: 0.3
}

impl AutoTuner {
    pub fn tick(&mut self, metrics: &SystemMetrics) -> TunableParams {
        self.history.push_back(metrics.clone());

        // Memory pressure → reduce scrollback, increase snapshot interval
        if metrics.rss_fraction > self.targets.target_rss_fraction {
            let pressure = metrics.rss_fraction / self.targets.target_rss_fraction;
            self.params.scrollback_lines = (self.params.scrollback_lines as f64 / pressure) as usize;
            self.params.snapshot_interval_secs = (self.params.snapshot_interval_secs as f64 * pressure) as u64;
        }

        // Latency pressure → reduce polling, increase pool
        if metrics.mux_latency_ms > self.targets.target_latency_ms {
            let pressure = metrics.mux_latency_ms / self.targets.target_latency_ms;
            self.params.poll_interval_ms = (self.params.poll_interval_ms as f64 * pressure) as u64;
        }

        self.params.clamp_to_ranges();
        self.params.clone()
    }
}
```

### Safety Rails
- All parameters have hard min/max ranges (never go below safety floor)
- Changes are gradual (max 10% change per tick)
- Hysteresis: don't oscillate — require sustained signal before changing
- Manual override: user can pin any parameter, auto-tuner skips it
- Telemetry: log every adjustment with reason

### Galaxy-Brain Card
```
+- Auto-Tuner ----------------------------------------------------------------+
| Panes: 47  |  RSS: 12.3GB (62% of 20GB target)                              |
|                                                                               |
| Adjusted Parameters:                                                          |
|   poll_interval:    500ms -> 750ms  (latency pressure: 1.5x)                |
|   scrollback_lines: 3500 -> 2800   (memory pressure: 1.24x)                 |
|   snapshot_interval: 300s -> 300s   (unchanged)                              |
|                                                                               |
| System adapting to 47-pane load. Reduced polling frequency                    |
| to lower mux server pressure.                                                |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

### Implementation Location
- New: crates/wa-core/src/auto_tune.rs
- Integration: main event loop reads tuned params each tick
- Config: tuning targets and parameter ranges

## Existing Code References
- backpressure.rs: has hardcoded thresholds (0.50/0.75) — auto-tuner can adjust these
- watchdog.rs: fixed timeout thresholds — auto-tuner adapts to load
- tailer.rs: adaptive polling with 1.5x backoff — auto-tuner sets base rate

## Configuration
```toml
[auto_tune]
enabled = true
tick_interval_secs = 30
target_rss_fraction = 0.5
target_latency_ms = 10.0
target_cpu_fraction = 0.3
max_change_per_tick = 0.1    # Max 10% change per tick
hysteresis_ticks = 3         # Sustained signal for 3 ticks before changing
```

## Dependencies
- Telemetry pipeline (wa-3kxe.5): provides system metrics (RSS, latency, CPU)
- Enhances continuous backpressure (wa-1qz1.6): auto-tuner can adjust center threshold
- Enhances adaptive watchdog (wa-1qz1.7): auto-tuner adapts sensitivity_k based on load

## Acceptance Criteria
- Proportional control loop adjusting 5+ parameters
- Hard safety ranges (never exceed bounds)
- Hysteresis to prevent oscillation
- Manual override per parameter
- Galaxy-brain transparency card
- Telemetry logging for every adjustment
- Unit tests: synthetic load curves, verify parameter adaptation
- Integration test: simulated memory pressure, verify scrollback reduction

## Benchmark Requirements
- **criterion benchmarks** with target `benches/auto_tuning.rs`:
  - `parameter_search_latency`: measure time for one full tick() cycle (read metrics, compute adjustments, clamp ranges). Target: <100us per tick with 5 tunable parameters and 100-entry history.
  - `hysteresis_evaluation`: measure time to evaluate whether sustained signal threshold is met across hysteresis_ticks window. Target: <10us per parameter.
  - `clamp_to_ranges`: measure range clamping for all parameters. Target: <1us (pure arithmetic).

## Property-Based Testing (proptest)
- **Tuning convergence**: for any constant SystemMetrics input repeated for 100+ ticks, parameters converge to stable values (change per tick approaches zero). The control loop does not oscillate indefinitely.
- **Range invariant**: for any sequence of SystemMetrics inputs (including extreme values like 0.0, 1.0, f64::MAX), all output parameters remain within their configured [min, max] ranges after clamp_to_ranges().
- **Monotonic response**: if `metrics.rss_fraction` increases monotonically over consecutive ticks, `scrollback_lines` decreases monotonically (or stays at minimum). Higher pressure always results in equal or more aggressive reduction.
- **Manual override respected**: if a parameter is pinned by the user, the auto-tuner never modifies it regardless of input metrics. `tuned_params.pinned_field == original_value` for all tick sequences.

## Cross-References
- **wa-1qz1.7** (Adaptive watchdog thresholds via Kalman filter): the Kalman filter in wa-1qz1.7 provides filtered, noise-reduced metric signals that the auto-tuner can consume instead of raw metrics. This prevents the auto-tuner from reacting to transient spikes. The auto-tuner's hysteresis and the Kalman filter's smoothing are complementary noise-rejection mechanisms.

description:
# Task: E2E script — secret redaction in audit/export

## Goal
Prove that end-to-end audit and export paths never leak secrets from action inputs.

This is a trust-critical property:
- users will paste artifacts into issues
- CI will upload artifacts
- we must ensure secrets are not present in these outputs

## Scenario
- Spawn a dummy pane that echoes received input.
- Ensure policy allows a send in a safe context.

Steps
1) Send a string containing a known fake secret pattern (e.g., `sk-FAKESECRET123`) via `wa send` or `wa robot send`.
2) Export audit trail slice for this run (or query audit feed).
3) Assert that:
  - the audit entry exists
  - the raw secret string does NOT appear anywhere in audit export output
  - a redacted placeholder DOES appear (to prove redaction happened, not omission)

## Assertions
- Audit emission records the action.
- Redaction rules remove the secret from:
  - audit DB row(s)
  - audit export output
  - E2E script logs + artifacts

## Artifacts
- Effective config used.
- Audit export JSONL.
- Script stdout/stderr.
- Grep-style proof output (counts of secret matches should be 0).

## Registry
- Register this case in the E2E case registry (`wa-4vx.10.20`), including prerequisites and default inclusion status.
- Ensure `./scripts/e2e_test.sh --all` includes this case (or mark non-default with justification).

## Acceptance Criteria
- The test is deterministic.
- Any failure clearly indicates whether the leak came from:
  - audit emission
  - redaction engine
  - export path
  - e2e script logging


## Testing
- Meta-validation:
  - The script must scan *all* produced artifacts (logs, JSONL exports, summaries) for the fake secret string.
  - Include at least two different fake secret patterns (OpenAI-style, GitHub token-style) to ensure redactor coverage isn’t overly narrow.

- Failure mode:
  - If a match is found, print the exact artifact filename + surrounding context (bounded) to make the leak diagnosable.

title: [EPIC] Session Recording and Replay for Debugging and Sharing
description:
# [EPIC] Session Recording and Replay

## Mission
Record wa sessions for **debugging, sharing, and analysis**—replay exactly what happened.

## Why This Matters
When something goes wrong, the #1 debugging question is: "What happened?"

Session recording provides:
- **Debugging**: Replay the sequence that led to a bug
- **Sharing**: Show others exactly what wa did
- **Analysis**: Study patterns across sessions
- **Training**: Learn from real examples

## Components

### 1. Recording Mode
Capture all events and state during a session:
```bash
$ wa watch --record
Recording session to: /path/to/.wa/recordings/2026-01-18_143201.warecord
...
^C
Session recorded: 1234 events, 45 minutes

$ ls /path/to/.wa/recordings/
2026-01-18_143201.warecord
2026-01-18_150000.warecord
```

Recording captures:
- All pane output deltas (optional, configurable)
- All detection events
- All workflow executions and step logs
- All policy decisions
- Timestamps for everything

### 2. Replay Mode
Replay a recorded session:
```bash
$ wa replay /path/to/session.warecord

Replaying session: 2026-01-18_143201
Duration: 45 minutes (1234 events)

[Press SPACE to step, ENTER to play, Q to quit]

14:32:01 > Pane 1 detected: codex.usage_limit_warning
14:32:05 > Policy check: send allowed (rate: 2/10)
14:35:12 > Pane 1 detected: codex.usage_limit_reached
14:35:12 > Workflow started: handle_usage_limits
...
```

Replay options:
- Real-time (1x speed)
- Fast-forward (10x, 100x)
- Step-by-step
- Jump to timestamp

### 3. Recording Formats
```
.warecord    - Binary format (compact, fast)
.warecord.json - JSON format (human-readable, diffable)
```

Export options:
```bash
$ wa recording export session.warecord --format json > session.json
$ wa recording export session.warecord --format markdown > session.md
```

### 4. Session Annotation
Add notes to recording:
```bash
$ wa recording annotate session.warecord --at 14:35:12 --note "This is where it went wrong"
```

### 5. Recording Sharing
Share recordings safely:
```bash
$ wa recording share session.warecord --redact
Created: session_redacted.warecord
Removed: API keys, passwords, sensitive paths
```

## Privacy Considerations
- Recordings may contain sensitive data
- Redaction mode removes known secret patterns
- Warning when recording includes sensitive paths
- Recording retention policy (auto-delete after N days)

## Storage
- Recordings stored in `.wa/recordings/`
- Configurable retention (default: 7 days)
- Compression for old recordings
- Size limits per recording

## Testing

# Phase 3: Full Agent Support

## Overview
This epic completes the agent-specific implementations for all three supported AI coding agents: Codex CLI, Claude Code, and Gemini CLI. After this phase, wa can fully monitor and automate all three agent types.

## Strategic Importance
The value of wa scales with the number of agent types it supports. Multi-agent orchestration requires consistent handling across agent boundaries. This phase ensures:
- Consistent pattern detection for all agents
- Workflow automation for all agents
- Browser automation for all auth flows
- Account rotation across all services

## Key Components

### 1. Complete Codex Patterns and Workflows
Patterns:
- codex.usage.warning_25 - "less than 25%"
- codex.usage.warning_10 - "less than 10%"
- codex.usage.warning_5 - "less than 5%"
- codex.usage.reached - "You've hit your usage limit"
- codex.session.token_usage - "Token usage: total=X input=Y ..."
- codex.session.resume_hint - "codex resume <uuid>"
- codex.auth.device_code_prompt - "Enter this one-time code"

Workflows:
- handle_usage_limits fully working
- Device auth flow fully automated
- Session resume tested end-to-end

### 2. Complete Claude Code Patterns and Workflows
Patterns:
- cc.compaction - "Conversation compacted"
- cc.session_start - "Claude Code v" (version detection)
- cc.usage_limit (evolves with Claude Code updates)

Workflows:
- handle_compaction fully working
- handle_usage_limits (if Claude Code exposes reset time)

Challenges:
- Claude Code's session identity is less clear than Codex's UUID
- May need cwd + start time correlation via CASS

### 3. Complete Gemini Patterns and Workflows
Patterns:
- gemini.usage.reached - "Usage limit reached for all Pro models"
- gemini.session.summary - "Interaction Summary"
- gemini.model.used - "Responding with gemini-"

Workflows:
- handle_usage_limits for Gemini
- Google auth flow via Playwright

### 4. Full Browser Automation
Complete the auth flows started in Phase 2:

#### OpenAI Device Auth (Codex)
1. Navigate to https://auth.openai.com/codex/device
2. Wait for and fill email
3. Handle authentication (password, OTP, or SSO)
4. Enter device code
5. Wait for success confirmation
6. Save profile state

#### Anthropic OAuth (Claude Code)
1. Navigate to console.anthropic.com/login
2. Handle Google OAuth or email/password
3. Complete any MFA
4. Persist session

#### Google Auth (Gemini)
1. Navigate to accounts.google.com
2. Complete Google login flow
3. Handle account selection
4. Persist session

### 5. Account Rotation Logic
- Track usage per account per service
- Select account with highest percent_remaining above threshold
- Round-robin fallback if all near limit
- Mark accounts as "cooling down" after hitting limits
- Notification when all accounts exhausted

## Agent-Specific Considerations

### Codex CLI
- Uses device code flow for auth
- Session ID is a clear UUID in resume hint
- Token usage clearly reported at session end
- "cod" command prefix (verify actual binary name)

### Claude Code
- Uses browser-based auth
- Session identity less obvious (cwd + time?)
- Compaction is the primary automation target
- Version banner at session start

### Gemini CLI
- Uses Google OAuth
- Model used is reported
- Session summary at end
- "/quit" to exit

## Success Criteria
- [ ] All patterns for all 3 agents are implemented and tested
- [ ] Workflows work end-to-end for all 3 agents
- [ ] Browser automation completes auth for all 3 services
- [ ] Account rotation selects best account across services
- [ ] Field testing confirms reliability in real usage

## Dependencies
- Depends on Phase 1 (Foundation) - patterns, storage
- Depends on Phase 2 (Workflows) - workflow engine, browser skeleton

## Testing Strategy
For each agent:
1. Golden corpus regression tests with captured real output
2. Workflow integration tests with mock panes
3. Manual end-to-end testing with real agent sessions
4. Browser automation tests with recorded sessions

## Open Questions to Resolve
- What undocumented behaviors do each agent have?
- How do we reliably detect session boundaries for Claude Code?
- How does Gemini's usage limit reset work?
- Which auth flows can be fully automated vs need human?

title: Correlation detection engine: heuristics for identifying related events
description:
# Correlation Detection Engine

## Purpose
Automatically identify relationships between events across panes using heuristics.

## Correlation Types

### 1. Failover Correlation
- **Pattern**: Usage limit reached → new session start (same agent type)
- **Window**: Within 5 minutes
- **Confidence**: High if same agent type, same project

### 2. Cascade Correlation
- **Pattern**: Error in pane A → recovery action in pane B
- **Window**: Within 30 seconds
- **Confidence**: Medium, needs manual validation

### 3. Temporal Clustering
- **Pattern**: Multiple events within N seconds
- **Window**: Configurable (default 10s)
- **Confidence**: Low (just temporal, not causal)

### 4. Workflow Group
- **Pattern**: Events handled by same workflow run
- **Source**: workflow_executions table
- **Confidence**: High (explicit relationship)

## Implementation
```rust
pub trait CorrelationDetector {
    fn detect(&self, events: &[Event]) -> Vec<Correlation>;
}

pub struct FailoverDetector;
pub struct CascadeDetector;
pub struct TemporalClusterDetector;
pub struct WorkflowGroupDetector;
```

## Confidence Scoring
- 0.9+: Definite correlation (explicit link)
- 0.7-0.9: Likely correlation (strong heuristic)
- 0.5-0.7: Possible correlation (weak heuristic)
- <0.5: Don't show

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Failover correlations detected accurately
- [ ] Temporal clustering groups close events
- [ ] Workflow groups link events to workflow runs
- [ ] Confidence scores are meaningful
- [ ] False positive rate < 10%

## Testing
- Unit tests for correlation heuristics and aggregation.
- Integration tests for timeline queries and rendering.
- E2E scenario verifies correlations with artifacts.

title: [EPIC] Proactive Suggestions: contextual hints and recommendations
description:
# [EPIC] Proactive Suggestions

## Mission
Provide contextual, helpful suggestions that guide users toward better outcomes without being intrusive.

## Why This Matters
Users often don't know what they could do:
- "What should I check when something fails?"
- "How can I optimize my setup?"
- "What's the next step after this event?"

Proactive suggestions:
- **Guide** users to successful outcomes
- **Educate** about available features
- **Optimize** usage patterns

## Scope

### Contextual Suggestions
Based on current state:
- After event: "Run `wa why` to understand this decision"
- After error: "This often happens when... Try..."
- On status: "Account X is at 85% - consider rotation"

### Suggestion Types
```rust
pub enum SuggestionType {
    NextStep,      // What to do next
    Optimization,  // How to improve
    Warning,       // Upcoming issue
    Tip,           // Useful feature
}

pub struct Suggestion {
    suggestion_type: SuggestionType,
    message: String,
    action: Option<String>,  // Command to run
    learn_more: Option<String>, // Doc link
    priority: Priority,
    context: SuggestionContext,
}
```

### Suggestion Engine
```rust
pub struct SuggestionEngine {
    rules: Vec<SuggestionRule>,
}

impl SuggestionEngine {
    pub fn suggest(&self, context: &Context) -> Vec<Suggestion> {
        self.rules.iter()
            .filter(|r| r.applies(context))
            .map(|r| r.generate(context))
            .collect()
    }
}
```

### Suggestion Rules
- Account at 80%+ usage → suggest rotation
- Repeated rate limits → suggest pacing
- No events detected → suggest pattern check
- First workflow → suggest dry-run
- Error without why → suggest wa why

### Display
- Non-intrusive hints in CLI output
- Optional in status/events
- Dismissable (don't repeat)

## Success Criteria
- Suggestions are helpful, not annoying
- Users discover features through suggestions
- Error recovery is guided

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Suggestion engine implemented
- [ ] Common suggestion rules defined
- [ ] Suggestions appear in relevant contexts
- [ ] Dismissal persisted
- [ ] Not overly intrusive
- [ ] Tests cover suggestion logic

## Testing
- Unit tests for suggestion rules and suppression.
- Integration tests for CLI rendering.
- E2E artifacts include suggestion rule IDs.

title: Implement HandleCompaction workflow (steps, guards, agent-specific prompts)
description:
# Task: Implement HandleCompaction workflow

## Goal
Ship a safe, deterministic workflow that reacts to compaction events by prompting the agent to refresh critical context.

This is the concrete implementation of PLAN Appendix D.1.

## Trigger
- Detection event `session.compaction` (from the relevant agent pack).

## Step plan (Observe → Act → Verify)
1. Acquire per-pane workflow lock.
2. Re-read pane tail to confirm the compaction anchor is still present (avoid acting on stale detections).
3. Guard: abort if pane is `AltScreen` or we have a recent output gap (`OutputGap`/`RecentGap`).
4. Stabilize (see `wa-nu4.1.2.2`):
   - wait a short stabilization window (default: 2s), OR
   - require a deterministic marker if we have one.
5. Send agent-specific refresh prompt (exact strings; include trailing newline):
   - Claude Code: `"Reread AGENTS.md so it's still fresh in your mind.\n"`
   - Codex: `"Please re-read AGENTS.md and any key project context files.\n"`
   - Gemini: `"Please re-examine AGENTS.md and project context.\n"`
6. Verify send:
   - prefer deterministic verification via OSC 133 prompt boundary after the send
   - otherwise accept prompt echo/agent UI marker as best-effort
   - on timeout: mark the workflow `paused` with a “next steps” payload (do not spam retries)
7. Record workflow result + mark event handled.

## Safety
- All sends are policy-gated.
- Rate limiting applies.
- Workflow is idempotent: repeated compaction detections should not spam prompts (dedupe/cooldown semantics apply).

## Failure modes (must be handled explicitly)
- Pane disappeared: cancel workflow.
- Policy denies send: record denied/aborted result; do not inject input.
- Verification timeout: pause with a next-step plan; keep the event visible but not “unhandled spam”.

## Testing
- Unit tests:
  - guards behave correctly (alt-screen/gap → abort)
  - anchor confirmation avoids acting when the anchor disappears
- Integration tests:
  - synthetic detection → one execution → event marked handled
  - “policy denied” path records denial and sends nothing
- E2E:
  - `wa-4vx.10.8` validates end-to-end behavior with verbose artifacts

## Acceptance Criteria
- When the compaction anchor appears in a pane, wa sends the prompt once and records a handled event.
- If policy denies, the workflow records a denied/aborted result and does not inject input.

title: Sync push/pull for config + binary (explicit, non-destructive)
description:
# Task: Sync push/pull for config + binary (feature sync)

## Goal
Implement the core sync operations for:
- `~/.config/wa/**` (config)
- optional `wa` binary (explicit opt-in)

The intent is to make it easy to keep multiple machines consistent **without ever surprising the user**.

## Design principles
- **Explicitness over magic**: no background sync; only `push`/`pull`.
- **Plan-first**: always compute and display a plan; require `--apply` for real changes.
- **No silent overwrites**: overwriting requires confirmation and clear diff metadata.
- **Secret-aware**: never sync forbidden paths; never print secret contents.

## Path selection rules
- Config root is the canonical wa config directory.
- Include only known-safe config artifacts.
- Exclude patterns like:
  - `**/.env*`
  - `**/*token*`
  - `**/*secret*`
  - keychains/SSH keys

(Exact allow/deny rules are authored in the sync spec bead; this bead implements them.)

## Conflict semantics
When both sides changed:
- classify as `Conflict` and refuse to apply automatically
- provide remediation:
  - show which file conflicted
  - suggest manual resolution steps
  - (future) offer an interactive merge/choose-side mode

## Binary sync
- Treat binary sync as a separate category:
  - opt-in in config
  - prefer syncing from a trusted build machine to others
- Validate binary integrity (hash/size) before replacing.

## Testing
- Covered by `wa-nu4.3.8.5` (sync tests):
  - offline push/pull planning and dry-run output stability
  - conflict classification (no silent overwrite)
  - secret/path deny rules

## Acceptance Criteria
- `wa sync push/pull` computes a deterministic plan for config + binary categories.
- `--dry-run` never modifies local or remote files.
- Applying changes requires `--apply` and refuses to overwrite without explicit confirmation.
- Conflicts are detected and surfaced as `Conflict` items (no auto-overwrite).

title: Event handling semantics: dedupe, handled/unhandled transitions, idempotency, cooldowns
description:
# Task: Event handling semantics (idempotency + UX)

## Goal
Make the event→workflow loop reliable and user-friendly:
- events don’t spam
- events don’t get lost
- users can see what is unhandled and why
- workflows are idempotent across restarts

## Concepts
### Event states
Minimum required lifecycle states:
- `unhandled`
- `in_progress` (optional; set when workflow starts)
- `handled_completed`
- `handled_aborted`
- `handled_failed`

User-facing safety/UX requires one more explicit concept:
- `handled_paused` (or `handled_aborted` with a `paused_needs_human` reason)

**Paused meaning:** automation intentionally stopped because continuing would be unsafe or impossible without human action (MFA required, missing prerequisite, ambiguous pane state). Paused events must:
- not show up in `--unhandled` (to avoid “spam/retry loops”)
- remain visible in the events feed with a clear status + “next steps” payload

### Next-step plans (for paused)
When pausing, workflows should persist a structured, redacted “next step plan” so humans/agents can recover without guessing:
- what happened (high-level, redacted)
- what action is required (e.g., “complete MFA in browser profile X”)
- when to retry (e.g., reset time)
- any relevant identifiers (resume id, external id) in redacted/hashed form

Store this in workflow step logs and/or event metadata, and surface via:
- `wa robot events`
- `wa events` (human)

### Idempotency
Workflows should be able to re-run safely:
- if an event is already handled/paused, workflow runner should normally skip
- `--force` can override skip, but still policy-gated
- after restart, runner must not “forget” handled/paused state

### Dedupe/cooldowns
For noisy patterns, we need suppression:
- `dedupe_key` stored on events
- cooldown window per `(pane_id, rule_id)`
- if within cooldown:
  - either don’t insert new event, or insert but mark as suppressed

## Deliverables
- Clear rules for when the watcher inserts events vs suppresses.
- Runner behavior for:
  - selecting next unhandled event
  - marking `in_progress`
  - marking handled with execution status
  - marking paused with an explicit next-step plan payload
- CLI/robot-visible semantics:
  - `wa events --unhandled` is stable
  - handled/paused events record which workflow handled them

## Testing
- Unit tests for dedupe + cooldown decisions.
- Integration tests that simulate repeated detections and confirm:
  - no event spam
  - correct handled/paused status transitions
  - paused events are visible but not “re-executed” automatically
  - restart/resume: persisted state prevents re-running handled events after restart

## Acceptance Criteria
- Repeated identical detections do not create an unbounded event backlog.
- After a workflow completes, the corresponding event no longer appears in `--unhandled`.
- When automation pauses, the event is clearly marked and includes a redacted next-step plan.

title: [Human command] `wa db repair` for database corruption recovery
description:
# Task: wa db repair

## Goal
Provide a recovery path when the database becomes corrupted or inconsistent.

## Use Cases
1. **SQLite corruption** (hardware failure, incomplete write)
2. **Schema inconsistency** (interrupted migration)
3. **Index corruption** (FTS5 issues)
4. **WAL/journal issues** (unclean shutdown)

## Command Design
```bash
# Check database health
$ wa db check
Database: /home/user/.local/share/wa/workspaces/default/db.sqlite

Running integrity checks...
  ✓ SQLite integrity: OK
  ✓ Schema version: 3 (current)
  ✓ FTS index: OK
  ✓ Foreign keys: OK
  ✓ WAL checkpoint: OK

Summary: Database is healthy

# With problems:
$ wa db check
  ✓ SQLite integrity: OK
  ✗ FTS index: CORRUPT (12 orphaned entries)
  ✓ Foreign keys: OK
  ⚠ WAL checkpoint: PENDING (large WAL file)

Problems found: 2
Run: wa db repair --dry-run

# Repair with preview
$ wa db repair --dry-run
Would perform:
  1. Rebuild FTS index from segments table
  2. Checkpoint WAL to main database
  
No data loss expected.

$ wa db repair
Creating backup: db.sqlite.bak.2026-01-18
Repairing...
  [1/2] Rebuilding FTS index... done (12,345 segments indexed)
  [2/2] Checkpointing WAL... done (50 MB recovered)

Repair complete. Run: wa db check
```

## Repair Operations
1. **FTS rebuild**: Drop and recreate FTS5 virtual table from segments
2. **WAL checkpoint**: Force WAL checkpoint + truncate
3. **Schema repair**: Re-run migrations to fix schema inconsistencies
4. **Vacuum**: Reclaim space after repairs
5. **Index rebuild**: Drop and recreate indexes

## Safety
- Always create backup before any repair
- `--dry-run` shows what would happen
- Require `--force` for potentially destructive operations
- Exit codes: 0=healthy, 1=repairable, 2=fatal

## Implementation Notes
- Use SQLite `PRAGMA integrity_check`
- Use SQLite `PRAGMA quick_check` for fast initial scan
- FTS corruption: `INSERT INTO segments_fts(segments_fts) VALUES('rebuild');`
- WAL checkpoint: `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE);`

## Testing
- Unit tests: each repair operation in isolation
- Integration: corrupt DB, repair, verify
- E2E: full repair cycle with logging

## Acceptance Criteria
- wa db check detects all common corruption types
- wa db repair fixes issues without data loss when possible
- Backup created automatically before repair
- Clear reporting of what was fixed

title: E2E script: timeline correlation (multi-pane events + correlation markers)
description:
# E2E script: timeline correlation (multi-pane events + correlation markers)

## Goal
Validate end-to-end that the timeline feature:
- aggregates events across multiple panes into a unified chronological view
- surfaces correlation markers for known correlation heuristics (failover, temporal clustering)
- provides stable machine-readable JSON output for automation

This is the integration proof for the timeline epic (`wa-6sk`) under the standard E2E harness.

## Key constraints
- Deterministic: no fixed `sleep N`. Prefer fixture-driven event generation or dummy panes that emit patterns immediately.
- No external credentials.
- Use standard harness contract (`wa-4vx.10.6`) and runner (`wa-4vx.10.11`).
- Artifacts must be redacted (no raw transcript leakage).

## Test setup
- Start a WezTerm mux server and spawn a small set of deterministic dummy panes.
- Run `wa watch` in an isolated E2E workspace.
- Produce a known set of events by having dummy panes emit known trigger strings that match the pattern packs.
  - The harness should ensure panes are labeled/inferred as the intended agent types where correlation logic requires it.

## Scenarios

### 1) Basic timeline aggregation
- Produce 3 distinct events across 3 panes (A/B/C).
- Query timeline in JSON mode:
  - `wa timeline --last 5m --format json` (preferred; aligns with global output flag)
- Assert:
  - all 3 events appear
  - ordering is chronological
  - `pane_id` fields match the expected panes

### 2) Failover correlation detection
- Produce a known “cause → effect” pair within the correlation window:
  - Pane A: `codex.usage_limit_reached`
  - Pane B: `session.started` (codex-backup)
- Query timeline with correlations enabled (default or explicit flag):
  - `wa timeline --last 5m --format json`
- Assert:
  - a correlation exists with `type == "failover"` (or the canonical name)
  - correlation references the two expected event ids
  - confidence is present (may be heuristic)

### 3) Temporal clustering correlation (compaction burst)
- Produce two compaction events in different panes close together:
  - Pane A: `session.compaction`
  - Pane C: `session.compaction`
- Query timeline.
- Assert:
  - correlation exists for temporal clustering (or `compaction_burst`), connecting the two events

### 4) Human-readable view sanity (optional snapshot)
- Run: `wa timeline --last 5m --format plain`.
- Assert:
  - output includes correlation markers (e.g., `[CORRELATED: …]`)
  - pane labels appear and are consistent

### 5) Performance guardrail (non-catastrophic in E2E)
Performance budgets should be enforced primarily by unit/bench tests (`wa-6sk.5`).
E2E should only catch catastrophic regressions:
- Option A (preferred): load a small-ish event fixture (e.g., 1k) into the E2E workspace DB.
- Run timeline query and assert it completes under a generous bound (e.g., < 1s) and emits a timing log line.

## Registry
- Register this case in the E2E case registry (`wa-4vx.10.20`) with prerequisites and default inclusion status.

## Artifacts
- `timeline_output.txt` (plain)
- `timeline_output.json` (redacted)
- `correlations.json` (extracted correlations)
- `query_timing.log`
- `wa_watch.log`
- `events.jsonl`

## Logging contract
Each step logs:
- scenario name
- which panes/events were seeded
- timeouts used
- summary counts (events, correlations)

Example:
```
[TIMELINE_E2E] seeded events=3 panes=[1,3,5]
[TIMELINE_E2E] correlations type=failover count=1
[TIMELINE_E2E] query_ms=45
```

## Testing
- Determinism:
  - no fixed sleeps
  - all waits bounded with timeouts
- Correctness:
  - aggregated events appear and are correctly attributed to panes
  - expected correlations are present in JSON output
- Schema:
  - JSON output validates against the documented timeline schema
- Performance:
  - E2E only asserts “non-catastrophic”
  - strict budgets (<100ms typical ranges) are validated in `wa-6sk.5` unit/bench tests

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Timeline includes events from multiple panes in order.
- [ ] Expected correlation markers appear (failover, temporal burst).
- [ ] JSON output is stable and schema-valid.
- [ ] Artifacts/logging make failures actionable.

title: [EPIC] Lua Performance Optimization — Eliminate WezTerm Lua Bottlenecks
description:
## Overview

This epic addresses a critical performance bottleneck: **Lua code running in WezTerm's event handlers dramatically slows down the entire terminal emulator**. The user has observed that any Lua-related code becomes THE bottleneck in WezTerm performance.

## Background & Context

wa (WezTerm Automata) currently injects two Lua snippets into wezterm.lua via the setup module (crates/wa-core/src/setup.rs):

### 1. USERVAR_FORWARDING_LUA (lines 37-47)
- **Hooks**: \`user-var-changed\` event
- **Purpose**: Forward OSC 1337 user-var signals from agents (Claude, Codex, Gemini) to wa daemon
- **Trigger frequency**: LOW - only when agents explicitly emit user-vars
- **Action**: Spawns \`wa event --from-uservar\` via \`wezterm.background_child_process\`

### 2. STATUS_UPDATE_LUA (lines 54-105) — **THE MAIN BOTTLENECK**
- **Hooks**: \`update-status\` event
- **Purpose**: Send pane metadata (cursor, dimensions, title, alt-screen) to wa daemon
- **Trigger frequency**: **EXTREMELY HIGH** - fires on nearly every render frame (potentially 60Hz+)
- **Rate limiting**: 2 seconds per pane, but **Lua handler runs on EVERY event** before rate-limiting kicks in
- **Action**: JSON serialization in Lua, then spawns \`wa event --from-status\`

## The Problem in Detail

The \`update-status\` event fires continuously in WezTerm (cursor blinks, new output, focus changes, etc.). Even with rate limiting, the Lua callback executes on every single event:

\`\`\`lua
wezterm.on('update-status', function(window, pane)
  -- THIS CODE RUNS ON EVERY update-status EVENT (60Hz+)
  local pane_id = pane:pane_id()           -- Lua method call
  local now_ms = os.time() * 1000          -- syscall
  local last = wa_last_status_update[pane_id] or 0  -- table lookup
  if now_ms - last < WA_STATUS_UPDATE_INTERVAL_MS then
    return  -- Rate limited, BUT we already paid Lua overhead
  end
  -- ... rest only runs every 2s, but above runs 60x/second
\`\`\`

**Cost breakdown per event (even when rate-limited):**
- Lua function call dispatch overhead
- pane:pane_id() method call across Lua-Rust FFI
- os.time() syscall
- Hash table lookup for rate limit state
- Integer arithmetic and comparison

**Cost when NOT rate-limited (every 2s per pane):**
- Multiple pane:get_*() Lua-Rust FFI calls
- String manipulation for JSON escaping in Lua (slow)
- string.format() for JSON construction
- wezterm.background_child_process - **spawns external OS process**

## Data We're Extracting & Alternatives

| Data | Current Lua Method | Lua-Free Alternative |
|------|-------------------|---------------------|
| Cursor position | pane:get_cursor_position() | Parse from terminal escape sequences in captured output |
| Dimensions | pane:get_dimensions() | \`wezterm cli list --format json\` (wa already polls this) |
| Domain name | pane:get_domain_name() | \`wezterm cli list --format json\` (wa already polls this) |
| Title | pane:get_title() | \`wezterm cli list --format json\` (wa already polls this) |
| Alt-screen | pane:is_alt_screen_active() | Detect ESC[?1049h/l in captured output stream |
| User-vars | user-var-changed event | **No alternative** - must keep Lua or modify WezTerm source |

## Strategic Options

### Option 1: Remove STATUS_UPDATE_LUA Entirely (Recommended First Step)
- wa's ingest loop already polls pane metadata via \`wezterm cli list\`
- Alt-screen can be detected via escape sequence parsing
- Cursor position rarely needed for wa's core mission
- **Immediate win with zero WezTerm modifications**

### Option 2: Vendored WezTerm with Native wa Integration
- If maintaining a WezTerm fork anyway, add native Rust event sink
- Feature-gated so changes are minimal and rebaseable
- Sub-millisecond latency, zero Lua overhead
- Requires careful design for upstream merge potential

### Option 3: Optimize Lua (Least Effective)
- Micro-optimizations won't solve fundamental Lua slowness
- Still pays function call overhead on every event
- Only consider if Options 1-2 are infeasible

## Success Criteria

1. WezTerm remains responsive with wa installed (no perceptible slowdown)
2. wa retains ability to detect agent state transitions in real-time
3. User-var signaling lane preserved for explicit agent communication
4. Changes are maintainable as WezTerm upstream evolves

## Dependencies

- Blocks: All wa workflow functionality that relies on status updates
- Related: wa-nu4.1.3 (handle_usage_limits workflow) — needs alt-screen detection

## References

- setup.rs: crates/wa-core/src/setup.rs (lines 33-105 for Lua snippets)
- PLAN.md §2.7: Status update specification
- WezTerm events: https://wezfurlong.org/wezterm/config/lua/window-events/

title: [EPIC] Top-15 pragmatic upgrades (robustness/perf/UX)
description:
# [EPIC] Top-15 pragmatic upgrades (robustness/perf/UX)

## Mission
Capture and execute the **top 15** most accretive, pragmatic upgrades that materially improve:
- robustness/reliability (fewer "mystery failures")
- performance (lower latency/CPU/memory)
- safety/trust (fewer footguns; clearer approvals)
- UX/ergonomics (faster diagnosis; better operator flow)

This epic exists to keep the project aligned on the **highest-leverage improvements**, without losing details or needing to re-read external plan docs.

## Why This Matters
wa is a high-power automation system operating in a high-stakes environment (typing into terminals). The biggest user outcomes we must optimize for:
- **Confidence:** users can predict and verify what wa will do
- **Recoverability:** when things go wrong, the system produces artifacts that make diagnosis/repro fast
- **Determinism:** tests and automation behave predictably (no flakey sleeps; bounded retries)
- **Performance:** background operation must be low overhead

## Scope (15 initiatives)
1. Incident bundle + `wa reproduce` (portable, redacted, self-contained repro artifacts)
2. ActionPlan/StepPlan: single source of truth for actions + verification + rollback
3. Deterministic time + quiescence: remove wall-clock sleeps; wait-for conditions with timeouts
4. Stable pane identity handshake (`pane_uuid`) across renames/reparenting/session churn
5. Storage/indexing perf hardening: durability and query speed at scale
6. Risk-scored policy decisions: better defaults + explainability + safer automation
7. Prepare/commit approvals with plan-hash binding (approval UX that is hard to misuse)
8. Noise control: dedupe/cooldown/mute and clear "needs attention" signal
9. `wa triage`: operator dashboard/command to prioritize and resolve issues quickly
10. Schema-driven docs + client generation (robot/MCP contracts as a real API)
11. FTS explainability: "why isn't this searchable?" and "what was indexed?"
12. Backpressure-aware watcher: bounded queues + graceful degradation under load
13. Crash-only + automatic crash bundle: crash is an event with artifacts, not a mystery
14. Rule match tracing: "explain match" for packs/rules/detections (human+robot)
15. Secure distributed mode: auth + encryption + safe defaults + rigorous tests

## Success Criteria
- Each initiative has a dedicated epic under this bead with:
  - explicit UX goals and user-perceived behavior
  - implementation plan and concrete interfaces
  - unit/integration tests (deterministic fixtures)
  - E2E scenario(s) with **verbose logs + artifacts** (and no fixed sleeps)
  - docs updates for human + robot + MCP
- Dependencies are explicit and cycle-free (`bd dep cycles` clean).

## Testing
- Every initiative includes:
  - unit tests for core logic
  - at least one E2E case registered in the E2E harness registry
  - artifact contract: on failure, emit a minimal repro bundle (logs + config summary + relevant DB slice)
- Determinism rules:
  - avoid wall-clock sleeps; use wait-for/quiescence with bounded timeouts
  - avoid network dependencies unless explicitly mocked

## Acceptance Criteria
- 15 child epics exist and are self-contained (no external-plan dependency).
- Each child epic includes explicit testing and E2E artifact requirements.
- `bd lint` passes with no template warnings.

title: [EPIC] Incident bundles + wa reproduce (portable, redacted repro)
description:
# [EPIC] Incident bundles + `wa reproduce`

## Mission
Make failures **easy to diagnose and reproduce** by producing a portable, redacted, self-contained "incident bundle" that future-us (or another machine) can replay.

This is the difference between:
- "it flaked once, shrug" and
- "here is a deterministic repro + trace + artifacts"

## User Value
- Users can file an issue with a single artifact.
- Maintainers can reproduce without having access to the user’s machine.
- Operators can self-serve: bundle → explain → recommended next steps.

## Design Overview
An incident bundle is a **compressed directory** with:
- **manifest.json**: versions, workspace info, time range, redaction summary, bundle "kind" (crash, policy-deny, workflow-stuck, ingest-gap, etc.)
- **config summary** (sanitized): relevant wa + wezterm integration knobs
- **logs** (sanitized + bounded): watcher logs with correlation IDs
- **DB slice** (optional, sanitized + minimal): recent events, gaps, and (when safe) small output excerpts needed for repro
- **decision traces** (sanitized): the policy decisions / explainability traces relevant to the incident
- **replay instructions**: what command to run and what outcome to expect

### Key property: portability
The bundle must be usable on a different machine:
- no absolute paths assumed
- no machine-local secrets
- deterministic replay for supported incident kinds

### Key property: safety
The bundle must be safe to share:
- aggressive secret redaction
- explicit "privacy budget" (max bytes, max lines)
- never include raw auth tokens or full transcripts unless explicitly opted-in

## Proposed UX
- `wa reproduce` (smart default):
  - detects the most recent "incident" (crash, denial, stuck workflow, repeated gap)
  - exports a bundle with stable naming
  - prints: where it wrote, what it contains, how to replay

- `wa reproduce --since <duration> --kind <...>`:
  - targeted export for a specific time window/kind

- `wa reproduce replay <bundle>`:
  - runs deterministic replay modes:
    - policy decision replay (same decision + trace)
    - pattern/rule replay on captured segments
    - workflow-step replay (synthetic) where possible

## Scope
This epic focuses on **repro and supportability**, not on full "production-grade telemetry".

## Dependencies / Related Work
- Build on diagnostics bundle work (sanitized export) and crash report work.
- Integrate with session recording/replay when available.

## Success Criteria
- A maintainer can reproduce at least 3 classes of incidents from a bundle:
  1) policy deny/require-approval
  2) pattern false-positive/false-negative (rule replay)
  3) watcher crash (crash bundle + last-N events)
- Bundles are safe-by-default: secrets are redacted, sizes bounded.

## Testing
- Unit tests:
  - redaction is applied (no secrets in any file)
  - bundle manifests are deterministic (stable keys/order)
  - replay modes produce stable outputs for fixtures

- Integration tests:
  - build bundle from deterministic fixture DB and assert it contains expected files

- E2E:
  - create a known policy denial, run `wa reproduce`, verify artifact + replay result

## Acceptance Criteria
- All items in the following sections are satisfied: Success Criteria, Scope.
- Bundle export + replay are covered by unit/integration/E2E tests with verbose logs and artifacts.
- The bundle format is documented (enough for a separate tool to parse).

title: Spec: incident bundle format + privacy budget + replay modes
description:
# Task: Spec incident bundle + replay

## Goal
Define the **incident bundle** format and replay contracts so implementation is deterministic, safe, and debuggable.

## Requirements
### Bundle format
- Bundle is a directory (zipped) with a stable top-level layout.
- Must include:
  - `manifest.json` (versioned)
  - `README.md` (human instructions)
  - `redaction_report.json` (what was redacted and why; counts only, no secrets)
  - `logs/` (bounded)
  - `db/` (optional, minimal slice; safe copy semantics)
  - `traces/` (policy + rule traces; sanitized)

### Versioning
- Bundle format version is explicit and bumpable.
- Replay tooling refuses unknown major versions with a clear error.

### Privacy budget
- Default behavior is safe-to-share.
- Define hard limits:
  - max bytes per file
  - max total bytes
  - max lines per log
  - max output excerpt length
- Define opt-in flags for more data.

### Replay modes
Define which incident classes are supported by deterministic replay:
- Policy decision replay (decision trace reproduction)
- Rule/pattern replay (detection engine on captured segments)
- Workflow trace replay (simulate step logs + verification where possible)

### Ergonomics
- Bundle naming conventions: include timestamp + kind + short id.
- Clear CLI output: where written, what's inside, how to replay.

## Testing
- Add fixtures for bundle layout + manifest stability.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Bundle layout + manifest schema are written down and unambiguous.
- Privacy budget rules are explicit and implementable.
- Replay modes have clear input/output contracts and error semantics.

Implement the core bundle builder that gathers, sanitizes, and packages incident artifacts according to the spec.

  - privacy budget enforcement (truncate behavior deterministic)
  - redaction: secrets never appear
  - manifest determinism across runs
- Integration tests:
  - build bundle from fixture DB/logs and assert required files exist

## Acceptance Criteria
- Bundles are created successfully with bounded size.
- Bundles contain no secrets by default.
- Bundle structure matches the spec and is deterministic.
